Now begins the first chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra:
[to] the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Pārvatī questioned the Supreme Lord, Īśa, who is supreme bliss.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, performer of the five sacrifices, omniscient one, easily accessible through devotion, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge. (2)
O Lord of the Kula, Supreme Sovereign, ocean of the nectar of compassion!
In this essence-less and terrible cycle of existence, we are stained by all manner of suffering. (3)
Infinite multitudes of living beings, residing in various kinds of bodies, are born and they die; for them, there is no liberation.
O Lord, those who are always afflicted by suffering are never happy anywhere;
O Lord of Gods, tell me, O Master, by what means are they liberated? || 5 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, a person is liberated from saṃsāra.
O Goddess, there exists Śiva, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman;
he is partless, omniscient, the creator of all, the Lord of all, stainless, and non-dual. || 7 ||

He is self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; those known as individual souls (jīvas) are His portions.
Conditioned by beginningless ignorance, like sparks from a fire, they are divided by limiting adjuncts such as the womb, as well as by actions, instruments, and so forth. || 9 ||
Constrained by their own merits and demerits, which bestow all manner of suffering,
they receive a body, a lifespan, and enjoyments born of karma, endowed with various corresponding species.
O beloved, those of deluded mind undergo that subtle liṅga-body at every birth; it is imperishable until liberation.
Immovable beings, worms, water-born creatures, birds, domestic animals, humans, gods, and likewise those seeking liberation, follow this sequence respectively. || 12 ||
Having assumed thousands of fourfold bodies again and again,
if a man becomes a knower through his good deeds, he shall attain liberation.
Among the eighty-four hundred thousand bodies of embodied beings, the knowledge of reality cannot be obtained except in a human body. (14)
In this regard, O Pārvatī, even after thousands upon thousands of births, a living being may perhaps obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit. (15)
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and serves as a staircase to liberation, who in this world could be more sinful than he who does not rescue himself? (16)
Furthermore, even after obtaining an excellent birth and the perfection of the sense faculties, he who does not know what is beneficial for himself would be a destroyer of his own self. || 17 ||
Without a body, the human goal (puruṣārtha) does not exist for anyone;
therefore, having obtained this wealth of a body, one should accomplish meritorious deeds. || 18 ||
One should protect oneself with one's whole being; the self is the vessel for everything.
One should apply effort toward its protection until one perceives reality. 19.
Again there are villages, again fields, again wealth, again a house;
again there is good and evil karma, but never again a body. || 20 ||
People always exert effort for the protection of the body;
indeed, they do not even desire the abandonment of the body due to diseases such as leprosy. (21)
That [teaching] should be guarded with effort for the sake of dharma and knowledge;
and knowledge is for the sake of the yoga of meditation, through which one is liberated without delay. || 22 ||
If the self itself does not restrain itself from what is harmful, who else is there to act for its welfare? Therefore, the self alone shall deliver the self.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, being afflicted by disease, what will he do? (24)
Who, being of evil mind, would dig a well within a house that is already ablaze?
As long as this body remains, one should practice the essential truth. || 25 ||
Old age approaches like a tigress and life departs like water from a broken jar;
diseases strike like enemies, therefore one should practice what is beneficial. || 26 ||
As long as one does not encounter suffering, as long as calamities do not arrive, and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should one practice what is beneficial. || 27 ||
Time is not perceived due to the various activities arising from saṃsāra;
devoted to pleasure and pain, the living being does not know what is beneficial for itself. (28)
Seeing the dull-witted, the afflicted, the dead, and those fallen into calamity—all deeply suffering—the world, having drunk the wine of delusion, never feels fear. (29)
Prosperity is like a dream, youth is like a flower, and life is as flickering as lightning; who in this world could possess steadfastness?
A hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short; half of it is stolen by sleep, and even that remaining half is rendered fruitless by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age. (31)
Why is one not slain by destroyers—being indolent when action must begin, slumbering when one should be awake, and placing trust in a situation that inspires fear? || 32 ||
While the body is like the froth of water and the life-force dwells within it like a bird, how can people remain fearless in this impermanent and unpleasant cycle of existence? || 33 ||

One who perceives what is harmful as beneficial, who considers the impermanent to be permanent, who mistakes misfortune for gain, and who does not recognize his own death—[such a person is deluded]. || 34 ||
Though seeing, he does not see; though hearing, he does not understand;
though reciting, he does not know—deluded by your māyā.
This world, sinking deep into the profound ocean of time,
which has death, disease, and old age for its crocodiles, does not perceive anything at all.
This body decays moment by moment, yet it is not perceived;
like an unbaked clay jar submerged in water, its disintegration is not noticed at all. (37)
It is as reasonable to attempt to wrap the wind or to break the sky, as it is to tie together waves or to place one's trust in life. (38)
By which the earth is burned and even Mount Meru is shattered;
by which the waters of the ocean are dried up—O Goddess, what need is there to speak of the body? (39)
"Offspring are mine, my wife is mine, wealth is mine, and kinsmen are mine"—while a mortal laments thus, the wolf of Time forcibly slays him. (40)
"This has been done, this is to be done, and this other thing is half-finished"—O beloved, Death devours the person who is thus occupied with such striving. (41)
What is to be done tomorrow should be done today; and what is to be done in the afternoon should be done in the forenoon. For death does not wait to see whether one’s work is finished or not.
Do you not see that you are approaching the path of old age, with its scorching heat, where fierce diseases are the soldiers and death is the enemy—you who are supposedly wise? (43)
Death devours the human being who has been pierced by the needle of hope, drenched with the essence of sense-objects, and cooked in the fire of passion and hatred. (44)
Death harms the young, those in their youth, the old, and even those still in the womb; indeed, this entire world is of such a nature.
The gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as all classes of living beings, inevitably pursue destruction; therefore, one should practice what is truly beneficial. || 46 ||

Through the transgression of the conduct prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life, through the acceptance of improper gifts, and through greed for the wives and wealth of others, the lifespan of men comes to an end. || 47 ||

Due to the lack of study of the Vedas and the scriptures, as well as from failing to honor one's guru, and from the failure to restrain the senses, there shall be a great loss of lifespan for men. (48)
Disease, mental anguish, poison, weapons, serpents, domestic animals, wild beasts, and death—by whichever of these beings are bitten, by that very means do living creatures pass away. (49)
Like a water-louse moving from one blade of grass to another, the living soul goes from one body to another;
having attained [the new body] by means of its supreme part, it abandons the previous body. (50)

Just as childhood, youth, and old age, as well as the transition to another body and so forth, occur, so too does the attainment of another body happen like one who has come from one house to another. || 51 ||
O Goddess, having performed actions here in this world, people experience happiness and suffering; lacking knowledge, they go and come again and again to the next world.
Whatever action is performed here is experienced in the next world;
the fruit of a tree watered at its root is seen upon its branches. || 53 ||
Poverty, suffering, disease, imprisonment, and calamities—these are the fruits for embodied beings of the tree of their own transgressions. (54)
Liberation occurs only through non-attachment, for all defects are born of attachment.
Therefore, having abandoned attachment, one who is established in reality shall be happy.
Even a man of knowledge is inevitably shaken by attachment; how much more so one of little wisdom? (55)
Attachment should be abandoned with one's whole being; if it cannot be abandoned, then it should be directed toward the virtuous, for association with the virtuous is indeed the remedy. || 56 ||
He who possesses neither the company of the virtuous nor discernment—those two stainless eyes—is blind; how could such a man not stray from the path? (57)
As many dear attachments as a living being forms with the mind, so many spikes of grief enter his heart. (58)
O Mistress of the Family, this living being departs even after abandoning its own body; for what reason, then, does it maintain attachment to wife, mother, father, sons, and other relations? (59)
For saṃsāra has suffering as its root; he who possesses it is suffering.
O beloved, he by whom its abandonment has been accomplished is happy, and no other. 60.
O Beloved, one should abandon saṃsāra, which is the source of all sufferings, the locus of all calamities, and the abode of all sins. (61)
O Goddess, it is a terrible bondage without fetters, a mixture of great poisons, and a destruction without weapons for those whose minds are attached to saṃsāra.
Since all this is suffering in its beginning, middle, and end, one should therefore renounce cyclic existence and, being established in reality, become happy. || 63 ||
Even one who is firmly bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released;
but one who is deeply attached to women, wealth, and the like is never released at all.
For one who is occupied with the cares of family life, virtues such as learning and moral conduct perish,
leaving only the physical body behind, like water in an unbaked clay pot.

The entire world has been utterly ruined by those whose minds are completely deceived—alas, woe!—by the thieves that are the senses within the body, which feed upon the objects of the senses. || 66 ||
Just as a fish greedy for flesh does not see the iron hook, so the embodied being greedy for pleasure does not see the torment of Yama. || 67 ||
O beloved, those who do not know what is beneficial or harmful, who constantly follow the wrong path,
and whose sole purpose is the filling of their bellies, are ignorant beings destined for hell.
Sleep, sexual intercourse, and food are common to all living beings;
however, O beloved, the human being who possesses knowledge is said to be wise, while one devoid of knowledge is a beast.
O beloved, during the day when the sun is at its zenith, human beings are afflicted by excrement and urine, as well as hunger and thirst; at night, they are oppressed by passion and sleep. (70)
All living beings are devoted to their own bodies, religious duties, wives, and so forth;
they are born and they die—alas! indeed, deluded by ignorance. (71)
O Pārvatī, all human beings who are devoted solely to the conduct of their own respective castes and stages of life do not know the supreme reality; being deluded, they perish.
Some, devoted to the exhaustion of ritual acts and engaged in the performance of sacrifices and the like, wander about as deceivers, their souls possessed by ignorance. (73)

Men who are satisfied with mere names and devoted to the ritualistic section [of the Vedas] are deluded by the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, and the like, as well as by elaborate sacrifices. (74)
Deluded and bewildered by your māyā, they desire that which is beyond perception through self-mortification such as eating but one meal a day and other ascetic observances. (75)
What liberation can there be for the undiscerning through the mere punishment of the body?
O Goddess, does a great serpent die simply from being struck on its ant-hill? (76)
Devoted to acquiring wealth and food, these hypocrites who merely wear the outward garb wander through the world like men of knowledge, leading even other people astray. (77)
One who is attached to worldly pleasures, who claims "I am a knower of Brahman," and who has fallen away from both ritual action and Brahman— that person one should abandon like an outcaste.
In this world, those who regard a house as equal to a forest, who are shameless and naked, and who wander about like donkeys and such—do they become yogis? (79)
O Goddess, if human beings were liberated merely by smearing themselves with clay and ashes, then would not those villagers who dwell in clay and ashes already be liberated? (80)
O Queen, those who subsist on grass, leaves, and water, who constantly dwell in the forest, and who [abstain from] gold and other such things—do they become yogins? (81)
And from birth until the end of death, do those dwelling on the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā—led by frogs, fish, and others—become practitioners of vows? (82)
O Goddess, parrots and mainas recite that which brings joy to the heart; for what indeed are the learned ones before common people? || 83 ||
O Supreme Goddess, do the pigeons that feed on stones and the cātakas not drink the water of the earth? Do they therefore become yogins? (84)
O beloved, do those who endure cold, wind, and heat, and who are indifferent toward what is fit or unfit to eat—such as pigs and other animals—become yogis? (85)
Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, ritual acts such as these merely serve to deceive the world; the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). || 86 ||
O Dear One, the bound souls (paśus) have fallen into the great well of the six philosophical systems;
constrained by the bonds of the bound soul (paśupāśa), they do not know the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 87 ||
In the terrible ocean of the Vedic scriptures, being tossed here and there and seized by the crocodiles of Time, the sophists indeed remain [struggling]. || 88 ||
He who knows the Vedas, Agamas, and Purāṇas, yet does not know the ultimate truth—even for such a person, all that is merely the cawing of a crow. || 89 ||

"O Goddess, those who are distracted by the thought, 'This is knowledge' and 'This is the object of knowledge,' recite [the scriptures] day and night while turning their backs on the supreme reality. (90)
Bound by the composition of sentences and meters, and beautified by poetic ornaments, the deluded remain distressed with anxiety, their senses agitated. (91)
People practice the supreme reality in one way, while it is otherwise;
they explain the true essence of the scriptures in one way, while it is otherwise. (92)
Some, struck down by egoism and devoid of instruction, speak of the state of Unmanī while they themselves do not experience it. (93)
They study the Vedas and the Shastras and debate with one another,
yet they do not know the supreme reality, just as a ladle does not know the flavor of the food it stirs.
The head bears flowers, and the nose perceives fragrance;
people recite the Vedas and Shastras, but one who understands the true inner nature is rare. || 95 ||
Not knowing the Reality that resides within himself, the fool is deluded by the scriptures;
like a dull-witted cowherd who looks for a goat hidden in the thicket while it is actually in the well. (96)
Verbal cognition is indeed not capable of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra;
darkness can never be dispelled merely by talk of a lamp. || 97 ||
Recitation by one devoid of wisdom is like a blind man looking into a mirror;
O Goddess, for the wise, the scripture is the cause of the knowledge of reality. || 98 ||
Some [stand] in front, some behind, and others on the sides;
they dispute with one another as to whether the truth is "thus" or "otherwise," even though they are men renowned for virtues such as true knowledge, generosity, and heroism.
There is no grasping through direct perception; how, then, could there be grasping through hearsay?
Thus, those who are deluded regarding the scriptures are undoubtedly far removed [from the truth]. || 100 ||
"This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge"—desiring to hear all of this from every side, O Goddess, one who lives for a thousand years would never reach the end of the scriptures. || 101 ||
The Vedas and many other scriptures are like millions of obstacles to a short lifespan;
therefore, one should discern the essence from them, just as a swan extracts milk from water. || 102 ||
Having studied all the scriptures and truly understood their essence, the wise person should discard all those scriptures, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. || 103 ||
Just as one who is satiated by nectar has no need for food, O Goddess, so one who knows reality has no need for scripture. (104)
There is no liberation from the study of the Vedas, nor even from the recitation of the Shastras;
for liberation comes only from knowledge, and not otherwise, O Goddess worshipped by heroes. (105)
The stages of life (āśramas) are not the cause of liberation, nor are the philosophical systems (darśanas) the cause;
likewise, all the scriptures are not the cause—knowledge alone is indeed the cause.

The singular word of the Guru bestows liberation; all other sciences are mere mockery. Compared to this labor of carrying a burden of wood, this [instruction] is the supreme means of restoration to life. 107.
But non-duality (advaita), as taught by Śiva, is free from the exertion of ritual action;
it can be attained through the mouth of the Guru, and not otherwise, even by millions of scriptures.
Knowledge is said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment.
That consisting of scripture is the lower Brahman; the higher Brahman is born of discernment. (109)
Some desire non-duality, and others desire duality;
yet they do not know my true nature, which is free from both duality and non-duality.
There are two words for bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine. A living being is oppressed by the thought "mine," while one who thinks "not mine" is liberated. || 111 ||

That action which does not lead to bondage is true knowledge, while that which leads to liberation is likewise knowledge; other action results in mere exhaustion, whereas other knowledge is merely skill in the arts.
As long as desire and the like burn, as long as the latent impressions of saṃsāra persist, and as long as there is fickleness of the senses, how can there be discourse on reality? || 113 ||
As long as the momentum of effort persists, as long as there is the conceptualization of mental constructs, and as long as there is no stability of the mind, how can there be talk of reality? (114)
As long as there is identification with the body, and as long as the sense of "mine-ness" exists, and as long as there is no profound compassion, how can there be discourse on reality? (115)

Austerity, vows, pilgrimage, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like, as well as the discourses of the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas, are all for that duration until one finds the ultimate reality. (116)
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort, in all states and at all times, one should remain established in reality if one desires liberation for oneself. || 117 ||
One who is scorched by the three types of suffering should take refuge in the shade of the tree of liberation, which has the flower of the knowledge of dharma and the fruit of the heavenly world.
What is the use of saying much more here? Listen to the secret, O Pārvatī:
without the Kula-dharma there is no liberation; this is the truth, there is no doubt. (119)
Therefore, O Goddess, having understood the truth from the mouth of the venerable Guru, one is easily liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra; this I tell you as the reality. 120.
Thus, O beloved Mistress of the Kula, I have briefly described to you a certain state of existence among living beings; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Abiding State of the Jīva," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the supreme among all scriptures, the great secret concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 1.
Now begins the second chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Kuleśa, O ocean of compassion for all living beings, I desire to hear [your teaching]."
O Lord, the family dharma has been indicated by you, but not fully revealed.
Tell me, O Lord, that doctrine which is the majesty of that Dharma, the supreme among all Dharmas, and the majesty of the Urdhvāmnāya; tell me, O Supreme Lord,
if you have compassion for me.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one shall become dear to the Yoginīs. (3)
I have not previously told this to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Guha, and the others;
out of affection for you, I shall now speak—listen with a one-pointed mind.
Transmitted through the lineage of succession and residing within the five faces, it is inexpressible in its ultimate sense; nevertheless, I shall speak of it to you.
Indeed, you too must keep this secret; it should not be given to just anyone.
It should be given to a devoted disciple; otherwise, there will be a fall.
The Vedas are supreme among all [scriptures], and the Vaiṣṇava [scripture] is indeed superior to the Vedas;
the Śaiva is superior to the Vaiṣṇava, and the Dakṣiṇa is superior to the Śaiva. || 7 ||
The left is superior to the right; the Siddhānta is superior to the left;
the Kaula is superior to the Siddhānta; and there is nothing higher than the Kaula.
O Goddess, this Kula, transmitted from ear to ear, is more secret than the secret, the essence of essences, higher than the high, and the direct bestower of Śiva. 9.
O Goddess, having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Āgamas with the staff of knowledge, I, who am a knower of the essence, have extracted the Kula-dharma.
On one side are all the dharmas, such as sacrifices, sacred fords, and vows;
on the other side is the family dharma (kuladharma), and therein the Kaula is superior, O Dear One.
Just as rivers, flowing straight or winding, enter the ocean,
even so do various phenomena enter into the family alone.
Just as all the footprints of living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too, O beloved, are all philosophical systems contained within this very Kula. 13.
If there were iron equal to that of Jāmbūnada gold, then by the law of the family, another agreement would be equal. || 14 ||
Just as all rivers are not equal to the celestial river of the gods,
so too all other traditions are not equal to our own family dharma.
Just as there is a vast difference between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly,
so too is the great difference between other systems and the Kula.
Even if there were a woman equal to you, and a man equal to me, who were identical in lineage and virtue, even so, it would never be [proper]. (17)
For that evil-minded person who, out of delusion, abandons his family dharma for another dharma, becomes bound by the noose of saṃsāra and will become dear to those of the lowest castes. || 18 ||
O beloved, he who out of ignorance speaks words that are contrary to the dharma of his family incurs a sin greater than the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. || 19 ||
Having boarded the vessel of the family dharma, the best of men travels to other islands such as heaven and attains the jewel of liberation. || 20 ||
In all philosophical systems, men attain liberation through long-term practice; however, in the Kaula system, they attain it immediately—of this there is no doubt. || 21 ||
What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O beloved of my life!
There is no dharma equal to that of the Kaula; I swear this to you, O Mistress of the Kula.
If one is a yogi, he would not be an enjoyer; if he is an enjoyer, he would not be a knower of yoga.
Therefore, O Dear One, the Kaula system, which consists of both enjoyment and yoga, is superior to all.
O Mistress of the Kula, when the Kula-dharma is observed, enjoyment itself directly becomes yoga, sin becomes merit, and even worldly existence becomes liberation.
O Goddess, even the preeminent sages and deities such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are devoted to their family duties; what then need be said of human beings?
Having abandoned all dharmas and the various doctrines of the gurus, one should know only the *kula* if one desires one's own success. || 26 ||

Through the practice performed in previous births, the knowledge of the Kula manifests without the need for instruction and the like, just like the conviction of one who has awakened from a dream. (27)
Whatever wisdom has been cultivated by men over thousands of previous births, that very same wisdom the creature obtains; instruction is therefore useless. (28)
For one whose mind is purified by mantras originating from Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, the Sun, Gaṇapati, and the Moon, the knowledge of the Kula shines forth. || 29 ||
O Goddess of gods, all dharmas are traditionally held to be subject to recurrence; however, those who abide in the Kula dharma are all non-returning. || 30 ||

O Goddess, for those men whose sins have been exhausted through austerities, charity, sacrifices, pilgrimages, recitations, and vows performed in the past, the knowledge of the lineage becomes manifest.
O auspicious goddess, for one with whom both you and I are pleased, the knowledge of the lineage shines forth through devotion to the deities and the guru. 32.
For one whose mind is pure, who is tranquil, diligent, and serves the guru,
and who is exceedingly devoted and secret, the knowledge of the Kula becomes manifest.
For one whose devotion is firm toward the venerable Guru, the Kula scriptures, the Kaulikas, and that which rests upon the Kula, the knowledge of Kula is revealed. || 34 ||
Through faith, discipline, joy, and the like, through firm vows of right conduct, and through dharmas that fulfill the commands of the guru, the knowledge of the lineage is attained. (35)
In one who is unworthy, family and knowledge never abide.
Therefore, having examined [the candidate], one should speak of the family and knowledge as declared by me. || 36 ||
One should not speak of that family dharma or the family precept to an unworthy person;
he who violates such an injunction shall incur the curse of the deity. || 37 ||

If, after having propitiated [the deity], one should speak of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) and the knowledge of the Kula, both that guru and that disciple shall become a beast (paśu) for the Yoginīs. || 38 ||
Having awakened the disciple, the Guru should reveal the knowledge of the Kula;
then both of them shall directly attain union with the Yoginīs and the Vīras. || 39 ||
He who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra without effort will be liberated upon knowing this family dharma; there is no doubt in this matter. || 40 ||
One who travels the great path of the Kula-dharma shall go to the city of liberation;
there is no doubt about this, it will happen before long. Therefore, one should take refuge in the Kaula. || 41 ||
O Pārvatī, he who disregards the Kula scriptures and practices the scriptures of the bound (paśu) is like one who abandons milk-rice in his own home and wanders for alms. 42.
He who abandons his own family tradition and becomes intent upon the traditions of others is like one who discards a jewel held in his hand and seeks glass located at a distance. || 43 ||
He who abandons the mantras of his lineage and recites the mantras of the beasts is like one who discards a heap of grain and desires to grasp a heap of dust. || 44 ||
He who abandons his own family lineage and looks toward another is like one afflicted by thirst who runs from a pond toward a mirage.
O Mistress of the Kula, just as illusions born from Indra’s net bring pleasure for only a moment, so too are the other traditions apart from the Śrīkaula. (46)
He who, ignorant of the dharma of his lineage, desires liberation from saṃsāra,
is like one who wishes to cross the shoreless expanse of the ocean with his two hands.
Or whoever desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems, he shall then become wealthy by means of riches obtained in a dream alone. 48.
O Pārvatī, just as the delusion of silver arises with respect to mother-of-pearl,
so too do enjoyment and liberation manifest from other conventional times.

O Mistress of the Kula, even one who is devoid of all ritual actions and free from the distinctions of caste and stage of life, yet remains rooted in his own lineage, becomes a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even one devoid of knowledge of the Kula may become a refuge through devotion to the Kula;
such a person attains a good destination—how much more so, then, one who is devoted to it as his ultimate resort? || 51 ||
O beloved, when a family tradition is destroyed, it destroys; when protected, it protects;
and when honored, it quickly honors in return. Therefore, one should not abandon it.
"Let all my kinsmen revile me; let my wife, sons, and heirs abandon me;
let people laugh at me upon seeing me, or let kings punish me. (53)
I serve, I serve, I serve again—you alone, O Supreme Deity!
I shall never abandon your dharma through the actions of my mind, speech, or body. || 54 ||
Thus, even for one who has fallen into calamity, if his devotion remains perfectly steadfast, he is honored by the gods in the hereafter and shall become Śiva himself. || 55 ||
O Śivā, even if one is constantly afflicted by disease, poverty, suffering, and the like,
that person who worships you with devotion shall attain the supreme goal.
Let people praise or revile; let fortune depart or remain;
whether death comes today or at the end of the age, one must never abandon one's family.
One should not abandon the family dharma out of greed, nor out of anger, nor out of hatred, nor out of envy; neither out of desire nor even out of fear.
That living being who, relying on the family dharma, does not worship you, is tormented from the very moment of birth by his own enemy, the spirit that destroys beings. || 59 ||
Those who are averse to the Kaula path are like chaff among grains, like moths among living beings, and like bubbles in the waters. (60)
For even trees live, and beasts and birds live;
but he alone truly lives whose mind is established in the dharma of his lineage.
For one who is devoid of the family dharma, days come and go;
though he breathes like a blacksmith’s bellows, he does not truly live.
Whether walking or standing, whether waking or even sleeping, for one who knows the Command of Kula, O Kuleśvarī, his life is like that of a bound soul (paśu). || 63 ||
Whether he be learned or foolish, virtuous or lacking virtue, whether he observes vows or does not observe them— any person who is averse to the Kaula path [is truly ignorant].
O Goddess, only those beings born in this world who are devoted to their family duties live as true virtuous lives; the rest are merely donkeys at the gateway.
That man is called by the virtuous one who is devoted to the dharma of his lineage;
the other, however, is the ultimate truth enveloped in a heap of bones and skin. (66)
O Dear One, one who knows his lineage, even if he is a master of the four Vedas, is lower than a dog-cooker;
whereas a dog-cooker who knows his lineage excels even a Brāhmaṇa. || 67 ||
But he who is endowed with the compassion of the Guru, whose sins have been shaken off by initiation, and who is devoted to the worship of the Kula— O Goddess, he alone is a Kaula, and not others.
Fie upon that Kaulika who does not perceive, does not find, and does not worship the knowledge of the Kula; his life is like that of a crow. || 69 ||
They are blessed, they are performers of meritorious deeds, they are virtuous, and they are yogis—those by whose good fortune, O Goddess, the knowledge of the Kula is revealed. (70)
They are to be revered, they are great-souled, and they have accomplished their purpose—those best of men in whose hearts arises the knowledge of the lineage as proclaimed by me. (71)
It is the traveling to all places of light, the bathing in all sacred fords, the performance of all sacrifices, and the entry into the dharma of one's own lineage. || 72 ||
Those men who are indeed virtuous enter the family of Dharma;
they never again enter the womb of a mother.
O Goddess, even if someone should utter the words "family, family" by mere chance, that family becomes purified through your grace.
O Mistress of the Kula, for one who possesses knowledge of the Kula, there is no need for other religious duties. (74)
To the great-souled Kaulikas who are devoted to the Kula and established in the Kula, I grant supreme knowledge at the time of death; of this there is no doubt. || 75 ||
People long for a time that yields little fruit despite much effort;
yet, alas, some abandon their own family, which effortlessly bestows all fruits! || 76 ||
For one who knows the Kula is indeed all-knowing, even if he has abandoned the Vedas and Shastras;
whereas one who knows the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas, but does not know the Kula, is truly ignorant. || 77 ||
Only those devoted to you know the greatness of your family, and no others;
only the cakora birds perceive the luster residing in the moon, and no other creatures.
O beloved, only those who know their lineage are satisfied upon hearing stories of their family;
small rivers swell with the moonlight, but not so the ocean.
Those who know the essence, the experts in the Kula tradition, do not look toward any other dharma;
like bees that serve the fragrance of the mandāra flower, they do not crave other flowers.
For those who know the essence honor family tradition, and not others; Śiva bears the lotus upon his head, while the son of Siṃhikā swallows it—how strange! (81)
Only those with supernormal knowledge perceive the lineage and appearance; those without such knowledge do not.
Does a crane know how to drink water mixed with milk like a swan? (82)
The world consists of Śiva and Śakti, and within that world the Kaula is established;
therefore, how could the Kaula—which is superior to all—be common to everyone? (83)
The six philosophical systems are my limbs—the feet, the belly, the hands, and the head.
Whoever should create division among them would be cutting off my own limb. (84)
For these very same [six] constitute the six limbs of the Kula as well;
therefore, O Dear One, know that the scripture whose essence is the Veda is also essentially Kaula. || 85 ||
O beloved, in this lineage, there is a single deity who bestows fruit upon all philosophical systems alike, and who grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men.
And that which is contrary to worldly norms, O Siddhayogīśvarī, dear one, attains the status of authoritative proof as the Kula, because it yields perceptible results. (87)
And direct perception is the means of valid knowledge for all living beings;
by the power of that apprehension, all sophists are defeated. || 88 ||
Who indeed knows what is hidden, or what will happen to whom? Only that which yields immediate fruit is the supreme vision. || 89 ||
"Knowing this family dharma, all human beings are liberated.
Thinking thus, O Maheśānī, the Kaula tradition was disparaged by me. (90)
For those devoid of compassion for you, who oppose the knowledge of their lineage,
and who are like beasts lacking discernment, the dharma of the lineage has been violated.
For one whose bondage of sinful karma is excessive in another birth,
neither the teacher’s compassion nor the knowledge of the lineage arises.
Just as the blind do not see the sun, the illuminator of all, so too they do not recognize your lineage, being utterly deluded by me. || 93 ||
Human beings constantly devote themselves with devotion to the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, and other philosophical systems, yet these yield only the fruit of futile exertion. || 94 ||
Alas, alas! Fools revile your vision, my beloved, which is declared by the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas to be the sole means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (95)
"O Goddess, I have indeed led the beasts astray through millions of scriptures;
they do not know the Kula-dharma, being vainly proud of their own knowledge. (96)
Indeed, all the scriptures of the animal-sacrificers were spoken by me alone, having assumed another form for the purpose of deluding the wicked-minded. (97)
Due to the power of great sins, a desire for those [lower realms] arises in men;
and for them, there is no return from them even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. || 98 ||
Even when urged on, the evil-minded person does not proceed according to his lineage;
even when restrained, the virtuous person adheres strictly to his lineage. || 99 ||
By means of the family dharma, the gods attained divinity,
and the sages, lords of yogis, and others reached supreme perfection.
Those on this earth who are devoted to animal sacrifices and the like, and who are hypocrites, are easy to find;
those who serve the Kaula path alone are great and exceedingly rare. || 101 ||
There are many men who know the meaning of false doctrines; O Maheśānī, one who is an expert in the Kula-tattva is rare to find.
Just as some men afflicted by disease, O Mistress of the Clan, do not partake of the divine medicine that destroys great maladies; || 103 ||
For they practice unwholesome conduct that increases that very disease, just as one takes bad medicine;
likewise, they perform worldly activities that cause birth and death. 104.
Devoid of your compassion, they constantly practice [wrongly]; they do not resort to the family-dharma that liberates one from the bonds of existence. 105.
And just as men, out of delusion, affectionately beg from merchants born in the forest, such as Marīca and others, O Mistress of the Family; || 106 ||
Indeed, no one asks for priceless jewels; likewise, they do not seek out the scriptures on animal sacrifice, which yield results bound by the fetters of karma. || 107 ||
Thus do those fools ask, deluded by your māyā;
they do not inquire about the family dharma that bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One might mistake musk for mud, camphor for salt, sugar for gravel, and a gem for glass. (109)
Just as common folk do not believe in what they have seen even when it is in their own hands,
so too do those bereft of your grace fail to understand the Kaula tradition.
Oh, the greatness of delusion produced by your māyā!
O Queen of the Gods, what ignorance could it not bewilder, even the immortals? || 111 ||
Having beheld the face of one's beloved, [one should partake of] drink, wine, meat, and food;
such is the practice, such is the recitation, by which the supreme state is to be attained. 112.
Such a vision of the Kula, obtainable through the compassion of the Guru, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; only those devoted to you know it, and no others.
Some who lack the instruction of a guru claim to be "great beings";
having themselves been previously deluded, they delude all people. || 114 ||
Some base people, devoted to misconduct, recite [this]:
"Of what nature is the master, so shall his servants be. (115)
Many who mock false knowledge invent the Kaula doctrine according to their own intellects, being devoid of the traditional lineage. || 116 ||
If a person were indeed to attain accomplishment through the drinking of liquor, then let all common folk who delight in the drinking of liquor likewise attain accomplishment. (117)
If a meritorious destiny were to result merely from eating meat, then indeed all those in the world who eat meat would be partakers of merit. (118)
If liberation were indeed to occur merely through the enjoyment of power (śakti), then all living beings in the world would be liberated simply by consorting with women. ||119||
O Great Goddess, the family tradition has never been censured by me anywhere;
it is those here who are devoid of proper conduct that are censured, and not others.
Otherwise, O Goddess, those fools who consider themselves wise wander about, disregarding the conduct that has been taught by me regarding the Kaulika Dharma. (121)
Surely, following the path of one's lineage is impossible—[as difficult as] walking upon the edge of a sword, hanging from the throat of a tiger, or carrying a venomous serpent. || 122 ||
O Goddess of the gods, drinking [liquor] in vain is called the drinking of *surā*;
that is to be known as a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), as established in the Vedas and other scriptures. || 123 ||
Wine, meat, and the flesh of animals— which are unfit to be smelled, unfit to be seen, unfit to be touched, and unfit to be drunk— constitute the great fruit for the Kaulikas.
There are eleven kinds of intoxicants that are impure for the twice-born;
the twelfth, however, is the "great intoxicant" (mahāmadya), which is the most excellent of all.
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called the dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.
Upon merely seeing liquor, one should gaze at the sun;
upon merely smelling it, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 127 ||
If one is submerged in water up to the knees, one should fast for a day;
however, if the contact with liquor reaches above the navel, the rule is a fast of three nights.
In the case of drinking liquor intentionally, one should cast that [hot iron ball] burning into one's mouth;
when one has been completely burnt by it, one then attains purification. || 129 ||
The rule for expiation regarding the fault of touching liquor and so forth has been declared.
O Dear One, he who, acting contrary to the injunctions, kills living beings for his own sake [is subject to this]. || 130 ||
That man of evil conduct shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the body of a beast; even after death, he is born among the animal species.

The one who consents, the one who trusts [the killer], the one who strikes, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats—it is these eight who are the slayers. (132)
The buyer destroys by means of wealth, the eater by consumption, and the killer by slaughter and imprisonment; such is this threefold destruction. || 133 ||
Having looked upon meat, one should behave as if looking upon wine;
therefore, one should never consume meat or wine except according to the prescribed rule. || 134 ||
O Goddess, when served according to the prescribed rule, you become quickly propitious;
it is indeed true, O fair-faced one, that [ignorance] is destroyed through lack of full understanding. 135.
One should never cut even grass without following the prescribed rule;
however, by killing a cow or even a twice-born man according to the rule, one is not tainted by the sins of slaughter.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to this one thing, my dear:
the means for the bliss of liberation while living, which is hidden within the Kula scriptures.
O Goddess, for one who desires liberation, that supreme knowledge which exists even in one born of a noble lineage and renowned for their spiritual heights is like the fragrance of gold. 138.
O Pārvatī, all the Kula scriptures have been spoken by me alone;
they are authoritative, of this there is no doubt, and they must not be refuted by means of logical arguments.

To the deities and to the ancestors: "The winds blow honey for the one who follows the cosmic order; with the sweetest and most intoxicating [essence], [they provide] milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. (140)
"Hiraṇyapāva and Khādi bound the Puruṣa as the sacrificial animal;
one should undergo initiation (dīkṣā)," and so forth—these are the scriptural authorities (pramāṇa), O beloved. (141)
Thus, O Mother, this greatness of the Kula has been briefly recounted;
O mistress of the Kula, what more do you wish to hear? (142)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Kula," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, which contains one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, and serves as the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Kula, I desire to hear that which is the most excellent among all dharmas.
O Lord, tell me about the Ūrdhvāmnāya, its mantra, and its greatness.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the deity becomes well-pleased.
Never before have I spoken [this], O Mistress of the Family;
out of affection for you, I shall now speak—listen, my beloved, to the Ūrdhvāmnāya.
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are to be made manifest, O Mistress of the Kula;
all the Śaiva and Śākta Āgamas are proclaimed to be secret.
O Pārvatī, the Kula scriptures are the most secret of secrets;
O Mother, this [scripture] is the secret even among those most secret of secrets. || 5 ||
Indeed, the supreme reality of the Ūrdhvāmnāya, which consists of the complete Brahman, has been carefully concealed by me; however, it is now being revealed.
And from my five faces, the five traditions (āmnāyas) have emerged:
the Eastern, the Western, the Southern, the Northern, and likewise the Upper tradition; these five are proclaimed as the paths to liberation. || 7 ||
There are many traditional lineages, but none are equal to the Upper Tradition (Urdhvāmnāya).
This is the truth, O beautiful lady; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 8 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, many secret traditions arising from the divisions of the four Vedas were previously proclaimed in this Tantra.
O beloved, there are many who know the four traditions; but those who know the reality of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) are rare, O goddess praised by heroes.
As many as are the grains of dust upon the earth,
so many were uttered the mantras born of each individual Vedic tradition, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And just as many secondary mantras have been proclaimed as essential;
they were indeed spoken by me alone out of a desire to grace the world. || 12 ||
O lady of pure smiles, it is declared that the deities of all mantras, who bestow their respective fruits, have arisen from a portion of the two of us.
I know all mantras; no one else knows them at all. By my grace, however, some among millions of men may come to know them. || 14 ||
He who knows even a single tradition is liberated; there is no doubt about this. How much more so one who knows the four traditions—he shall become Śiva himself. || 15 ||
O Dear One, the Higher Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya) is superior to the knowledge of the four traditions;
therefore, one who desires his own perfection should know that alone. || 16 ||
Because all phenomena are upward-tending, the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya) is praised; it leads those situated below to the heights, and is thus called the "Upper Tradition. || 17 ||

O Kuleśānī, because it arises from the higher reality (ūrdhva-tattva) and has destroyed the ocean of saṃsāra, and because it is to be served exclusively by those in the higher worlds, it is known as the Ūrdhvāmnāya. || 18 ||

Therefore, O Goddess, know that the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), which is higher than the highest, is the direct and sole means to liberation and yields a fruit superior to all other traditions. 19.
O Dear One, O Śivā, just as I am indeed worthy of worship by everyone in all the worlds,
so too is the Ūrdhvāmnāya among all the Āmnāyas.
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, as the sun is among luminous bodies, as Kāśī is among sacred fords, and as the celestial river is among streams; || 21 ||
Just as Meru is among mountains, as sandalwood is among trees, as the horse-sacrifice is among rituals, and as a gem is among stones; || 22 ||
Just as sweetness is among tastes, gold among metals, the cow among quadrupeds, and the swan among birds; || 23 ||
Just as the mendicant is among the stages of life, as the Brahmin is among the social classes, as the king is among men, and as the head is among the limbs; || 24 ||
Just as musk is the preeminent among fragrances and Kāñcīpurī among cities, so too, O beloved, is the Ūrdhvāmnāya superior among all dharmas. (25)

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one may understand the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) through the arising of the fruit of meritorious deeds accumulated over various births; it cannot be known otherwise. || 26 ||
Among hundreds of thousands of men, one is fortunate who knows the vision of the lineage;
and among those hundreds of thousands, there may be someone who understands the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya). || 27 ||
Not by the Vedas, nor by the Āgamas, nor by the scriptures, nor by the very extensive Purāṇas;
not by sacrifices, nor by austerities, nor by millions of pilgrimages and vows. || 28 ||
O Goddess of the gods, the upward-pointing tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) is not known through other means—such as mantras and medicinal herbs—without the mouth of the venerable Guru. 29.
One should seek out that very person there— the omniscient one, a treasure-house of compassion,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and proficient in the meaning of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya).
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, O Mistress of the Kula, one should understand the Upper Tradition from him.
O Goddess, that man who understands the tradition (āmnāya) according to its true nature attains the desired perfection; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. (31)
The man who correctly understands the Ūrdhvāmnāya from the mouth of the venerable Guru according to the path of the scriptures is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (32)

O Goddess, he who understands such a tradition in its true essence—he is the venerable true guru; he is to be honored; he is the knower of the divine; he is the master of mantras; he is to be served; he is to be praised; he is to be beheld; he is the one established in sattva. || 33 ||
He is the observer of vows, he is the ascetic, he is the practitioner, and he is the worshiper;
he is the master of all sciences, including the Vedas, the Āgamas, and the Śāstras. || 34 ||
He is the teacher, he is the wise one, he is the ascetic, and he is the Kaulika;
he is the performer of sacrifice, he is the purified soul, he is the reciter of mantras, and he is the adept. || 35 ||
O Dear One, he is the yogi, he has accomplished his purpose, he is the hero, and he is the most excellent;
he is the meritorious soul, he is the omniscient one, he is liberated, and he is Śiva. || 36 ||
O Goddess, that family is sanctified; that mother is considered blessed;
and that father, O Beloved, has achieved his life's purpose, for his ancestors are liberated.
All those born in his lineage are meritorious, and his friends and kinsmen are purified. (37)

What need is there for much speaking here? For one who is devoted to the Upper Tradition (Urdhvāmnāya), even remembering, chanting, seeing, bowing down, or conversing with [such a person] yields a fruit greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 38 ||
O Goddess, wherever he dwells, there shall be the victory of Śrī;
there shall be freedom from disease, abundance of food, good rain, and absence of calamity. || 39 ||
Therefore, O Goddess, that best of men who, through the grace of the Guru, knows the Ūrdhvāmnāya according to its true essence—he shall become most dear to me. || 40 ||
O Goddess, the Eastern Tradition is of the nature of emanation, the Southern is of the nature of maintenance, the Western is withdrawal, and the Northern is grace.
They know mantra-yoga as the eastern, bhakti-yoga as the southern,
karma-yoga as the western, and likewise jñāna-yoga as the northern.
Twenty-four conventions of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) have been declared; twenty-five conventions of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) have been declared. (43)
The conventions of the Western Tradition are declared to be thirty-two;
the wise know that there are thirty-six conventions in the venerable Uttara-āmnāya.
O Kulanāyikā, these [impurities] do not exist in the Ūrdhvāmnāya;
because it is the very nature of Śiva himself, no ritual action whatsoever exists there. || 45 ||
"I alone know the greatness of the Ūrdhvāmnāya, and no one else;
because of my affection for you, O fair-faced one, you too know this truth. (46)
O Mistress of the Kula, I have thus related to you in brief the majesty of the Ūrdhvāmnāya; now the majesty of the mantra is being declared. (47)
O Pārvatī, I have never before spoken this to anyone;
out of affection for you, I shall now tell it—listen, O beloved of my life! (48)
He who knows our supreme form, which is established in the Śrīprāsāda-parā-mantra and the Ūrdhvāmnāya, is himself Śiva. (49)
O Dear One, from Śiva down to the smallest insect, this mantra exists within the life-force of all living beings in the form of inhalation and exhalation through the path of the vital breath.
Just as a cloud does not move in the sky without the wind,
O beloved, so too the world cannot exist without the mantra of supreme grace.

O Goddess, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sewn together by the mantra of Parāprāsāda; in reality, it is non-different from it, just as the wind is non-different from the palm-leaf fan.
The sprout is in the seed, oil in the sesame, heat in fire, radiance in the sun, moonlight in the moon, fire in wood, fragrance in the flower, and fluidity in water. (53)
The meaning resides in the word, power in Śiva, fat in milk, flavor in fruit, sweetness in sugar, and coolness in camphor. (54)
Just as the power of restraint and favor resides in a mantra, as a deity resides in an image,
as a reflection resides in a mirror, and as motion resides in the wind,
so too does this entire phenomenal world abide within the mantra that is the supreme grace. || 55 ||
Just as a tree exists in subtle form within a banyan seed, so too does the entire universe reside within this Parāprāsāda mantra. || 56 ||
O Kuleśvarī, just as food that is well-cooked and delicious does not produce any taste for the eater when devoid of salt, so it is with these substances. (57)
Those mantras which are not conjoined with the Parāprāsāda mantra do not bestow their fruit, being devoid of power. (58)
The supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda should be guarded with great effort. || 59 ||
Having reflected upon the meanings of the Purāṇas arising from various systems of philosophy and scriptural traditions, I perceive myself as swallowing the mantras and diverse treatises. (60)
The gods, beginning with the thousand-eyed Indra, wander among various scriptures;
deluded therein, they are utterly bewildered by your māyā.

They are born and they die, sharing in the afflictions of saṃsāra; O Mistress of the Kula, those who do not chant the supreme mantra of the glorious temple do not indeed attain liberation, being deluded by your māyā. || 62 ||
He in whom firm devotion toward the venerable Guru, who is my own form, arises, becomes liberated upon knowing the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda. || 63 ||
He who, throughout thousands of previous births, has been diligent in the Śaiva and other traditions, and who shall honor the mantras born of the four Āmnāyas and the command of the Guru; || 64 ||
Freed from the cloak of evil, pure in soul, and devoted to his guru, he understands the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda; it cannot be otherwise.
O Dear One, [there were] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the preeminent gods led by Śakra, the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, the Guardians of the Quarters, Manu, Candra, and others. || 66 ||
The sages headed by Mārkaṇḍeya, the lords of sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, the masters of yoga headed by Sanaka, and those liberated while living such as Śuka and others; || 67 ||
Yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others,
having obtained this meritorious mantra which yields immeasurable fruit arising from the supreme mantra of the Śrī-prāsāda, continue to recite it even today, O Pārvatī. (68)
Capacity, honor, learning, splendor, happiness, freedom from disease, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation belong to one who recites [this mantra] with the grace of the Supreme One. (69)
The state of even Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Viṣṇu remains far beyond reach for one who,
though devoid of all ritual actions, knows the mantra of the supreme temple; the destination he attains with ease is not reached by all the performers of sacrificial rites.
For one who recites the *parā-prāsāda* mantra, the wish-fulfilling gem, the cow of plenty, and the desire-tree reside in his home, and Kubera himself is his manifest servant. (71)

Just as iron becomes gold through contact with a divine gem, so too may a bound soul (paśu) become the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati) through the recitation [of mantras] originating from the Supreme. || 72 ||
He who understands the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda in its true essence understands both me and you; he is exceedingly dear to us both. || 73 ||
O Pārvatī, one who knows the mantras for the supreme temple, even if he be an outcaste (śvapaca), is certainly capable of installing deities in images and the like; of this there is no doubt.
He who knows even just the mantra known as Parā-prasāda shall be liberated, even if he be an outcaste; how much more so one who knows its ritual procedure! || 75 ||
O Great Goddess, whatever one who knows the mantra of supreme faith performs, whatever he desires, and whatever he speaks—all that becomes austerity, meditation, and recitation. || 76 ||
O Great Goddess, he who knows the Parā-prāsāda mantra, preceded by initiation and endowed with the traditional lineage, is none other than I; of this there is no doubt.
The fourteen worlds, together with all that is moving and unmoving, eternally abide within the body of one who knows the mantra of the Supreme Temple (Parā-prāsāda). || 78 ||
O beautiful lady, wherever one who knows the mantra of Parāprāsāda resides, that place is designated as a divine field extending ten yojanas in every direction. || 79 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, those who know the true meaning of the mantras that inspire supreme devotion are saluted by gods and asuras alike; how much more so, then, by humans and others? || 80 ||
O Pārvatī, wherever one who knows the mantra of Parāprāsāda resides, that place becomes a field of accomplishment belonging to me, together with hosts of sages and gods. (81)
He knows all mantras originating from Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, the Sun, Gaṇapati, and the Moon— he who is a knower of the supreme mantra of grace.
Even an outcaste is liberated merely by the sight of one upon whose tongue-tip the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda resides. || 83 ||
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or an outcaste, pure or impure, O beloved—one who recites the *parā-prāsāda* mantra is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. || 84 ||
Whether walking or standing, whether waking or even sleeping,
O Goddess of Gods, this mantra of the Supreme Abode is never fruitless.
There are thousands of mantras that bestow each fruit only after a long time;
O Mistress of the Family, this king of mantras, however, swiftly grants all fruits. (86)
This mantra of Parāprāsāda is the most excellent among all mantras; whether worshipped with knowledge or without knowledge, this mantra grants the desires of those who practice it. || 87 ||
Śacī and Indra, Rohiṇī and the Moon, Svāhā and Agni, Prabhā and Ravi, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, Night and Day; || 88 ||
O Goddess, Kuleśvarī, Agni and Soma are the Bindu and Nāda; they are Prakṛti and Puruṣa, known as the support and the supported, and are Bhoga and Mokṣa. || 89 ||

In this beloved [reality], the out-breath and in-breath, speech and its meaning, as well as injunctions and prohibitions, and whatever dualities such as pleasure and pain are seen or heard by me—in all the worlds, all that is none other than the two of us; of this there is no doubt. (90)
Indeed, all forms of male and female are portions of us two;
therefore, this mantra of Parāprāsāda shall be the soul of all.
O Mistress of the Kula, the Supreme Brahman is formless, attainable through meditative cultivation, partless, stainless, eternal, devoid of qualities, and resembling the sky. || 92 ||
The infinite and imperishable reality, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech, is fully revealed through the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra of the supreme palace. || 93 ||
Therefore, O Goddess, this mantra is known as Parā-prasāda, because its essential nature is the Supreme Reality (paratattva), characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). || 94 ||
And because it consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and because it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is both with action and without action, and both with attributes and without attributes. || 95 ||
By reciting the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda, the crest-jewel of all mantras, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. || 96 ||
What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O beloved, to the very essence of all things:
there exists no mantra equal to the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda. 97.
This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme austerity;
this alone is the supreme meditation; this alone is the supreme worship. || 98 ||
This alone is the supreme initiation; this alone is the supreme recitation;
this alone is the supreme reality; this alone is the supreme vow. || 99 ||
This alone is the supreme sacrifice; this alone is higher than the highest. This alone is the supreme good; this alone is the supreme fruit. || 100 ||
"This alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the highest goal;
this alone is the supreme secret—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Having realized this, O beloved, one should always remain devoted to that, O best of men. (101)
Following the procedure taught in the scriptures and preceded by the sequential worship (kramapūjā), one should recite the Śrīprasādaparā mantra one hundred and eight times.
One is thereby liberated from the five great sins, including the killing of a Brahmin. || 102 ||

O Goddess, he who should recite two hundred times the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra, even through eighty-four hundred thousand [recitations] accompanied by dhāraṇās and ritual practices, [attains success]. || 103 ||

[They are] surrounded by the limbs born from their own source, accumulated through countless births, [experienced] in old age, youth, and childhood, and during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. || 104 ||

Whether committed through action, mind, or speech, and whether performed knowingly or unknowingly, one is liberated from the multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) and tens of millions of minor sins (upapātaka); there is no doubt in this, O fair-faced one—this is the truth. || 105 ||

O Goddess, whoever should recite three hundred times the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra, [they obtain] whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving. || 106 ||
O Goddess, one obtains that fruit which is the merit found in all vows and the fruit found at all sacred fords; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 107 ||

Whoever recites four hundred times the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda, the eight siddhis beginning with aṇimā—endowed with all accomplishments—will always attend upon him at the door of his house; of this there is no doubt. (108)
Whatever the mind desires, that it obtains without a doubt;
dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are directly held in its hand. (109)
O Goddess, O Mistress of the Kula, the practitioner shall obtain the fourfold liberation, headed by *sālokya*;
this is the truth, there is no doubt. (110)
O Mistress of the Kula, I am not able to describe the fruit of that person who recites the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda five hundred times. || 111 ||
Therefore, with every effort, in all states and at all times, one should recite the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 112 ||
There is no reality superior to the Guru; there is no deity greater than Śiva. There is no knowledge superior to the Vedas; there is no vision equal to that of the Kaula. || 113 ||
There is no knowledge superior to noble birth, no happiness superior to knowledge, no worship superior to the eightfold path, and indeed no fruit superior to liberation.
This is the truth, this is the truth; truth, truth—of this there is no doubt. (114)
O lady of excellent hips, I am not able to describe here the greatness of the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Just as a mustard seed on a mountain or the sands in the ocean, so has the majesty of the mantra been described by me to you in brief. (116)
"O Goddess, I have thus related to you the majesty of the Śrīprāsāda-parāmanu of the Ūrdhvāmnāya. What more do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Supreme Prāsāda Mantra," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, containing one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, which serves as the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa. 3.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Kula, I desire to hear the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda.
One should recite the King of Mantras together with the ritual placements (nyāsa), meditations (dhyāna), and so forth. || 1 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the form of Śiva arises.
Until now, I have not spoken this mantra to anyone at all;
out of affection for you, I speak it today—listen, O beloved of my very life!

The supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda consists of the world of infinite moons (anantacandrabhuvana) joined with the pair of the moon-drop (indubindu); it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 4 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, the mantra of Parāprāsāda is said to begin with the letter *sā*,
because it consists of the nature of light and bliss and because it bestows manifest results.
Because he brings the tranquil mind under his control, because he defines the meaning of what is well-established,
because he pacifies past sins, because he destroys the suffering of those who have sought refuge,
and because he swiftly bestows grace, he is celebrated as Prāsāda.
Because it is the very nature of the supreme reality, because it reveals the Supreme Self, because it generates supreme bliss, and because it demonstrates the supreme attributes. || 7 ||

Because it bestows results that are beyond the senses, because it is the cause of supreme sovereignty, and because it is superior to all mantras, it is called the "Supreme Mantra" (Parāmantra). || 8 ||
O Goddess, listen to this family mantra; I shall tell you the ritual placement (nyāsa).
First, having risen in the morning, one should contemplate the Guru and the Deity. (9)
Having fixed the mind upon the root-center (kanda), one should perform the evacuation of feces and urine;
then one should carry out purification, cleansing of the mouth, bathing, the twilight rites (sandhyā), and libations (tarpaṇa).
In a secluded place, the worship of the door, the warding off of the three obstacles, the entry into the place of worship, and likewise the sitting upon the seat. || 11 ||
O Īśvarī, [the sequence consists of] meditation on the temple for the worship of the Goddess, salutation to the gurus beginning with Śiva,
the seat, and salutation to Gaṇapa and Kṣetrapāla.
O Dear One, [the practice consists of] the recollection of the sandals, the worship of the Lord of Day (the Sun),
the purification of the hands and limbs, and breath control within one's own Brahmarandhra.
The binding of the directions, the pair of limbs joined with the ritual procedure, the Mātṛkā,
the script known as the tenfold Bhūta, and that which is designated as Kamaṭha.
The seer of this [mantra] is the supreme Śambhu; the meter is Gāyatrī preceded by the Unmanifest (avyakta); and the deity here is the supreme Parā, the sovereign of all mantras. 15.
The root mantra, the seed, the power, and the pin are each joined with the three long vowels;
and the six limbs, O Pārvatī, are formed by the root seed-mantra joined with the six long vowels.
Having thus assigned [the mantras] of Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta,
and Vāmadeva to the five fingers, one should assign the forms to the faces.
O Ambikā, one should likewise perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon the five Brahmans,
beginning from Ādhāraśakti and ending with the Pīṭha-mantra.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform the *alpa-ṣoḍhā* according to the path previously described;
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the rite of placement (*nyāsa*) called *mahā-ṣoḍhā*,
by means of the procedure that will be explained hereafter, for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.

This has not been taught to anyone at all; out of affection for you, I shall speak it. The universe, the forms, the mantras, the deities, and the Mothers—this ritual placement (nyāsa) called the Great Ṣoḍhā is the most excellent among all ritual placements. (20)

Therein, first, O Supreme Goddess, the placement of the manifestation (prapañcanyāsa) is described: the manifestations consist of continents, oceans, mountains, cities, and sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 21 ||
The field consists of forests, hermitages, caves, riverbanks, crossroads, and fissures; those born from sweat, eggs, and wombs are said to be the sixteen types.
Śrī, Māyā, Kamalā, Viṣṇuvallabhā, Padmadhāriṇī, Samudratanayā, Lokamātā, and Kamalavāsinī. || 23 ||
Indirā, Mā, Ramā, Padmā, as well as Nārāyaṇapriyā,
Siddhalakṣmī, Rājalakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī—
these are proclaimed as the Śaktis of the worlds and the presiding deities of the vowels. (24)
A lava, a truṭi, a kalā, a kāṣṭhā, a nimeṣa, and indeed a śvāsa;
likewise a ghaṭikā, a muhūrta, a prahara, and a day. (25)
The twilight, the night, the lunar day, the day of the week, and the asterism;
the yoga, the karaṇa, the two fortnights, the month, the zodiac sign, and likewise the season. || 26 ||
The solstices, the years, the yugas, and the dissolutions— these twenty-five [principles] are declared to have their fixed locations within the heart.
Āryā, Umā, Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Śivā, Aparṇā, Ambikā, Satī, Īśvarī, Śāmbhavī, Īśānī, Pārvatī, and Sarvamaṅgalā. || 28 ||
Dākṣāyaṇī, Haimavatī, Mahāmāyā, Maheśvarī, Mṛḍānī, Rudrāṇī, Sarvāṇī, and Parameśvarī. || 29 ||
Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, and Bhavānī are thus proclaimed;
they are the powers (śaktis) and the presiding deities of the subtle elements beginning with smell (gandha).
The fixed positions for these are said to be within the heart.
One should meditate upon the five elements, the subtle essences, the organs of knowledge and action, the qualities, the states of the internal organ, and the ten faults that are the winds. 31.
Brāhmī, Vāgīśvarī, Vāṇī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Vākpradā, Śāradā, and Bhāratī— O beloved, these are the embodiments of knowledge, the sovereigns who pervade the five elements. (32)

The Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], Bhuvaneśī, and the Lakṣmī-bīja, followed by the three Tārakas; then the Mūla-vidyā with the three Tārakas at its end, and beyond that, the letters of the Mātṛkā. || 33 ||

One should say, "Salutation to Śrī, whose form is the manifest world (prapañca)," and so forth in sequence. Having joined the letters with the *prapañca* [mantras] and others, one should join them with the Śaktis.
O Dear One, one should thus perform the placement (nyāsa) in the very locations prescribed for the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Having uttered "Obeisance to the Primordial Goddess Parāmbā," who is by her very nature the root of the three *tāras* and the entirety of phenomenal manifestation, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*).
The ritual deposition of the worlds (bhuvananyāsa) is said to be precisely the ritual deposition of the manifold (prapañcanyāsa).
At the end of the three *tāra*s and the root mantra, one should utter "A ĀṂ IṂ AṬALAṂ. (36)
Then, O Dear One, one should utter "lokaṃ ca nilayaṃ caiva śatakoṭipadaṃ tataḥ," followed by the root mantra of the Yoginī beginning with "guhyā. (37)
One should utter "vadedādhāraśaktyambādevyai" and assign it to the two feet.
Then, having uttered "ī uṃ ūṃ vitalaṃ guhyataraṃ cānantasaṃjñakam śeṣañca" as before, O Goddess, one should assign it to the two ankles. (38)
"Ṛṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ, as well as Sutala, the most secret, and that which is named Avicintya—having uttered these and the remainder as before, O Dear One, one should place them on the two shanks. (39)
Then, O Goddess, having uttered "Ḷṃ Eṃ Eṃ Mahātalaṃ ca Mahāguhyaṃ Padam" and the remainder as before, one should place [the mantra] upon the knees.
Oṃ auṃ, O Goddess, [the mantra] "Talātalam" is the supreme designation of the secret;
having recited the remainder as before, O Queen of the Gods, one should place it upon the two thighs. 41.
Aṃ Aḥ—having likewise uttered Rasātala, the secret known as Jñāna, and Śeṣa as before, one should place them in the private region. || 42 ||
One should also recite "kavargāya," "pātālāya," "lokāya," and "nilayāya," and having spoken the remainder as before, one should place it in the mūlādhāra.
The secret consists of the *ca*-group, the ground of the elements (*bhūtala*), and also the *ḍākinī*;
having spoken of the remainder as before, one should place it in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, O Dear One. (44)
O Dear One, having uttered the syllable *bhuvaḥ* along with the *ṭa*-group, as well as the *rahasya* [Veda] and Rākiṇī,
and having spoken the remainder as before, one should place them on the navel.
Having uttered the *tavarga*, the *sva* [vowel], the *paramarahasya*, and *lākinī*, as well as the remainder as before, one should place them in the heart, O Dear One. (46)
Having likewise uttered the labial class (pavarga), Maharloka, Rahasya, and Kākinī,
as well as Śeṣa as before, one should place [them], O Dear One, at the root of the palate.
O Dear One, having uttered the *ya*-group, the word *jana*, the term *guptatara*, and also *śākinī*,
as well as the remainder as before, one should place them within the command (*ājñā*).
Having uttered the *śa*-group, the *ta*-group, the extremely secret [mantra], and Hākinī as well—the remainder being as before—one should place it on the forehead, O Dear One. (49)

"Laṃ kṣaṃ, O Dear One, [reciting] 'Truth,' 'The Great Secret,' and 'Even the Yakṣiṇī,' and having spoken the remainder as before, one should place it in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head)."

At the end of the root mantra consisting of three *tāra*s, one should utter "to the fourteenth earth. Then, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) for the Goddess Śrī Parā, who is the sovereign (*adhipāyī*). || 51 ||
Having thus performed the assignment of the worlds (bhuvana-nyāsa), one should then perform the assignment of the forms (mūrti-nyāsa):
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu.
And he who is named Madhusūdana; then Trivikrama and Vāmana;
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara;
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. || 53 ||
Akṣaroṣṭhā, Ceśānī, and likewise Ugroddhvamukhī;
Ṛddhi, Rūpiṇī, Luptā, and Lūnadoṣaikanāyikā. || 54 ||
Eṅkāriṇī, Caughavatī, Sarvakāmāñjanaprabhā, and Asthimālādharā—these are proclaimed as the deities of the vowels. 55.
Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra,
Mahādeva, Bhīma, Īśa, and the one called Tatpuruṣa.
Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva are thus proclaimed. || 56 ||
Karabhadrā, Khagabalā, she who bestows fruits such as heaviness (garimā),
Ghaṇṭādhara, Ugranayanā, Candradhartrī, and after that Chandomayī, Jagatsthānā, and after that Jvalattārā. || 57 ||
Jñānadā, and Ṭaṅkadharā, and Dhṛti are declared as the twelfth; these are the deities of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*. (58)
Brahmā, Prajāpati, Vedhā, Parameṣṭhin, Pitāmaha, Vidhātṛ, Viriñci, Sraṣṭṛ, and Caturānana.
Those beginning with Brahmā are called Hiraṇyagarbha and so forth, in their respective order, making ten.
Yakṣiṇī, Rañjinī, Lakṣmīvajriṇī, Śaśidhāriṇī,
Ṣaḍādhāralayā, Sarvanāyikā, Hasitānanā, Lalitā, and Kṣamā— these are declared to be the deities of the letters beginning with *ya*. (60)
At the end of the three-syllable root mantra, one should place the Viṣṇus together with their Śaktis— conjoined with the dative case ending and the word "namaḥ"— upon the head and the face.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place [the mantras] upon the shoulders, sides, hips, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet, proceeding from the right to the left. 62.
The practitioner of mantra should place Bhava and the other [deities], joined with their respective vowels and conjoined with their Śaktis,
in the feet, sides, arms, throat, and the five faces;
and he should place Brahmā and the others, joined with their Yādi-Śaktis, in the ten supports (ādhāras).
At the end of the root mantra with three *tāra*s, one should utter "Śrī Trimūrttyambikām. Then, with "Āyai Parāmbādevyai Namaḥ," one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*).
Having thus performed the placement of the forms (*mūrti-nyāsa*), one should proceed with the placement of the mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*).
The root of the three *tāras* is *aṃ*, *āṃ*, and *iṃ*; [one should recite] one hundred thousand and ten million [times].
And there is the division [of mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*, consisting of single syllables, from among all mantras.
Then, for the presiding deity (adhidevatā), one should offer the complete [mantra] which bestows all fruits;
likewise, one should utter "Oṃ, obeisance to Āyai Ekakūṭeśvaryambādevyai. (66)
The supreme *dvikūṭa* [mantra] beginning with *ī*, *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, and so forth, starting from *haṃsa*, is as before;
the supreme *trikūṭa* beginning with *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, and so forth, starting from *vahni*, is as before. || 67 ||
Ḷṃ Eṃ Eṃ, four hundred thousand times; as before, the supreme [mantra] beginning with Candra.
Oṃ Auṃ Aṃ Aḥ, five hundred thousand times; as before, the supreme [mantra] beginning with Sūrya. (68)
Kaṃ, khaṃ, and gaṃ—six hundred thousand times each; Skanda and the others as before, followed by the supreme.
