Ghaṃ, ṅaṃ, and caṃ—seven hundred thousand times each; Gaṇeśa and the others as before, followed by the supreme. (69)
Chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ, eight hundred thousand times, for Vaṭuka and the others as before;
ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ, nine hundred thousand times, for Brahmā and the others as before. (70)
Ḍaṃ, ḍhaṃ, and ṇaṃ for ten hundred thousand [recitations], beginning with Viṣṇu as before; and taṃ, thaṃ, and daṃ for eleven hundred thousand, beginning with Rudra as before. (71)
Dhaṃ, naṃ, and paṃ—twelve hundred thousand times each; Vāṇī and the others as before, followed by the Supreme.
Phaṃ, baṃ, and bhaṃ—thirteen hundred thousand times each; Lakṣmī and the others as before, followed by the Supreme. (72)

Maṃ, yaṃ, raṃ—one hundred and forty thousand times; Gaurī and others as before, followed by the supreme. Laṃ, vaṃ, śaṃ—one hundred and fifty thousand times; Durgā and others as before, followed by the supreme.
Ṣaṃ, saṃ, haṃ, laṃ, kṣaṃ—one hundred and sixty thousand times; Tripurā and others, and the sixteen [deities]. (73)

Then, [one should worship] the goddess presiding over all mantras as the essence of the syllables (akṣarātman), followed by the goddess who bestows the fruit of the entire [practice]; likewise, one should again worship the sixteen [syllables] of Kūṭeśvarī.
O Maheśvarī, the mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) for Ambādevī is said to be performed at the ādhāra, the liṅga, the navel, the heart, the throat, and also in the two eyes. 75.

O Mistress of the Kula, one should place [the mantra] in the nibodhikā, the half-moon, the bindu, the kalāpada, the unmanī, the viṣṇuktra, the nāda, the nādānta, and in the region of the dhruvamaṇḍala.

At the end of the root mantra with three *tāra*s, one should place the word "consisting of all mantras" (*sarvamantrātmikā*), followed by "to Āyai Parāmbādevyai," as the pervasive [mantra] upon the heart. (77)
Having thus performed the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), one should perform the placement of the deity (daivatanyāsa).
At the end of the root mantra preceded by the three tāras, [one should utter] "aṃ āṃ sahasrakoṭi" and so forth.
O Dear One, at the end of the word *yoginīkula*, one should utter the word *sevitāyai*;
then one should pronounce the word *nivṛttyambā* for the Goddess, followed by *namaḥ*. (79)
IṂ ĪṂ: one should recite the consecration of the Yoginī and the remainder as before.
UṂ ŪṂ: [one should recite] the ascetic and the Vidyā, and the remainder as before. (80)
Ṛṃ ṝṃ [represent] Śānta and likewise Śānti; one should recite the remainder as before.
Ḷṃ ḹṃ [represent] Muni and Śāntyatītā; one should recite the remainder as before. (81)
"Eṃ E Devañca Hṛllekhāṃ," one should utter the remainder as before.
"Oṃ Auṃ," at the end of the word "Rākṣasa," [one should utter] "Gaganāṃ" as before, followed by "Param.
"Aṃ Aḥ Vidyādharaṃ Raktāṃ," one should utter the remainder as before. (82)
One should utter "kaṃ khaṃ," followed by Siddhimahocchuṣmā, and recite the remainder as before;
then "gaṃ ghaṃ," followed by Sādhyakarālā, and recite the remainder as before. || 83 ||
One should recite "ḍaṃ caṃ" for the Apsaras Jayā, and the remainder as before; "chaṃ jaṃ" for the Gandharva Vijayā, and the remainder as before. || 84 ||
Jhaṃ Ñaṃ, following the word "guhyaka," [one should utter] Ajitā; the remainder is as before.
Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ, following "yakṣa," one should utter Aparājitā; the remainder should be recited as before. (85)
Ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ, and the left-hand Kinnara; the remainder should be recited as before. Ṇaṃ taṃ, and the eldest of the Pannagas; the remainder should be recited as before. || 86 ||
One should utter *thaṃ*, *daṃ*, *caṃ*, and *pitṛraudrāmbāṃ*; the remainder should be recited as before.
*Dhaṃ*, *naṃ*, *gaṇeśa*, and *māyāṃ*; the remainder should be recited as before. (87)
Paṃ phaṃ, at the end of the word Bhairava, [one should worship] Kuṇḍalī as before;
baṃ bhaṃ, [one should worship] Vaṭuka and Kālī, and the remainder should be recited as before. (88)
After the word *kṣetreśa*, one should recite *maṃ yaṃ* and *kālarātri* as before;
then *raṃ laṃ* and *pramathabhagavatī*, and the remainder should be uttered as before. (89)
"Vaṃ śaṃ [is for] Brahmasarveśvarī; the remainder should be recited as before.
Ṣaṃ saṃ [is for] Viṣṇu and Sarvajñā; the remainder should be recited as before. (90)
Haṃ Laṃ, Rudra, the creator of all; one should recite the remainder as before.
Kṣaṃ, the power of the moving and the unmoving; one should recite the remainder as before. || 91 ||
In the thumbs, ankles, shanks, knees, thighs, hips, sides, breasts, armpits, hands, shoulders, ears, and head, respectively. (92)
O Kulanāyikā, one should place [the mantra] ending with "day" on the right side;
at the end of the three-syllable root mantra, [one should place] the word "sarvadevātmikām. (93)
One should place the pervasive [mantra] in the heart for Āyai and Parāmbādevī;
having thus performed the placement of the deities (devanyāsa), one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).
At the end of the three-syllable root mantra: "O you who are the earth of infinite millions following the *ka*-group, served by the family of *carī*, Āṃ Kṣāṃ! Hail to the state of Maṅgalā! (95)
One should utter "Ambādevyai namaḥ," then "Āṃ Kṣāṃ Brahmāṇyai," and thereafter one should speak of the lineage (kula) consisting of infinite crores of beings belonging to Ambādevī.
Then one should utter "aṃ kṣaṃ" for Sahitā and Maṅgalanātha;
one should pronounce "aṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ" for Asitāṅgabhairavanātha. || 97 ||
The cavarga, Khecarī, the syllable *ī*, *lāṃ*, Cacīkā, and Maheśvarī;
Vetāla, *iṃ*, *laṃ*, Cacīka, Ruru, and Śeṣa, as before. || 98 ||
One should utter the *ṭa*-group, "pātālacarīm," "ūṃ," "hāṃ," "yogeśvarīm," and "kaumārīm"; then "piśācam," "uṃ," "haṃ," and "yogeśacaṇḍakau. (99)
The *tavarga* [consonants], *dikcarī*, *ṛṃ*, *sāṃ*, and the *vaiṣṇavī* *harasiddhā*;
for epilepsy (*apasmāra*), *ṛṃ*, *saṃ*, and the *harasiddha* beginning with *krodha*, as before. (100)
The Pavarga [consonants], Sahacarī, ḶṂ, and ṢĀṂ follow Bhaṭṭi and Vārāhī; then comes Brahmarākṣasaka, ḶṂ, and ṢĀṂ, with Bhaṭṭa, Unmattā, and the others as before. (101)
The *yavarga* [mantra] consists of *giricarīm*, *eṃ*, *śāṃ*, and *kilikileti*;
likewise, *indrāṇīm*, *ceṭakam*, *eṃ*, *śaṃ*, *kiliḥ*, and *kāpālikaḥ*. (102)
The letter *śa* is the forest-dweller (*vanacarī*); *oṃ vāṃ* is Kālādirātri;
*cāmuṇḍā* is the corpse (*preta*); *oṃ vaṃ* is Kālarātri; and *bhīṣaṇa* is [the letter] *ca*. (103)
One should utter "laṃ kṣaṃ jalacarīṃ aḥ lāṃ," and then "vaścañca bhīṣaṇām. Following that, one should say "mahālakṣmīṃ śākinīśca aṃ laṃ" and then "bhīṣaṇam. (104)
One should likewise recite Saṃhārabhairava and the remainder as before, [placing them] in the Mūlādhāra, the Liṅga, the navel, the Anāhata, and the Viśuddhi. || 105 ||

One should thus place [the mantra] upon the forehead, the heart, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), at the end of the root mantra consisting of three *tāra*s, using the words "Mātṛ-Bhairava. (106)
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the mantra "Adhipāyai Parāmbā Devyai Namaḥ.
O Maheśānī, one who is composed should thus perform the Mātṛ-nyāsa. 107.

Thus, O Goddess, having deposited his body [in the sacred sites], he should meditate on the God with undivided mind upon a most beautiful jewel-island rising from the midst of the ocean of nectar. 108.
Within a pavilion of rubies situated in the midst of a forest of wish-fulfilling trees,
[he sits] upon a lotus at the center of a glorious lion-throne made of the nine precious gems.
Seated within the triangle, possessing the splendor of ten thousand moons and suns, joined with Ambikā who is half his size, and adorned with distinct ornaments. || 110 ||
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, eternally sixteen years of age, with a lotus-face of gentle smiles, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-jewel. 111.
Adorned with divine garments, garlands, and unguents, and decorated with divine ornaments,
he holds in his hands a vessel of the nectar of consciousness, a trident, and a book.
She who bears the perfect accomplishment of knowledge, whose face and eyes are ever-blissful,
and who is served by the entire host of deities arisen from the Great Sixteen.
Thus, one should meditate upon Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara within the lotus of the heart;
O Goddess, one may contemplate him in male form or reflect upon him in female form.

Or else, O Goddess, one should meditate upon the partless [Brahman], characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, consisting of pure luster, and having the form of all that is moving and unmoving. 115.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should display the ten mudrās:
the yoni, the liṅga, the surabhi, and the four mudrās of the weapon (heti).

One should recite the root mantra of the forest garland (vanamālā), the great seal (mahāmudrā), and the sky seal (nabhomudrā) in sequence according to one's capacity, as well as the mantra of the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā). O Goddess, one should contemplate the venerable Guru, whose form is Śiva, upon the crown of one's head.
In a thousand-petaled lotus, he who possesses the luster of the full moon, whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness, who is clothed in pure fragrant flowers,
whose face and eyes are serene, and who embodies the form of all deities.
One should remember the Guru, seated upon a swan on the head, preceded by his name.

When the nyāsa has been performed in this manner, O Goddess, the practitioner of mantra becomes manifest as Paraśiva himself; there is no doubt in this regard, for he is capable of both restraint and grace. (119)
I bow to him who performs day after day the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Mahāṣoḍhā; all the gods pay homage to him—of this there is no doubt.
O Pārvatī, wherever one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Mahāṣoḍhā,
that place is declared to be a divine field (divyakṣetra) extending ten yojanas in every direction.
O Goddess, O Beloved, wherever a man goes after performing this nyāsa, there he shall have victory, gain, honor, and prowess.
O Śivā, he who performs the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa and is thus saluted meets death within six months, even if Śiva himself were his protector.

Whoever performs this ritual placement (nyāsa) named Vajrapañjara [becomes protected from] those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, on the earth, in the mountains, in the waters, and in the forests. 124.
O Mistress of the Kula, fierce spirits, vetālas, gods, rākṣasas, grahas, and the like do not even look upon him with minds seized by fear.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as the sages and the lords of munis, bow down to one who has performed the Mahāṣoḍhā ritual placement (nyāsa).
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? This nyāsa is dear to me.
O Goddess, one should not speak of it to one who is not a son, nor should one reveal it to one who is not a disciple.
One attains the perfection of command; therefore, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
There is no protection superior to this, which grants the accomplishment of the state of divinity;
there is no doubt about this in the world. This is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. (128)
Entry into the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), contemplation upon the Supreme Palace (parāprāsāda), and the thorough knowledge of the Great Ṣoḍhā—these are not the fruit of meager austerity. (129)
Thus, O Goddess, O beloved, the extraction of the mantra and so forth has been told to you in brief, O Mistress of the Kula. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Great Ṣoḍhā," in the fifth section of the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the *Śrīkulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The Goddess said:
[Please explain] the characteristics of the Kuleśas, the supporting vessels, and the various meats.
The creation, the division, and indeed the greatness of the family property. || 1 ||
I wish to hear all about the sin that arises from non-performance and the fruit that arises from performance; tell me this, O ocean of compassion.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one attains equality with the gods.
Without a support there is a fall, and yet the Mothers are not satisfied;
therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should prepare the support according to the rule.
They say the base should have three feet, or six feet, or four feet;
or else, O Goddess, one should make it circular in shape and beautiful to the mind.
[The vessel] may be made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, skull, gourd, or clay;
or it may originate from coconut, conch, copper, pearl-oyster, or mother-of-pearl. || 6 ||
A wise person should fashion an alms-bowl from a tree grown of merit;
one should avoid that which is too thin, too thick, cracked, or broken. (7)
Vessels made of gold, silver, and copper bring about all accomplishments;
for rites of pacification, a stone vessel is used, and for rites of immobilization, one made of clay.
The coconut shell is for subjugation (vaśya), and that from a tortoise is for malevolent rites (abhicāra);
the conch-shell bestows knowledge, and the mother-of-pearl shell grants the favor of the Goddess.
Skulls and gourd vessels bring about the accomplishment of yoga,
while vessels made from sacred trees remove all sins.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should prepare a single vessel from among those mentioned here.
I shall now declare the family substances; listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess!
There should be twelve *prasthas* of water and half a *prastha* of buttermilk. (11)
One should place four prasthas of rice and two prasthas of grain, together with sprouts the size of a handful, into a single jar.
One should place it for two days in a location free from cold and other such elements;
then, having applied fire to it, one should cook it until it resembles mud.
Having sown it again, one should then bring it to a cool state;
having ground it with three-quarters of a *prastha* measure, the wise person should then mix it together with his hands.
On the following day, one should take half a *prastha* of rice grains;
having thoroughly mixed them with buttermilk (*takra*) and stirred them during cooking, one should combine them.
This is renowned as *paiṣṭī*, honored by gods and demons alike. (15)
O Kuleśānī, ten *prasthas* of water boiled with *gauḍī*, white *barbara*, and the bark of *jambu*, along with auspicious *dhātakī* flowers [should be used]. (16)
One should also add one prastha of coconut blossoms, along with *harītakī* fruits measuring eight *niṣkas* in weight. (17)
One should add one niṣka each of fire (cinnabar) and the three pungents (trikaṭuka) separately;
then, one should combine them with eighty parts of jaggery in a single jar.
One should rotate it properly with the hand, both clockwise and counter-clockwise,
one hundred and eight times at each of the three junctions of the day every day.
The digestion [of the poison] occurs in twelve days; one should protect [the patient] during the thirteenth.
This is called the Gauḍī [type of mercury], which is the cause for attaining union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
One should mix double the amount of water with the flower-nectar in a jar;
the cooking will be complete in twelve days. The remainder is as previously described. This is designated as Mādhvī, which brings delight to the deities.
One part of ginger, two parts of cinnamon, three parts of black pepper, four parts of dhātakī flower, five parts of flowers [of the pārijāta tree], and six parts of honey. (22)
Mixed with eighty pieces of jaggery, the remainder is as previously described.
This captivating substance is the supreme drink for the Yoginīs. || 23 ||
Half a *drona* of *sārddhendupālaka*, one *prastha* of buffalo milk, and a hundred ripe plantains— this preparation is an auspicious intoxicant (*madirā*).
Having mixed and combined that, one should cook it in a bamboo tube smeared with mud for forty-eight days in a mire born of lotuses. (25)
Having placed it [there] and extracted it with the rays of the sun, one should thoroughly dry it;
and when it has become solid, the person should collect it. (26)
The auspicious vessel, filled with water to the measure of a *guñjā* fruit, should be filled according to one's own desire; it bestows supreme, ultimate bliss. 27.
O beloved, this too is a supreme substance dear to all the gods;
one should prepare these other intoxicants which cause exhilaration. (28)
The intoxicating drinks derived from the jackfruit, grape, honey-tree, date-palm, and sugarcane;
those produced from honey, *śīdhu*, *mādhvīka*, *maireya*, and coconut. (29)
These eleven types of liquor grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
however, O Beloved, the twelfth, *surā-madya*, is the best of them all.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from flour (paiṣṭī), that made from molasses (gauḍī), and that made from honey (mādhvī).
Paiṣṭī bestows all accomplishments (siddhi), while gauḍī grants enjoyment (bhoga). || 31 ||

Honey-wine (mādhvī) should be known as the bestower of liberation; liquor (surā) is dear to the gods; sugarcane wine (aikṣavī) should be known as the giver of knowledge; and grape wine (drākṣī) shall be the bestower of sovereignty.
The *tālaja* [variety] is praised for immobilization; the *khārjūrī* destroys enemies;
that which arises from the coconut bestows prosperity; and the *pānasī* grants auspiciousness. (33)
That which is born of the Madhūka tree bestows knowledge; that of the Mādhvīka plant destroys disease;
and that known as Maireya, O Kuleśānī, always removes sin. (34)
Liquor produced from milk-trees, that which originates from bark, that which arises from honey-flowers, and fermented gruel made from rice; || 35 ||
O Goddess, that liquor which possesses unchanging bliss and a captivating fragrance is the most excellent, bestowing delight upon the gods. (36)
One should fill the vessel according to one's desire, which increases supreme bliss;
O Dear One, this substance known as āmodaka is beloved by all the gods.
By the mere sight of the Surā, one is liberated from all sins;
by the mere smelling of its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. || 38 ||
By the mere touch of the wine, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy places;
O Goddess, by drinking it, one directly attains the fourfold liberation.

The power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in the fragrance of the wine, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in its taste, and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in its savor; while the Supreme (parā) power abides in its exhilaration.
Wines that reach the Brahman are said to be the means for purifying the mind;
having procured one of them, one should perform the rite of worship. (41)
Having thoroughly mixed fish, meat, and the like with *vijayā* well-blended with the eight fragrances (*aṣṭagandha*), the wise practitioner should knead it into pills and collect them;
then, in the absence of wine, he should satisfy [the deity] by mixing the pill with water. 42.
One should satisfy [the deity] with buttermilk mixed with jaggery and honey; or one may do so with *sauvīra* (sour gruel). One must not omit this rite;
if it is omitted through negligence, one shall incur the curse of the deities. (43)
O Dear One, meat is said to be of three kinds: that which moves in the sky, on the earth, and in the water.
Even if only one is available according to circumstances, one should prepare it for the purpose of satiation.
By the mere sight of meat, the fruit is obtained just as by the sight of wine. 44.
In sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, ritual violence is ordained;
however, O beloved, the killing of living beings for one's own sake is never enjoined.
One should never cut even a blade of grass without purpose;
however, having killed [an animal] for the sake of the deities or for the sake of the twice-born, one is not tainted by sin.
O Śāmbhavī, whatever merit or sin may arise from speaking while disregarding me, let him commit that sin for my sake; it shall become merit. 47.
By the very same substances through which [ordinary] falling occurs, accomplishment is likewise enjoined even in the venerable Kaula system by the high-souled Bhairava. (48)
If there should be no lapse in the performance of my rites for those men who carry them out, then the seven crores of lordly sages shall perform those rites for you. (49)
O Dear One, having consecrated the sacrificial animal with this mantra, one should slay it;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), otherwise one would go to hell.
"This body has been cut away by Śiva; therefore, you have attained the state of Śiva.
Understand this, O bound soul (paśu), for you are not [merely] Śiva—you are indeed Śiva. (51)
Brahmā resides in the flesh, Viṣṇu in the fragrance, and Rudra in its taste;
the Supreme Self resides in its bliss. Therefore, O beloved, this [wine] should be consumed.
In the absence of meat, however, O Goddess, one should take garlic, fresh ginger, or ginger-root (nāgara) and perform the worship; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
One should not satisfy [the deity] even with liquor that is devoid of fish and meat;
one should not perform worship with any substance lacking fish and meat. 54.
By offering even a piece of flesh the size of a sesame seed, or even half a sesame seed with a single drop,
through that single act of satiation, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
There is no other merit in the three worlds equal to the worship of one's own family;
therefore, he who worships with devotion becomes a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. //56//
Even if he has not studied and is ignorant of the scriptures, one who is devoted to his guru, firm in his vows, and intent upon the worship of the lineage—such a person shall be most dear to me. (57)
O Goddess, when she is worshipped, she bestows the desired fruits upon all four castes and stages of life, as well as upon men, women, and eunuchs.
O Goddess of Devas, when worshipped, you bestow fruits both in this world and the next, like a virtuous wife; but when not worshipped, you cause suffering, like a wicked wife. (59)
But that person of evil intellect who performs [this] without the worship of his lineage goes to a terrible hell along with twenty-one generations of his family.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the worship of the Kula;
one obtains all accomplishments—of this there is no doubt. || 61 ||
If one is unable to perform the propitiation, one should offer the means for worship;
if one is not even able to give those, one should at least behold the act of worship.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by performing a hundred sacrifices correctly, that same fruit one obtains by performing the *kramārcana* just once. (63)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by performing the sixteen great gifts, that same fruit one attains by beholding the Śrīcakra. 64.
O Goddess, by performing the Krama-worship even once, one obtains that same fruit which one would attain by bathing in thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? He who, according to his devotion, gives kuladravya for the sake of worship to the Kulācārya, is a knower of dharma.
Whether in the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, or Sugata-darśana (Buddhist) traditions; likewise in the Bauddha, Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, Vrata, or Kula-mukha systems. || 67 ||
O Pārvatī, in the Siddhānta of the six right and left [traditions], as well as in the Vedic and other systems,
worship performed without wine (ali) and meat (piśita) shall be fruitless.
O Goddess, one who performs the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), austerity, or vows while deprived of the family wealth shall find it fruitless, just like an oblation poured into ashes.
Just as those who move within the inner circle of a king are dear to him, not those who move outside,
so too, O Goddess, those who are devoted to the internal sacrifice are dear to me, and no others.
Those who offer meat and wine to us with devotion, and who produce joy, are my beloved Kaulikas. (71)
The supreme form of us two, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss,
manifests through the enjoyment of the substances of the Kula, and not otherwise.
The radiant splendor of internal experience, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech, arises through the enjoyment of the substances of the Kula, O Dear One, and not otherwise. (73)
When the substance of the Kula has been consumed, one who perceives the true meaning of the Kula-tattva experiences the possession of Bhairava, seeing with equanimity everywhere. (74)
Just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen by means of a lamp,
so indeed the self, shrouded by māyā, is seen through the drinking of the substance.
O Dear One, those people who drink the family substance (kuladravya) purified by mantra and consumed by the Guru and the Devas, for them there is no further need to drink mother’s milk.
The god Bhairava is indeed wine, and wine is declared to be Śakti;
oh, the enjoyer of wine could delude even the immortals! (77)
O beloved, that man who, having drunk that *maireya* liquor, does not undergo transformation, but becomes solely intent on meditation—he is liberated and he is a *kaulika*. (78)
Wine is Śakti, meat is Śiva, and he who eats it is Bhairava himself;
the bliss arising from the union of these two is called liberation.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
wine is its manifestor, and therefore it is drunk by yogis.
Do the people of this world not see Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara bearing their water-pots, conch-shells, and skull-bowls filled with honey? (81)
Free from doubt, fearless, heroic, shameless, and devoid of curiosity,
having fully ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, one may drink the boon-granting wine of Varuṇa.
O Pārvatī, through the drinking of nectar purified by the refinement of mantras, the state of the deity arises, which brings liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. 83.
It is always to be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya, at the onset of battle; for a Vaiśya, upon the acquisition of cattle; and for a Śūdra, at the time of funeral rites. || 84 ||
O Goddess, having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed in the scriptures,
one who drinks liquor and eats meat while remembering the Guru incurs no fault.

For the sake of satisfying the ancestors and the gods, and for the purpose of stabilizing meditation on Brahman, one may consume honey and meat; however, if one does so out of mere craving, he is a sinner.

One should practice the drinking of honey for the sake of the meaning of the mantra, for the purpose of mental radiance, as a cause for the stability of the mind, and for the cessation of the bonds of worldly existence. 87.
He who consumes liquor and other such substances for his own pleasure is a sinner;
one who is free from personal desire should partake of them for the sake of pleasing the deity. 88.
O beloved, the consumption of intoxicants such as fish, meat, wine, and the like,
at any time other than during a sacrificial rite, is declared to be a fault.
Just as the drinking of Soma is prescribed for the wise during sacrifices, so too should the drinking of wine be performed at the proper time, as it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 90.
Having thoroughly understood the latent tendencies from the Kula scriptures of the glorious Guru, one should practice the five mudrās; otherwise, one shall fall.
If one does not worship the Āvṛtti, the lineage of gurus, and Vaṭuka and the others,
even a hero who drinks here in vain shall incur the curse of the deities.
Without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation of the mantras,
even a hero who drinks according to the rite for the consumption of the *paśu* shall go to hell.
If anyone should engage in this scripture without knowing the Kaulika conduct and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru, you will certainly afflict him. 94.
For he who, being unaccomplished in the Kaula knowledge, desires to consume that substance, should be known as a great sinner, excluded from all dharma. (95)

For one who has fallen away from the conduct of the samaya, who acts according to his own whims, and who is evil-minded, there are no accomplishments; he suffers a fall from his lineage. Therefore, one should not associate with him. 96.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims, attains no success in this world, nor the supreme goal in the hereafter. (97)

For one who indulges according to their own whims and is devoid of the purificatory rites of initiation (dīkṣā), there is no attainment of the supreme goal anywhere, despite asceticism, pilgrimages, vows, and the like.
One who drinks unfermented liquor, engages in sexual intercourse by force, or eats meat killed for one's own pleasure, shall go to the Raurava hell. (99)
If Kaulas are devoted to the vows of the fettered (paśu), they mock both sides; for as many hairs as they possess, for that many years they remain in the Raurava hell.
He who, having resorted to another doctrine, consumes the ritual substances of his own family,
is born among the sources of elemental beings for as many times as there are hairs on his body.
And one whose self is obscured by intoxication understands nothing at all;
there is no meditation, no austerity, no worship, no dharma, and no virtuous action. 102.
Neither fate, nor the guru, nor self-inquiry can save him; he who is merely attached to sense objects falls, without a doubt. 103.
He who is addicted to liquor, who does not seek worship, who eats meat, who indulges with women, and who is devoid of the Kaula instruction—such a person shall go to an inexhaustible hell. 104.
But he who is devoid of ritual practice (*asaṃskārin*) yet employs the five mudrās, O Mistress of the Family—though he may be devoted to Brahmā—he incurs censure. (105)
One who knows the distinctions of the three genders and discerns the six supports (ādhāras),
having reached the locations of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), should proceed to the Great Lotus Forest (mahāpadmavana).

Having gone repeatedly from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), there arises the bliss of the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the moon of consciousness (*ciccandra*) and the power of Kuṇḍalinī. 107.
The man who delights in drinking the nectar flowing from the lotus of the sky is said to be a drinker of nectar; others are merely drinkers of wine. 108.

Having slain the sacrificial animal of merit and demerit with the sword of knowledge, the knower of yoga leads the consciousness to dissolution in the Supreme; he is called a "consumer of meat" (palāśī).
Having restrained the group of senses with the mind, one should unite them within the self;
O Goddess, he who eats thus becomes a "fish-eater" (matsyāśī), while all others are destroyers of living beings.
The power of the beast is unawakened, whereas that of the Kaulika is awakened;
he who serves that power shall be a true servant of power. || 111 ||

He who remains filled with the bliss arising from the union of the couple consisting of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) and the Self—that is true sexual union; others are merely those who indulge with women.
O Goddess, Mistress of the Kula, he who, having learned the latent impressions (vāsanā) of these five mudrās from the mouth of the Guru, practices them, is liberated. 113.
Thus, O Goddess, the characteristics of the Kula substances and so forth have been told to you in brief, O Mistress of the Kula. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Kula," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 5.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Kuleśa, I wish to hear the characteristics of the worshiper.
O Lord, tell me about the consecration of family property and other such items, as well as worship.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one is praised by gods and dānavas. (2)
There, men who have cast off all sins and perform meritorious deeds,
who are well-endowed with noble lineage and knowledge, and who are firm in their vows, offer their devotion.
Endowed with the full consecration, knowing the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras,
devoted to the deity and the guru, and self-restrained, one should perform worship, O Dear One.
O Mistress of the Kula, one who knows the secrets of the family lineage (kulāgama), who is eager to propitiate the deity, and who is endowed with the instructions of the guru, should perform worship.
O Dear One, one who is pure in soul, exceedingly joyful, free from anger and greed, averse to animal sacrifices and similar rites, and possessing a gracious countenance, should perform the sacrifice.
O beloved, when, after a long time, that man has accomplished his purpose,
through my grace there shall arise for him a firm union with devotion.

For that purpose, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with substances as proclaimed by Śrī Bhairava, according to the method of the Guru’s instruction; otherwise, a fall [from grace] will occur. || 8 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the worship of the Śrīcakra through the yoga of mantra;
that I myself shall accept with reverence along with you. (9)
"Through the realization that 'I am Bhairava,' one becomes endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
Having reflected thus, the lord of yogis should become devoted to the worship of Kula. (10)

O Goddess, he who, endowed with such characteristics as these, is a follower of the Kaula path and firm in his vows, and worships you— he shall become a recipient of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Seated on a comfortable seat in a solitary, secluded forest region free from disturbances, facing either the east or the north. || 12 ||
In the ocean of nectar, on the island of jewels, at the foot of the Kalpa tree,
one should remember a ruby pavilion resplendent with walls of gems.
Richly adorned with canopies of flower garlands, covered and enclosed by curtains,
radiant with camphor lamps, and fragrant with the scent of incense.
O Goddess, having meditated with an undisturbed mind upon oneself as situated within that pavilion, one should perform the Kula worship by the command of the venerable Guru.
The purification of the deity through the absence of substances residing within oneself is the fifth [stage].
As long as the practitioner of mantra does not perform this, how can there be worship of the deity? (16)

O Dear One, self-purification is said to be accomplished through thorough bathing, the purification of the elements, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth, as well as by the placement of all the six limbs and other [mantras]. (17)

The purification of the site is said to consist of sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other such acts, making the ground as smooth as the surface of a mirror; it is further adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, flowers, and garlands, and decorated with patterns made from five-colored powders.
Having interwoven the letters of the Mātṛkā with the syllables of the root mantra,
both in forward and reverse order and by repeating them twice, this is declared to be the purification of the mantra.

Having consecrated the articles of worship with the root mantra and the weapon mantra according to the rules, one who knows the ritual procedure should display the *dhenu-mudrā*; this is declared to be the purification of the articles.

Having established the deity upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the knower of mantras, radiant in spirit, should sprinkle [the deity] three times with the root mantra and with water from the substances used for nyāsa; this is declared to be the purification of the deity. 21.
Having thus performed the fivefold purification, one should thereafter perform the sacrifice;
that worship is said to be fruitful, otherwise it becomes fruitless. (22)
"O Dear One, it is said that worship without a mandala is fruitless;
therefore, having drawn the mandala according to the rules, one should perform worship therein. (23)
That which stands pervading the universe with the form of an unbroken circle,
by which the three worlds are adorned— that mandala is eternally auspicious.
Uḍḍīyāna is a quadrangle, Kāmarūpa is circular, Jālandhara is a half-moon, and Pūrṇagiri is triangular. || 25 ||
After worshipping the mandala, one should subsequently place the supporting vessels in their proper order:
the common vessel, the vessel for the venerable Guru, the vessel for enjoyment, and the vessel for the bali offering—thus making five.
One should not cause [the vessel] to be made with two, three, or even a single foot;
rather, having placed it from one's own right to the left and having worshipped it with liquor (āsava), [one should proceed].
Having filled it with the root mantra, O Kuleśvarī, one who knows the ritual placement should deposit therein fish and meat in the measure of a māṣa. 28.
If [the water] has been drunk from causes such as being lost, stale, leftover, foul-smelling, or overcome by odors,
or if it is contained in another vessel, it becomes fruitless.
O Mistress of the Family, one should not fill the vessels with those things which are unpleasant;
rather, O Great Goddess, the libation becomes fruitful when performed with delightful substances that are most delicious, intoxicating to the lips, and like unto nectar. (30)
Wine is unrefined; it bestows evil, strife, disease, and suffering.
It is the destroyer of life-span, prosperity, fame, good fortune, wealth, and grain. (31)
Therefore, having duly consecrated the family property according to the rules, one should then perform the worship;
otherwise, both the giver and the consumer go to hell, without a doubt. (32)
O Dear One, one should neither recite nor meditate without dwelling upon the substance and so forth;
those foolish men who do so experience suffering at every step. (33)
Without liquor there is no mantra, and without mantra there is no liquor;
since they are mutually contradictory, how can worship be performed? (34)
O beloved, having understood the removal of those doubts from the mouth of the Guru, [one performs] inspection, sprinkling, meditation, and purification through mantra and mudrā;
thus the substance becomes fit for libation and causes delight to the deity. (35)
Through the twenty-four mantras dedicated to Agni, Sūrya, Indu, Brahmā, Indra, Viṣ� liquor is indeed the supreme nectar (parāmṛta). || 36 ||
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. (37)
O Mistress of the Kula, the sixteen digits born of the vowels—Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and the rest—are said to be gentle and bestowers of desires. (38)

Tapanī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Rodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā— these twelve, beginning with Ka and Ha and ending with Ṣa and Tha, are said to bestow wealth and belong to the Sun. (39)
Dhūmrā, Arci, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā—
these ten fiery kalās, beginning with the letter 'ya', bestow the fruit of dharma. || 40 ||

Sṛṣṭi, Medhā, Smṛti, Ṛddhi, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirā, Sthiti, and Siddhi—these are declared to be the ten kalās of the *ka*-group. Originating from the letter *a* and born of Brahmā, these kalās are for the purpose of creation. (41)
Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, and Īśvarī; Ratikāmikā, Varadā, Āhlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā—these are born from the *ṣ*, *ṭ*, and *t* groups.
Originating from the letter *u* and born from Viṣṇu, these digits (kalās) exist for the purpose of maintenance (*sthiti*).

Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣut, Krodhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu— these are said to be the ten digits (kalās) of the *pa*-group. Originating from the letter *ma*, these digits born of Rudra are for the purpose of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*).
The four [powers] belonging to the *ṣa*-group are yellow, white, reddish, and black;
these digits (*kalās*) are born from Īśvara for the purpose of concealment (*tirodhāna*), while those born from the *bindu* are for the sake of liberation.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā. (45)

Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānā, Amṛtā, Āpyāyinī, Vyāpinī, and Vyomarūpā— these are the sixteen digits (kalās) born from the vowels. Arising from Sadāśiva, they are the digits of grace (anugraha-kalās) following the sequence from Nāda.
First is *Prakṛteḥ haṃsaḥ*, followed immediately by *Tat viṣṇoḥ*;
the third should be *Tryambakaṃ*, and the fourth begins with *Tat padam*. (47)
May Viṣṇu fashion the womb; this is the fifth mantra of the Kalpanā-manus.
These ninety-four mantras bestow the attainment of the state of the deity who is one's own self. || 48 ||
The recitation of mantras and the self-praise are proclaimed [to be performed] with five;
O Mistress of the Kula, those five mantras which are proclaimed here—[they are as follows]. (49)
O you whose nature is the supreme nectar, the source of unbroken, singular-flavored bliss;
O you who possess the form of Akula, bestow upon me here the spontaneous radiance of your own will.
O Supreme One, who abides in the non-clan (akula), whose form is nectar, and who bestows the knowledge of accomplishment—
grant the state of immortality in this reality that has a moist nature.
Having brought about a state of oneness with that form, [offer] the *arghya* to her who possesses that very nature;
having become the form of supreme nectar, cause the vibration of consciousness to arise within me.
Vāgbhava is situated at the side; Bhūmi is Puṣṭi conjoined with Indu;
and Sthiti is adorned by Artha and Indu following Pāvaka.
One should utter the word *amṛte* joined with *sthire*, *indhike*, and *indau*, followed by *śvete* accompanied by two dots (*bindu*), and after that, the words *amṛtodbhave*. (54)

Having thus spoken "Amṛteśvarī," one should then utter the nectar-showering syllables. A pair that causes nectar to flow, ending with the seed-syllable *dviṭha* (svāhā), effects the purification of substances.
This mantra of Amṛteśī is said to consist of thirty-five syllables.
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of words, and "Vāgvādinī" followed by the Vāgbhava;
then the Kāmarāja [syllable], and "Klinne," "Kledini," and "Kledaya. (56)
After that, [one should utter] "mahāmokṣam" followed by the pair "kuru"; then the "kāmarāja" [mantra];
and after the word "mokṣa," one should then utter the third [mantra] followed by the pair "kuru. (57)
It may end with the word *prāsādaparā* and consist of thirty-seven syllables; O Dear One, it is called the *Dīpanī-mantra*, which bestows all accomplishments.
These [syllables] are the Kalās, as well as the Mātṛkās, the Mantras beginning with Akhaṇḍendu and Āṇḍaika,
Amṛteśī, Dīpanī, and also the Mūla-mantra, in due order.
O Mother, having recollected [the mantra] one, two, three, four, or five times, or twice or four times, and having performed worship, one should honor the vessel with the *dhenumudrā*.
O you who bring forth the essence of nectar, fill this great vessel— produced from a fragment of the cosmic egg and filled with the entirety of all essences.

O Dear One, one should worship oneself with pure substances, and with that [substance], as well as with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, using all the mantras prescribed for the ritual placement (nyāsa). 62.
On the crown of the head, one should contemplate the lineage of the venerable gurus, and at the *mūlādhāra*, the *pādukā*.
In the divine stream (*divyaugha*), there is Ādinātha, his Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
His wife is Īśvara, his wife is Rudra, and his daughter-in-law is Viṣṇu; his beloved is Brahmā, and his wife is [the last]; these twelve are thus proclaimed.
In the lineage of the Siddhas: Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta, and Ṛbhukṣaja. || 65 ||
Dattātreya, Raivataka, and Vāmadeva after him;
then Vyāsa and Śuka—these eleven are proclaimed. (66)
Mānavaugha, Nṛsiṃha, Maheśa, Bhāskara, Mahendra, Mādhava, and Viṣṇu—these six are proclaimed [as the forms]. || 67 ||

O Goddess, one should join the supreme Śiva at the end of the *namas* in the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), Mahāśiva in the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), and Sadāśiva in the Human Current (*mānavaugha*). || 68 ||
Then, having worshipped the pedestal, O Dear One, one should invoke the Goddess:
"O Supreme Goddess, who dwells within the forest of great lotuses, whose form is the bliss of the Cause, who is intent on the welfare of all beings, O Mother, come, come hither! (69)
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion and endowed with all protective coverings,
remain steadfast here for as long as I worship you.
Having invoked the Goddess with this mantra, one who is single-minded should worship her;
having meditated upon her and displayed the mudrās, one should honor her with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
The conceptualization of forms for Brahman— who is composed of consciousness, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, and bodiless— is for the benefit of spiritual practitioners.
On a linga, a sacrificial mound, fire, water, a ladle, a wall,
a cloth, a mandala, a wooden board, on the head, or in the heart— these ten locations are proclaimed.
In these places, O Goddess of the gods, men devoted to the ritualistic section of the Vedas worship the supreme Śivā, having rendered her who is formless into one possessing form. (74)
Just as milk produced from all the limbs of a cow flows forth from the openings of her udders,
so does the omnipresent Lord manifest within images and other such forms.
Due to the beauty of the image, the excellence of the worship, and the faith of the practitioner, the deity becomes present. (76)
Milk residing within the body of cows does not nourish their own limbs;
however, when given away, it nourishes that very same body through the performance of its own action. (77)
Thus, O Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign resides within the bodies of all as the Sapīrvī;
yet, without worship, O Goddess, She does not bestow fruit upon men.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having kindled its vital breaths and the senses, one should install and worship [the deity], O Goddess; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.

Whatever may be deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in procedure— one should rectify all such deficiencies, as well as any missing limbs or steps, through confession (kṣamā).
Whatever action one performs in excess of the prescribed rule,
no fruit whatsoever is accomplished for him due to the fault of violating the sequence.
Deficient or excessive rituals never bear fruit;
indeed, virtuous deeds performed here according to the prescribed rules do bear fruit.
May the ritual action performed according to those rules—such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—bring delight to the deity and bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 83.
O Śāmbhavī, for those who do not know the pervasion of the mantra within the God who is the very form of the mantra, all acts such as worship and the like become entirely fruitless.
The yantra is said to consist of mantra, and the deity has the form of mantra;
O Goddess, when she is worshipped within the yantra, she becomes pleased instantly.
Because it restrains all sufferings arising from defects such as desire and anger, they call this a "yantra" (instrument/machine); when worshipped, the Divine is pleased within it.
O beloved, just as the body is to the living soul and oil is to the lamp,
so too is the yantra established for all the gods.

Therefore, O Dear One, having either drawn the yantra or meditated upon Śiva together with his retinue, and having learned everything from the mouth of the Guru, one should worship according to the prescribed rite.

He who performs the worship of different deities on a single seat without using separate yantras, having abandoned the relationship of principal and subordinate, shall incur the curse of the deity. (89)
O Mistress of the Kula, one should worship the deities, together with their retinues, according to the prescribed rules, each individually upon their own respective yantra on a single seat.
If one, having invoked a single deity, should worship another deity, that practitioner with a fickle mind incurs sin from both. (91)
O Dear One, having learned these characteristics from the guru and from the scriptures, one should properly worship the deity according to the prescribed rite; then the deity becomes well-pleased.
One should worship Śiva, together with his limbs and his retinue, using the root mantra and the sixteen types of offerings, such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains. || 93 ||
O Śāmbhavī, one should worship the entire retinue arisen from the Mahāṣoḍha [rite] with their respective names, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. || 94 ||
One should satisfy [the deities] with drops of nectar by means of the path taught in the scriptures.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform this according to the rule from the flow of one's own vessel, with the nectar issuing upward from the nails of the thumb and ring finger. 95.
Having performed a single libation and recited the root mantra and the *pāduka*,
one should raise the internal power (*antaḥśakti*) and offer libations to the deities of the body.
The thumb is the god Bhairava, and the ring finger is Caṇḍikā, O beloved;
by the union of the ring finger and the thumb, one should satisfy the lineage of the Kula.
O Dear One, one should offer libations with the thumb and ring finger for the rite of subjugation;
with the combination of the index finger and thumb for malevolent rites (abhicāra);
and with the combination of the little finger and thumb for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).
Having thus satisfied [the deities], O Goddess of the gods, with the kula-substances according to the rule, one should worship the deities in front of oneself and the lineages of gurus, O Goddess,
having correctly understood them in the sequence of three lines with an undistracted mind. (99)
Holding the *cinmudrā* and a skull-cup filled with honey in her two hands,
she resembles molten gold, wearing red flowers, unguents, and garments;
her side-glances are full of compassion, her eyes are crimson, and her matted hair reaches to the heavens.
Let him worship the lineage of gurus, which has descended through the sequence and is attended by the multitudes of Siddhas. || 100 ||
Having thus performed worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings,
one should present liquor mixed with meat, various kinds of edibles,
fruits such as plantains, and betel leaf. (101)

Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the characteristics of the Kula practice; [I have also explained] the purification through the processing of the products of the cow and so forth. What else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Purification of Substances," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāyatantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrīkulārṇava*— the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. Chapter Six.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The Śrī Devī said: O Kuleśa, [please explain] the bali offering for the Baṭukas and others, as well as the characteristics of the Śakti.
O Treasure of Compassion, tell me how that which is not a substance can indeed be accepted as one's own. || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is revealed.
O Kuleśvarī, as long as one does not offer [the oblation] to the *vaṭuka*, all the deities are not satisfied, even through remembrance or sacrifice. || 3 ||
Therefore, one should worship Vaṭuka and the others with perfumes, flowers, wine, and meat;
by means of their respective mantras and ritual procedures, one shall obtain the favor of the deities.
O Mistress of the Kula, whatever collection of offerings has been brought for the sake of worship or as a cause for enjoyment, that is given with devotion to the Lords of the Field (kṣetrapas).
O Mistress of the Kula, listen as I shall declare the mantras of the Vaṭukas; by the mere recitation of which all calamities are destroyed. (6)
Then, with three high-pitched tones, [one should call out]: "O Son of the Goddess! or "O Baṭuka!
or "O Nātha!"—you who are tawny and radiant with the mass of matted hair.
The word *trinetra* comes first, followed by the word *jvālāmukha*;
then [the words] *imāṃ pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa*, O beloved of Agni!
This mantra of Vaṭuka, consisting of forty-four syllables, has thus been declared. (8)
Satisfied by this offering of sacrifice, may the young ascetic (baṭuka), the bestower of all perfections, who is attended by spirits and vetālas, grant me constant peace. || 9 ||
Then one should utter the three *tāra*s, followed by the word "to all yoginīs.
After that, [one says] "to all beings" (*sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*) and "the sovereign over all beings" (*sarvabhūtādhipati*). 10.
One should utter the word "pada" for those ḍākinīs and śākinīs;
then one should utter the word "trailokye" and then "vāsinībhya imām. || 11 ||
"O Maheśānī, this fifteen-syllable mantra of the Yoginī, ending in *svāhā* and beginning with 'Accept the worship and the offering (*bali*)', has been declared. (12)
Whatever Yoginī there may be—whether fierce, gentle, most terrible, or supreme;
whether moving in the sky, moving on the earth, or moving in the void—may she always be pleased with me. 13.
One should utter "tāra" three times, followed by "sarvabhūtebhyaḥ sarva eva hi.
After that, joined with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), there is the seventeen-syllable mantra for the lords of beings (bhūtapatibhyaḥ). || 14 ||
Those beings of various forms—divine, terrestrial, or moving in the atmosphere—who reside in the netherworld, some have been purified by me through the yoga of Śiva. (15)
May Dhruva and the others, who are true to their vows, and Indra and the others, who are established in heaven, be satisfied with joyful minds and accept this bali offering. 16.
One should utter the three *tāra*s (oṃ), then the pair *dehi*, then the word *devī*.
Then [one says] *putrāya baṭukanāthāya*, followed by *ucchiṣṭahāriṇe*.
After that, the word *sarvavighnān*, and likewise the pair *nāśaya*. (17)
"Take, take" (gṛhṇa-yugmam), followed by the word "ruru" and then the word "kṣetrapāla.
Then one should say: "Accept this worship along with all the ritual offerings (sarvopacāra) and the bali-offering.
"Take, take," ending with the syllable *svāhā* (dviṭha)—this, O Dear One, is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla. (18)
Consisting of sixty-four syllables, he is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments.
He who dwells in this sacred field as a servant of the Kṣetrapāla—may he, being pleased by this offering of bali, grant me protection from all dangers. || 19 ||
One should utter the three *tāras*, the *tāra*, and the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda; preceded by *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ* in pairs, and [the words] "to the one presided over by Bhairava. (20)
After Akṣobhyānanda, the supreme bestower of heart's desires follows; then, having addressed the stage of Siddhārtha, there are two subsequent descents.

Next is the station of the Protector of the Field (kṣetrapāla), then the station of the Greatly Peaceful (mahāśānta); next is the station of Mother and Son (mātṛputra), and likewise the station of the Son of Good Family (kulaputra). || 22 ||
And in this [mantra], there is the word *siddhiputrapada*, followed by the word *sthānādhipapada*;
then there should be *grāmādhipataye* in this [mantra], and after that, *deśādhipataye*. || 23 ||
One should utter "Baṭukanātha," then the word "Devīputra," followed by the word "Meghanāda," and thereafter the word "Pracaṇḍogra. || 24 ||
After the word "Kapālī," one should utter the word "Bhīṣaṇa.
[Then] "to the Lord of All Obstacles" (sarvavighnādhipataye); one should utter "this offering" (imāṃ pūjāṃ) and "bali. || 25 ||

One should utter: "Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa, kurudvandva, mama dūrayayugmakam, jvalayuk-prajvalayugam, sarvavighnān! (Seize, seize! O pair of Kurus! Distantize my pair! O flaming one, pair of blazing ones! All obstacles! 26.
One should utter "kṣāṃ kṣaṃ" to destroy the pair [of obstacles], and afterwards say "buddhi".
Then, "kṣetrapālāya vauṣaṭ hrūṃ"—this is the mantra of one hundred and sixty syllables.

After that, one should utter the three *tāra*s (OM), followed by "Amuka Kṣetrapāla," "Rājarājeśvara," and "accept this worship and offering" (*imaṃ pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa*); this mantra, ending with two *svāhā*s, consists of twenty-eight syllables. || 28 ||
By this offering of bali, may the Lord, the King of the Kings of Kings, who is accompanied by the lineage of Vaṭu, be forever gracious to me. || 29 ||

O Mistress of the Kula, one should offer an oblation to the god Vaṭuka in the west, an oblation to the Yoginīs in the north, an oblation to the Bhūtas in the east, and to the Kṣetrapāla in the south; one should worship the Lord of the Kings of Kings in the center.
The offering for Baṭuka is prescribed with the thumb and the ring finger;
the offering for the Yoginīs is made with the index, middle, ring, and thumb fingers.
O beloved, the offering to the Bhūtas is said to be made with all the fingers;
the offering to the Kṣetrapāla should be made with the thumb and forefinger;
and that for the Lord of the Kings of Kings (Rājarājeśvara) should be made with the thumb and middle finger.
Having thus worshipped the *baṭuka*s and others, one should display the *kuladīpa*s (family lamps) made from slightly reddened fine flour,
measuring four finger-breadths in size.
One should prepare nine, seven, or five lamps shaped like hand-drums (ḍamaruka), triangular and very beautiful, which hold a karṣa of ghee.
Having unified the inner light and the outer light into those of immeasurable radiance, one should offer the family-lamps (kuladīpa) by waving them three times above the Goddess. || 35 ||
O Mistress of all wheels and wheel-lords, O Goddess of gods, O Soul of all things— O Goddess,
accept this *ārātrika* for my spiritual success.
Then, having displayed the family lamps (*kuladīpa*), one should perform the worship of Śakti.

Having caused one’s own consort or a hero-consort (vīraśakti) who has been initiated according to the path of the Guru to drink [the wine], one should partake of the drink; such is the certainty of the scripture. (37)
O Ambikā, one should perform the immediate consecration for an uninitiated woman by means of the ritual procedure for mantra-initiation; she becomes pure in no other way.
Therefore, having worshipped the auspicious Śakti with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, regarding her as the deity itself, one should offer the vessel of enjoyments. (39)
At the conclusion of that, having honored the maidens and the charming women with the thought that they are deities, one should give the vessel individually to each.
But he who consumes the family substance (kuladravya) without first offering it to Śakti—his worship is fruitless, and the deity does not become pleased with him. 41.
The Caṇḍālī, the Carmakārī, the Mātaṅgī, the Pukkasi, the Śvapacī, the Khaṭṭakī, and the Kaivarttī—these are the women of the world. || 42 ||
This is declared to be the group of eight families; now the group of eight non-families (akula) is described:
the ball-maker, the vintner, the one who lives by weapons, and the dyer. (43)
The female singer, the washerwoman, the artisan, and the weaver as the eighth— these,
endowed with the tantras and mantras, are observers of the conduct of the samaya.
A maiden, one established in her vow, or even one who bears the *yogamudrā*—
if she arrives spontaneously at the time of worship, she should be known by the wise as the *sahajā*.
In the absence of a woman of the aforementioned caste, one should worship a woman from any of the four castes—one who is beautiful, youthful, tranquil, endowed with noble conduct, and pure. (46)
Free from doubt, endowed with devotion, modest, subsisting on the scriptures, free from greed, virtuous, smiling-faced, and speaking kindly. (47)
Devoted to the Guru and the deity, pure, and fond of the Kaulika path;
free from envy, possessing specialized knowledge, and eager in the worship of the deity; captivating, of virtuous conduct—this is the Śakti endowed with auspicious marks. (48)
She was wicked, fierce, harsh, cruel, miserable, a defiler of her family, ill-behaved, dependent on others, fearful, greedy, afflicted, and lazy. (49)
One who is addicted to sleep, extremely dull-witted, deficient in limbs, afflicted by disease, foul-smelling, contemptible, foolish, aged, insane, or a traitor of secrets.

One should exclude from the sacrifice such a female practitioner who is characterized by fallacious reasoning, loathsome speech, shamelessness, and a fondness for quarreling; who is deformed, follows the wrong path, is stubborn, and has a face like that of a cripple, a blind person, or one with a distorted countenance—even if she is joined with the mantra and possesses power. (51)
Then, preceded by the mantra-water, the practitioner of mantras should offer all the worship and other rites to the Goddess from this point on, beginning with the eastern direction, using the mantra.
Prior to this, there are the three *tāras*; after that, *prāṇa* and *buddhi*;
[these exist] according to the authority of the body and its attributes throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
One should speak of that Supreme with the mind, the intellect, speech, and action;
then with the two hands, then with the two feet, and thereafter with the belly. (54)
"Whatever has been remembered later regarding the penis, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done—one should say at the end, 'May all that be drunk by me along with the Guru.
O Dear One, this mantra ending in 'svāhā' is said to consist of seventy-three syllables. (55)
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly, O Śivā, whatever is performed by me—knowing that all this is your own work, please forgive me. (56)
Having thus made this prayer, O Goddess of the Gods, and having praised and bowed with devotion,
one should worship the retinue within the form of the principal deity.
In this manner, one should meditate upon the Goddess, together with her enclosures, within the lotus of one's own heart.
Having offered it to Śeṣikā, one should purify it with one's own root mantra.
First is Vāgbhava, then Hṛdaya, followed by Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī. (58)
"O Mātaṅgī, bring everything under my control!"—this is declared to be the Śeṣikā mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables. || 59 ||
With this mantra, one should offer the remains of the floral offerings (*nirmālya*) to Śeṣikā;
one should meditate upon the Goddess Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī, the enchantress of the three worlds. (60)
She is devoted to the diversion of lute-playing and song, radiant in her blue silken garment;
she has lips like the *bimba* fruit and feet moist with fresh lac-dye; her tresses and locks are disheveled;
her limbs are soft; she wears white conch-shell earrings and is resplendent with ornaments of rubies.
I bow to Mātaṅgī, the goddess with a beautiful smile, who is dark as a parrot.
Then, having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should offer it together with its companion to the one who is the embodiment of the venerable Guru and is Paraśiva himself.
One should perform worship together with heroes who belong to one's own tradition;
having performed mutual salutations, one should drink [the nectar] with their permission.
Having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the mudrā with the right,
one should take it up with the second hand according to the rule while reciting the mantra.

One should purify the three aspects of one's own body by means of the triad: flesh in the measure of a *māṣa*, a substance in the measure of a handful (*culluka*), and the reality (*tattva*). || 65 ||
O Dear One, filled with youthful joy and possessing a serene face and eyes,
the Guru, having summoned his disciples, should bestow the three principles (tattvas).
Having taken the disciple’s offering— flowers and so forth— the pure-souled one, free from stinginess regarding wealth, should then present it according to his ability.
Having prostrated with the eight limbs outside, O beloved, and having entered slowly within,
one should devotedly offer a gift to Śiva in the form of the Guru.
Having joined the two hands with the thumbs interlaced and the tips of the index fingers touching,
and having gone to the ground with both knees, one should prostrate before the guru with the five limbs.
Having touched the extended right hand with the left thumb and ring finger, with a purified heart and head slightly bowed; || 70 ||
O Dear One, with his left thumb and ring finger, the venerable Guru [bestows] upon the disciple, O Dear One, by means of the twenty-four elements beginning with Prakṛti and ending with Earth. (71)
O Kuleśvarī, one should purify the gross body by means of the vowels, the impure principles, and the Ātmatattva joined with the Vāgbhava [syllable]. || 72 ||

The knower of mantras should purify the subtle body by means of the seven principles beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣa*, which are both pure and impure; and by means of the principles called *sparśa*, the phonemes, and the *vidyātattva* joined with the *kāmarāja*. (73)
With the pure, all-pervading five principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā, and with the Supreme Śiva-principle, one should thoroughly purify the supreme body. (74)
O Dear One, with the Mālinī consisting of thirty-six principles,
one should purify all the principles by means of the seed-syllable which is the support of all principles.
The Guru should give the command "Purify" and the vessel containing the *amṛta* along with its companion.
Reciting "I purify," the disciple, bowing with devotion, should drink the *amṛta* three times silently from the handful offered by the Guru. (76)
One should touch the body with both hands while reciting all the essential mantras;
one should contemplate the body as pure, from the head down to the feet. (77)
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) extends up to the gross (sthūla); the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) has the subtle (sūkṣma) as its range;
and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) extends up to the supreme (parā). Thus, the universe consists of these three principles.
"Having thus learned from the Guru the knowledge of the three principles, he who practices it shall be liberated even while living; so it was spoken by Śaṅkara. (79)
Then, having accepted [the remainder] from the disciples, the Guru shall become the giver of the remnant (śeṣada).
Having taken what was given by the Guru, one should drink it together with the consort.
O Mistress of the Kula, it is the determination of the scriptures that one should not drink liquor while seated in the presence of the venerable Guru, elders, or those worthy of worship. 81.

He who practices without understanding the characteristics of the division of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the manifestation of their fruits, the prostration, and their stability, shall become a vessel for calamities. (82)
One should not drink liquor without a mantra; an expiation is prescribed for doing so.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, it must be performed according to the ritual injunctions of the mantras. 83.
I drink this purifying nectar, the medicine for existence, proclaimed by Bhairava, which is the cause for severing the bonds of the individual soul. 84.
Because the essence of sovereignty resides in the mind, and because the self consists of that bliss,
and because all entities are composed of that [bliss], all entities are contained within the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
For the sake of expansion up to the end of the Suṣumnā, the nectar (sura) is drunk by him;
therefore, I, being full, drink you, this goddess Sura. (86)
O Goddess of the Gods, the knower of mantras, with an undisturbed mind, should slowly and gradually perform the drinking of the nectar using this root mantra. (87)

One should offer the substance accompanied by the mantra into that which resides in the triangle at the root of one's own self, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, and having the nature of consciousness in the form of Kuṇḍalī.
This supreme nectar, filling the great vessel,
is characterized by the acceptance of the oblation in the fire consisting of supreme subjectivity (parāhaṃtā).

One should contemplate with the intellect the identity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra until the state of intense spiritual exaltation is reached; according to the instruction, one should drink the honey [of realization].
The churning is said to bestow success, the lamp is the giver of knowledge, and from drinking comes the attainment of the supreme state; thus is the triad described in the Kaula tradition.
Poison at the end of a meal, and food at the end of liquor—liquor is like poison;
one should know that food which is accompanied by wine is nectar. 92.
O beloved, drinking accompanied by chewing is said to be nectar;
drinking without chewing merely increases poison. (93)
Drink is said to be of three kinds, according to the sequence of the divine (divya), the heroic (vīra), and the animal (paśu).
Divine drinking is that which takes place in the presence of the Goddess; heroic drinking is that performed upon the seat of the mudrā. (94)
That which is drunk according to one's own will like a beast is called "beastly drinking" (paśupāna). || 95 ||
O Dear One, the divine drinking of the hero (vīrapāna) bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the drinking of the beast (paśupāna) is said to result in hell; such is the fruit of drinking. 96.
As long as there is no delusion regarding the view, mind, speech, and body, one should consume the drink; beyond this is the drinking of the animal (paśu). || 97 ||
As long as there is no impairment of the senses and no disfigurement of the face, for that long one may drink liquor; otherwise, downfall occurs. (98)
O Goddess, drinking is prescribed for those who are endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
Having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should remember the root mantra and the pādukā;
drinking the substance up to the throat, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (99)
Having drunk again and again, drinking until one falls to the ground, and rising once more to drink, there is no further rebirth. || 100 ||
The Goddess is satisfied by the bliss, Bhairava himself by the fainting, and all the gods by the vomiting; therefore, one should perform these three.
The bliss that belongs to the noble yogis who delight in divine drink does not exist even for a sovereign king. 102.
O fair-faced one, that happiness which belongs to those devoted to their family through the enjoyment of family assets—that very happiness shall indeed be liberation; this is the truth. (103)
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have briefly described to you something of the worship of Vaṭu, Śakti, and the others. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of Baṭuka, Śakti, and Others," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, containing one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, concerning the gateway to the liberation of Nirvāṇa. Chapter Seven.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said: O Lord of Kula, ocean of the nectar of compassion, I desire to hear [this].
O Lord of Gods, [I shall describe] the different types of ecstatic joy (ullāsa-bheda) and the gathering of ritual substances, vessels, and so forth. || 1 ||
O Supreme Lord, tell me the time for the departure of Rati, the very abiding of the Śrīcakra, and the activity of the Kaulika Śaktis.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, a divine disposition arises. (3)
The beginning, the youthful, the adolescent, the mature, its end, the state beyond the mind, and then the seventh, which is the outpouring (ullāsa). || 4 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, the undertaking is said to consist of the three principles;
O Mother, the youthful effulgence has been described, and youth is bliss.
When there is a perfect blossoming of the mind, a firm stability toward the beloved,
and yet occasional lapses in sight, thought, and speech, it is called "mature" (prauḍha).
In the wheel intent upon intense radiance, one who desires the union of vessels (pātramelana) should never, at any time, bring about a premature or excessive radiance;
rather, even therein, the union of vessels should be performed according to one's qualification.

One should not form associations with those who are uninitiated, who lack proper conduct, who do not know the tantras or the deities, who are detractors, or who have fallen from their commitments (samaya).

One should not form an association with those who consider themselves possessors of supernormal knowledge, who uphold the vows of conceptual proliferation, who are like cattle, and who are established in trivial rites.
One should not form an association with those who hate women, those cursed by their gurus, those devoid of devotion, the wicked-souled, or those lacking noble lineage and traditional instruction.

One should completely avoid the company of those who, though they may be knowers of grammar, logic, and epistemology, and understanders of the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti, are nevertheless ignorant of the duties of their own lineage. || 11 ||
Even if they are born of noble lineage, elderly, and possessed of good conduct,
if they are averse to your worship, one should abandon association with them.
O Pārvatī, O beloved, one should avoid the company of women, sons, friends, and kinsmen, even if they are affectionate, if they are ignorant of the traditional conduct of their lineage. 13.
And one should not form a connection with goods from those who have not been seen personally, who reside in another country, and who lack a formal agreement. 14.
One should not use a single vessel even if it belongs directly to the Lord of the Family;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step. (15)
And one should not offer the substance remaining in one's own vessel to Bhairava;
if one were to offer it, O Mistress of the Kula, one would incur the curse of the deity.
One should never share a seat, food, vessel, clothing, bed, or similar items with those who are ignorant or unworthy. || 17 ||
Alternatively, the Kaulika may perform the union of the vessels according to the division of the currents:
by unifying the east with the south, and likewise the north with the west. || 18 ||

In that [mandala], one should perform that worship with heroes who are devoted to sequential worship and are similar to oneself, as well as with beloved women, at the fourfold confluence of the streams.
O Dear One, one should drink the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) offered by yogins and yoginīs, which has been consecrated with the root mantra of one's own mother’s sandals.
O Goddess, having received a vessel of honey obtained by chance at some time, one should take it with devotion, recite the mantra as before, and drink it while remembering the Guru. 21.
O Pārvatī, one should eat the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) of the Guru, the Śakti, and the sons; of the elder and younger brothers of the Guru; and also of one’s own elder brother, but not of anyone else.
One should drink the substance that is the Śakti’s leavings and chew that which is the Hero’s leavings.
One must not give one’s own leavings, nor should one consume what belongs to another. (23)
One may eat the leavings of women, but one should not offer leavings to them;
even within the center of the Cakra, O Goddess of Gods, otherwise there will be a fall.
O Ambikā, one should give the remnants of food to one's own junior disciples;
he who gives them out of affection to others shall become a vessel for calamities.
But whoever, out of delusion, affection, greed, or even fear, takes up a vessel containing the remnants of the *āsava*, shall incur the curse of the deity. (26)
O Kuleśānī, when the intense joy has arisen, one should perform the dismissal of the bali offering;
one should do so outside the worship chamber, or within the house in a triangular area.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should meditate upon Ucchiṣṭabhairava—three-eyed, holding a mace, a trident, a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and a vessel in his hands;
one should meditate upon Bhairava, who is dark-hued and the dispeller of all obstacles. (28)
Having uttered the three *tāra*s, one should thereafter recite *ucchiṣṭabhairava*,
followed by the pair *ehi*, the pair *baliṃ gṛhṇa*, and *phaṭ* ending with *dviṭha*.
This is the mantra for the dismissal of the bali offering, consisting of twenty-two syllables;
thereafter, one should recite the Peace Hymn (śāntistava) and offer libations with drops of honey.
The goddesses worship the lotus-feet of Hara,
which bestow the nectar of liberation through their gracious splendor,
and which awaken one to the essence of infinite philosophical systems.
And I bow to the host of the sixty-four yoginīs. || 31 ||
I bow my head to the Lord Bhairava, the beloved of Bhairavī, who stands in the midst of the circle of Yoginīs and is surrounded by the mandala of Mothers. 32.
Homage to the illustrious Lord-Physician, who alone destroys the darkness of beginningless and terrible saṃsāra, and who provides the medicine for the kula.
May all those calamities, misfortunes, and diseases resulting from the transgression of conventional conduct be dispelled by the union with the divine wheel. (34)
May there be long life, health, sovereignty, fame, gain, happiness, and victory; may there be enchanting beauty, and may all the deities protect [us]. (35)
For those who worship and protect the lords of ascetics,
the lords of yogis, and those whose wealth is penance—
for them, as well as for the country, the kingdom, the family, and the king.
May the Blessed One, the Lord of the Family, grant peace. || 36 ||
May those who reveal the non-duality of the assembly of practitioners rejoice;
may those who reside upon the lion-throne and belong to the great Śākta lineage rejoice; and may those others who are devoted to all the Kula and Kaula traditions rejoice.
And others who are distinguished by various specific terms belonging to the Śāmbhava [tradition]. || 37 ||
May the Siddha-gurus rejoice— those who know that lineage, the elders of the tradition, the initiates, the young men, and the maidens—
who were born into the noble family of the Yoginīs and Heroes.
May the lords of the earth, cows, the twice-born, and the virtuous rejoice! || 38 ||
