Just as one protects wealth, grain, and so forth from thieves, O beloved, so too, O Goddess, should one thoroughly protect the family dharma from those who are uninitiated (paśus). 82.
Internally a Kaula, externally a Śaiva, and among the people a Vaiṣṇava—
one should well conceal the Kaula doctrine, O Goddess, like the water inside a coconut fruit.
One should always and with great effort conceal all things, such as family secrets and the like, in every situation, just as one would hide the pregnancy of a mother’s lover.
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are as manifest as courtesans;
but this knowledge of Śambhu is hidden like a woman of noble family.
The deities favor those who observe the well-guarded Kaulika conduct;
they bestow the fulfillment of their desires and destroy those who reveal [the secrets]. 86.
Those who know the Kula scriptures, who are devoted to the Kula worship,
and who serve you in secret, they abide in your presence.
The wise one should reveal the guru, but he should guard the mantra with effort;
through revealing what should not be revealed, both prosperity and lifespan are destroyed. (88)
One who has fallen away from all proper conduct should take refuge in the conduct of his own family;
one who has fallen away from the conduct of his family shall go to the Raurava hell.
In the scriptures, a means of expiation is seen even for those who have committed the great sins;
but for one who has fallen from his lineage, O Goddess of Gods, no expiation is seen anywhere.
O beloved, for that great sinner who, relying on the family dharma, does not maintain proper conduct and acts according to his own whims— 91.
Calamities, misfortune, diseases, poverty, strife, fear, the wrath of the Yoginīs, and stumbling at every step—[all these arise]. (92)
Falling away and utterly ruined, deprived of luster and exceedingly foolish,
censured by all and hated by everyone, agitated and abandoned by his associates, he wanders from country to country, and his undertakings always meet with failure. (93)
Even there, the Śākinīs who abide on the path of the Kula and protect the Kula will devour them first; for a boon was granted to them by me alone.
Therefore, O Goddess, one who possesses proper conduct shall be dear to the Yoginīs;
those lacking in conduct destroy the four Vedas, O Mistress of the Kula. (95)
Those who know the essence of the sandals alone and are restrained by right conduct attain divinity through that right conduct— the union of Yoginīs and Vīras;
whereas Kaulikas, by the opposite of this, fall into the state of animals.
This Kaula system is perfected through the Command; it perishes through improper conduct.
Through the observance of proper conduct, truly, the perfection of the Command will come to pass. || 97 ||
Neither consecration, nor mantra, nor the study of scriptures and the like is the cause of the Kula-dharma; O Mistress of the Kula, it is right conduct alone.

He who knows the supreme impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding the Śrīpādukā, the three principles (*tattva*), conduct (*ācāra*), and so forth, shall be a *samayin*, a *kaulika*, and also a *śāmbhava*. (99)
O Goddess, one is not a Kaulika as long as one has not been made a Samayin;
upon the fall of the body, liberation occurs through the observance of the conduct of the Samaya.
O Goddess, due to being devoid of ritual refinement, by transgressing the words of the Guru, and by abandoning proper conduct, a Kaulika becomes fallen. (101)

The constant and occasional rites, the ritual substances, and the loss of mantras, yantras, and so forth, as well as the occurrence of improper contact with unworthy persons (paśus) and the confusion of mantras; || 102 ||
O Dear One, regarding these and other such faults—whether committed secretly or openly, and whether produced by knowledge or ignorance—the gravity or lightness of the sin [must be determined]. (103)
Having correctly ascertained the place, time, age, and wealth according to the prescribed rule, the preceptor shall grant the penance for the purification of all sins. (104)
The disciple should also perform the expiation prescribed by the guru;
alternatively, the chanting of the guru’s name is remembered as the remedy for all sins. (105)
Just as the impurity of Jāmbūnada gold is purified by fire, one should burn away the defilement of improper conduct with the fire of penance. 106.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to the secret, O Pārvatī:
the conduct of all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life bestows a happy state.
O Mistress of the Kula, the Guru should explain the conduct three times;
if the disciple does not accept it, then no sin accrues to the Guru.
Just as the fault of a minister reaches the king, and the fault of a wife reaches the husband,
so too, O beloved, the sin of a disciple undoubtedly reaches the teacher.
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have told you something in brief regarding the ritual procedure of the Kula conduct, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear? 110.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Kula Conduct," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, which contains one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses and concerns the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said: "O Lord of Kula, I desire to hear the characteristics of devotion to the Pādukā."
O Lord of Gods, O ocean of compassion, please tell me also about the proper conduct (ācāra). || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, O Lord of Creatures, devotion arises swiftly.
The Vāgbhava [syllable] is at the root-circle, wherein the threads and other elements are swallowed;
thus, in the Kulārṇava, knowledge is established within the Pādukā.

Recollection of the venerable *śrīpādukā* is superior to ten million times ten million great gifts, to ten million times ten million great vows, and to ten million times ten million great sacrifices. (4)
O Goddess, the remembrance of the supreme Śrīpādukā is superior to the recitation of ten million mantras, to bathing at ten million sacred fords, and to the worship of ten million deities.
In great disease, in great calamity, in great fault, in great fear,
in great adversity, and in great sin— the *pādukā* remembered protects [one].
In misconduct, in foul speech, in evil association, in improper acceptance,
and in both misconduct and evil intent— the sandals are remembered as providing protection.
By him has been studied, remembered, known, sacrificed for, given, and honored;
for him whose remembrance of the Śrīpāduka is always upon the tip of his tongue.
O Goddess, whoever recites the Śrīpādukā mantra even once with devotion becomes free from all sins and attains the supreme goal. || 9 ||
Whether pure or impure, he who remembers the sandals with devotion attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa without effort. 10.
O Dear One, one should daily offer salutations with devotion toward that direction in which the lotus feet of Śrīnātha shine.
There is no mantra superior to the Pādukā-mantra, and no deity superior to the Śrī-guru;
there is no initiation higher than the Śākta, and no merit greater than the worship of the Kula.
The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of mantra is the word of the Guru; and the root of liberation is the grace of the Guru.

O Mistress of the Kula, all ritual actions in this world have their root in the Guru; therefore, for the sake of attaining perfection, he should always be served with devotion by those endowed with faith. (14)
Fear, grief, greed, delusion, confusion, and the like persist only so long as one does not seek refuge in the glorious Guru, who is affectionate toward his devotees. (15)
O Goddess of the gods, embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, defiled by all manner of suffering, for as long as they lack devotion toward a true guru. 16.
The mantra, endowed with the fruit of all accomplishments, becomes pure and auspicious;
this great sequence of the supreme reality has its root in the grace of the Guru. || 17 ||
Just as he grants boons when he is satisfied, pleased, and favorable toward the mantra, so should one diligently satisfy the guru with devotion, wealth, and even one's life. 18.
When the supreme teacher bestows his own self upon his disciple, then the disciple becomes liberated; thereafter, there is no further rebirth. || 19 ||
The disciple should continue to propitiate [the guru] until he becomes pleased;
when the guru is pleased, the disciple’s sins are instantly destroyed. || 20 ||
Whatever desires those who live in dependence do not even long for in their minds,
their masters— who are affectionate toward their devotees— fulfill them all.
When the Guru is satisfied, there is no doubt that the deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the sages and yogis, become pleased and bestow their grace.
The disciple who is instructed by a compassionate Guru pleased by his devotion shall be liberated from karma and become a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The disciple should likewise act in such a way that the Guru is satisfied; and thus gratified, O Goddess of Gods, he should do what is pleasing through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (24)
But if a teacher, being pleased, should command his own disciple anywhere, "You are liberated," then he too shall attain liberation, O Dear One. (25)
Alternatively, by means of some state free from conceptual proliferation, the Lord effects the liberation of bound souls from their fetters through the form of a Guru.
Neither one who has mastered the four Vedas nor even a dog-eater is dear to me if he is not my devotee;
to him [the devotee] gifts should be given and from him they should be accepted, for he is to be honored just as I am.
If a Brahmin, though endowed with the six qualities, is devoid of devotion, he is not praised;
even a Mleccha, though lacking in qualities, is called a disciple if he possesses devotion. (28)
For one devoid of devotion to the guru, austerity, knowledge, lineage, and vows—all perish right there; even their ornamentation is merely for the sake of pleasing the world. (29)

One whose impurities of evil intellect have been thoroughly burnt away by the fire of devotion to the Guru is worthy of honor by others even if he be an outcaste; but a learned man who is an atheist is not so honored.
O Goddess, for one whose devotion to the venerable Guru is always steadfast through all goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and even mokṣa itself—is held in the palm of his hand. (31)
"He is Śiva, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon me in the form of my guru"—for him who remembers this with devotion, success is not far off. (32)
O Mistress of the Kula, for one who has supreme devotion toward the God, and toward the Guru as toward the God, the meanings explained by you indeed become manifest.
O Great Goddess, just as devotion is to be shown toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, one’s parents, and the king, so too must it be shown toward one’s own guru.
One should contemplate Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, Girijā and Śiva, as well as the venerable Guru, the wife of the Guru, and one's own parents. (35)
O Goddess, beloved, all perfections are attained through devotion to the Guru in a manner that cannot be achieved by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, pilgrimages, vows, and the like. (36)
O Mistress of the Kula, just as unwavering devotion toward the venerable Guru increases, so too does his realized knowledge increase. (37)
What is the use of visiting sacred fords and other such great hardships, or of vows that wither the body? O Goddess of Gods, this sincere service to the true Guru is indeed true devotion. (38)
O Goddess, whatever fruit is obtained through great physical hardship or even through intense austerity, that same fruit one obtains easily by serving one's guru. (39)

O Goddess, for those seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation, and for those desiring the stations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, devotion to the Guru alone is the path; there is no other, so says the Śruti. (40)
And in an instant, devotion burns away inauspicious deeds and those born of great sins, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. (41)
Salutations to that Trustworthy One, the bestower of all accomplishments,
by whom clay, wood, and stone bear fruit that is not fruitless.
Neither yoga, nor austerity, nor any sequence of ritual worship dissolves away;
in this illusion-free path of the Kula, devotion alone is preeminent. (43)
O Goddess, since the entire interior of the world is directly composed of the Guru, in what field of those possessed of devotion would a mantra not be successful? (44)
One who perceives the teacher as a mere human being, the mantra as a mere collection of syllables, and the images as mere stone shall go to hell. (45)
One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; for if one were to perceive him so, there would never be success through mantras or through the worship of deities.
O Dear One, for those who remember or speak of the Śrī Guru together with common worldly people, all their merit indeed becomes sin.
For parents, being the causes of one's birth, should be honored with great effort;
but the teacher, who reveals what is dharma and what is adharma, is especially worthy of worship. || 48 ||
The Guru is the father, the Guru is the mother, and the Guru is the god Maheśvara.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Indeed, that which is received from the Guru must be performed through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
O Goddess, by practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement.
Those who deceive the glorious Guru by means of their body, wealth, and life-breaths, undoubtedly attain the state of worms, insects, and moths. (51)
From abandoning the mantra, death occurs; from abandoning the guru, poverty results;
and from abandoning both the guru and the mantra, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
One should sustain the body for the sake of the guru; one should acquire wealth for his sake.
Even by sacrificing one's own life, one should carry out the guru’s work.
One should contemplate the harsh words spoken by the guru as a blessing;
even when struck by him, one should remember it as his grace. (54)
O Mistress of the Kula, one should offer all objects to be enjoyed and consumed to the Guru; considering them as his remnants, one should then partake of them. 55.
One should not perform austerities, nor observe fasts, vows, and the like, in the presence of the Guru;
one should not undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites, nor bathe for the sake of personal purification.

One should never cause separation from the guru, nor should one ever address him as "you" (yuṣmad). Having become a disciple, one should by no means engage in lending or receiving money, nor in the buying or selling of goods, together with the gurus. (57)
O Goddess, one should not engage in debate with nihilists, nor even converse with them;
having seen them from afar, one should depart, and never sit together with them anywhere.
O Ambikā, he who worships another while the Guru is present goes to a terrible hell; that worship shall become fruitless.
One who bears the lotus feet of the Guru should not carry a burden on his own head;
rather, everything must be done by the Guru’s command, for the Guru is traditionally remembered as being the very embodiment of the command.
Whatever one has heard elsewhere regarding the mantras, āgamas, and so forth, one should report that to [the teacher];
one should receive it by the command of the guru and avoid what is forbidden. || 61 ||
One should not speak of the secret meaning taught in one's own scripture to just anyone;
if one should speak it, there is no doubt that he has fallen from his commitment (samaya).
One should constantly contemplate non-duality and never duality with the Guru;
O Mistress of the Kula, one should act for the benefit of all beings as if they were oneself. 63.
Service, O Goddess, is fourfold according to the presence of one's own purpose and mental disposition. With such service and with a focused mind, the disciple should satisfy the guru. (64)
He who is devoted to the service of his guru, the gods, and great-souled beings, undoubtedly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step. (65)
O beloved, service to the guru alone brings about your grace;
if it is accompanied by true devotion, it bestows the fruit of all desires.
O beloved, through service to the Guru, all sins are destroyed, heaps of merit increase, and all undertakings reach fulfillment.
Whatever object is beneficial to oneself, one should employ that very thing for the benefit [of others];
as for one who worships the Guru and the Devas, their merit cannot be calculated.
Whatever is performed with devotion according to one's means for the sake of the Guru—whether it be small or great—the merit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor. (69)
Even if a disciple were to give away all his possessions to the guru while devoid of devotion, he does not obtain the fruit; for devotion alone is the cause.
One should not experience that substance for which the guru has a longing;
however, if there is an unavoidable desire, one should experience it only by his command.
He who, out of greed or delusion, lives off even half a sesame seed or half of that as his teacher’s property, shall be cooked in the twenty-one hells.
O beloved, he who takes even a very small amount of a guru’s property without it being given becomes an animal and is devoured by carnivorous creatures.
One who covets the property of a guru and is eager to approach the wife of a guru—for such a fallen *kṣullaka*, no expiation exists. (74)
Disobedience of commands, misappropriation of wealth, and acting unfavorably toward the guru—these they call "offense against the guru"; he who commits such acts is a sinner. (75)
One should not employ one's own wealth without first offering it to the Guru;
for he who acts without having offered it becomes a slayer of Brahman. || 76 ||
He who destroys the station of the guru, the tradition, or its dharma, should be expelled by the gurus; he is to be punished and even put to death by the executioners.
From angering the guru comes destruction; from betraying the guru comes sin. From reviling the guru comes untimely death; from doing what is harmful to the guru come great calamities.
A man who has committed no offense against his guru may live even if he has entered fire, or drunk poison, or even fallen into the hands of death.
O Ambika, wherever there may be censure of the venerable Guru, one should cover one's ears and immediately depart from that place so as not to hear it again;
thereafter, one should remember the name of the Guru— this is the remedy for hearing such things.
One should not show contempt toward teachers, friends, companions, female servants, male servants, and others;
nor should one revile his commitments (samayas) or the Vedas, scriptures, Āgamas, and so forth. 81.
Adorning the sandals of the Guru, remembering the name of the Guru, and the recitation [of mantras];
carrying out the commands of the Guru is one's duty, as is service and devotion to the Guru. (82)
Desiring to enter the abode of the Guide with a tranquil mind and great devotion,
one should discard vehicles, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, fans, and the like,
as well as betel, collyrium, and [fine] attire, and enter slowly.
Upon seeing the sandals, the seat, the garment, the vehicle, the parasol, or the fly-whisk of the guru, one should offer salutation; one should not desire them for one's own enjoyment.
Washing the feet, bathing, anointing with oil, cleaning the teeth, urination, spitting, shaving, lying down, and sexual intercourse with women; || 85 ||
The heroic posture (vīrāsana), harsh speech, instruction, laughter, and weeping;
the loosening of hair, the turban, the bodice, and likewise nakedness. || 86 ||
O beloved, [these include] stretching out the feet, debate, quarreling, finding fault, contorting the limbs, playing with the body as an instrument, clapping the hands, and shaking [the limbs]. (87)

O Ambikā, one should not engage in gambling, curiosity, wrestling, combat, dancing, and the like, nor travel to the seats (pīṭhas), sacred fields (kṣetras), and hermitages (āśramas) of the gurus, yogins, and great siddhas; if one should so act out of delusion, one shall incur the curse of the deity.
One should remain in attendance before the guru with respectful demeanor; one should not enter [his presence] without his consent.
One should serve him while looking at his face and should practice exactly what he has said. (89)
O beloved, one should not show indifference toward tasks whether commanded or unspoken by the Guru;
whatever the Guru says with his head [as a gesture of command], that should be performed without hesitation.
Whether in punishment or in favor, the Guru is the cause of everything;
whatever has issued from the mouth of the Guru is called the entire scripture. 91.
O beloved, even if he is himself capable of performing the guru’s work, he should not send another;
for even if he is accompanied by many servants, he should remain exceedingly devoted.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, reciting, offering oblations, or performing worship,
one should carry out only the command of the Guru with an inner self that has gone unto him.
One should not harbor pride on account of birth, learning, wealth, and so forth;
a disciple should always and constantly serve in the presence of his preceptor. 94.
Having abandoned desire and anger, disciplined, humble, and full of devotion, O Goddess, he should remain on a seat of earth and perform the service of the Guru. 95.
Whether it be his own business or the business of another, a disciple who knows the mind of his guru should remain humble and cheerful of countenance when in the presence of his guru. || 96 ||
If one should perform that which is prohibited in general while in the presence of the Guru,
the fault for all of it shall become ten millionfold.
He who, turning his face away, disregards the words of his guru and does not listen—
whether they be beneficial or even harmful— shall go to the Raurava hell.
Whatever sin one may incur by killing a cow or a Brahmin, that same sin one incurs by speaking untruth in the presence of a guru. 99.

Even when the teacher has gone elsewhere, or is in distress, or situated in a difficult situation, one should never abandon the venerable guru; rather, O beloved, one should proceed only as directed by him.
When the guru is seated below, one should never remain above him;
one should not walk in front of him, nor stand when the guru has risen.
One should not step over the shadow of the Śakti, the shadow of a deity, or the shadow of the Guru;
one should not cast one's own shadow upon them, nor should one sleep in the presence of the Guru. 102.
One should not engage in speaking, teaching, singing, eating, sleeping, or similar activities unless commanded, nor should one do so without first performing a salutation.
By fulfilling the command of the guru, one may even commit a hundred murders of Brahmins;
without the guru’s command, a disciple should not place his trust in any other instruction. 104.
One should perform everything according to the guru's command and must not disparage his wife, O beloved;
having bowed with devotion, one should rise with palms joined in reverence, O beloved. (105)
One should depart from the teacher's house by the rear door after having paid homage;
one should not sit on the same seat as the teacher or those equal to him.

O Goddess, one should not sit upon a seat in the presence of a deity or a guru. A lion-throne should be offered to the guru; the best seat to the elders; a lower seat to the juniors; and an equal seat to others. || 107 ||
Whether he be noble by birth or enriched with learning and wealth, upon seeing his guru from afar,
he should joyfully perform a single prostration like a staff and circumambulate him three times.

Then, O Dear One, one should salute the *praguru* three, six, twelve, or even just once, according to the sequence beginning with the *jyeṣṭha* [guru], by means of the connection with the *gurupraguru*. 109.
Then he should bow to his guru, or else not disregard the guru’s command. In the presence of the supreme guru, the disciple should bow mentally to his own guru.

One should bow to every deity with the thought that they are the Guru, or as one would to a blade of grass; however, one should not bow to an image made of metal or clay with the thought that it is the deity itself.
One should offer three prostrations to the guru, one to the elders,
a salutation with joined palms to those worthy of honor, and likewise a verbal greeting to others.

O leader of the family, one should bow down to the gods, the gurus, the family preceptors, those advanced in knowledge, those whose wealth is austerity, those superior in learning, and those established in their own dharma. 113.

One should not bow down to one who hates women, one cursed by gurus, a heretic, a self-styled scholar, a rogue, one who follows forbidden occupations, an ungrateful person, or one who does not belong to any stage of life (āśrama).
He who eats without having first offered food to his guru, even if residing in the same village, that food becomes impure; upon death, he is born as a pig.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
a disciple residing within the distance of one *krośa* should bow to the guru every day.
A disciple who travels half a yojana should prostrate on the five festival days;
this applies starting from one yojana up to twelve yojanas.

O Dear One, for as many days or months as that number [of breaths], the disciple who resides in a distant land should prostrate before the illustrious Guru with devotion, having approached his presence.
In that regard, one should prostrate to the Guru once a month for every number of *yojanas* [of distance].
If the disciple has traveled a very great distance, he may go [to see the Guru] whenever he so desires. || 119 ||
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth according to one's ability. (120)
O Goddess, he who does not act in this manner shall become a Brahmarākṣasa.
The Guru’s Śakti and his son are [treated as] such; the elder brother is also traditionally considered a Guru. || 121 ||
One who knows the Self should protect his younger [disciple] like a son.

O Goddess of Gods, one should perform salutations to the family preceptor (kulācārya), to the elder and younger gurus, and to one who is like a guru, just as one would to one's own biological teacher. 122.
The eldest by sacrifice, the eldest by lineage, the third, the eldest by family, and the son of the eldest guru, O Goddess—thus is the group of four "eldests. (123)
Through the salutation of the eldest of sacrifices and by means of the sequential eight-limbed yoga, the Guru and the Kula-tree are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rule. (124)

Toward all those who belong to the highest category of worship—such as one's father, mother, and other kinsmen—one who remains unmanifest (unresponsive) by failing to rise, prostrate, and so forth, incurs blame externally. 125.
But when he manifests himself in the form of a teacher, then he becomes a partaker of fault [if one fails to show] rising to meet him, prostration, and so forth. (126)
He who, having become a master, shall offer salutation to his animals,
is called a "great beast" and shall incur the curse of the deities.
O Dear One, he who has attained the status of a Guru by the number of his sandals should be regarded as a Guru; he is to be saluted by the elders, not merely as a friend.
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have briefly described to you something of the characteristics of devotion to the sandals (pādukā). What more do you wish to hear? 129.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sandals," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, which contains one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses and serves as the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Kula, ocean of the nectar of compassion, I desire to hear [this].
O Lord of Gods, you should deign to explain the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the state of being a guru arises.
One born of a wicked lineage, wicked, devoid of virtues, deformed, a disciple of another, a heretic, a eunuch, and one who considers himself a scholar; || 3 ||
With limbs deficient, excessive, or deformed, and possessed of impaired members;
lame, blind, deaf, filthy, and afflicted by disease. (4)
O beloved, Durmukha has also been released; he assumes whatever appearance he desires at will, and his bodily movements, gait, speech, and gaze are difficult to imitate.

One who is possessed of sleep, lethargy, dullness, laziness, and vices such as gambling; whose body is always hidden behind doors, walls, pillars, and the like; who practices devotion inwardly while being base and devoid of outward devotion. (6)
One who speaks falsely, the stubborn, one who has gone abroad, a messenger, the deceitful,
one devoid of wealth, wife, or purity, and one habituated to forbidden acts— [these should be avoided].
Or one who reveals secrets, O Goddess, or one who destroys the task at hand; one who behaves like a cat or a crow, and is intent on seeking out faults.
One who is deceitful, ungrateful, one who gives secretly while hiding the inner intent, a betrayer of trust, a traitor to his master, and a doer of evil—(these should be avoided). || 9 ||
One who causes distrust, one who is of a doubting nature, one who desires success [by improper means], an assailant, one who seeks to seize, one who is provoked to anger, and a false witness.
O Goddess, he is a deceiver of all, possessed of the conceit of being superior to all, untruthful, addicted to cruelty, and one who speaks much of vulgar matters and the like. || 11 ||
One who indulges in difficult debates and fallacious reasoning, who is fond of quarreling, who makes groundless accusations, who is foolish, fickle, and a mocker with words; || 12 ||
One should know that a person who speaks ill behind one's back but speaks kindly in one's presence, who professes the sacred word with his voice yet is a thief, is a self-praiser. (13)
O Mother, he is intolerant of virtues, disrespectful, distressed, and wrathful;
he is loquacious, a friend to the wicked, and despised by all the world.

One who is slanderous, who torments others, who is devoid of affection and intimacy, who speaks of his own afflictions, who betrays his master, and who deceives himself—[one should avoid such a person]. 15.
O Goddess, he is devoted to his tongue and genitals, behaves like a thief, acts like a beast, and causes groundless hatred, laughter, affliction, anger, and the like. || 16 ||
One who tells excessive jokes, one who mocks the vital points [of others], one who is lustful and utterly shameless, and one who indicates false and wicked conduct; || 17 ||
It was joined with envy, intoxication, avarice, hypocrisy, and egoism;
it was filled with jealousy, harshness, malice, wretchedness, anger, and pride.
One who is lacking in fortitude, suffering, fearful, powerless, distressed, dull-witted, sluggish, deluded, agitated by anxiety, or a libertine; (19)
O beloved, he is possessed by craving and greed, wretched and discontented, a beggar for everything; he eats excessively, is deceitful, a deceiver, and crooked.
Devoid of devotion, faith, compassion, tranquility, and righteous conduct, he mocked his mother, father, teacher, and the wise words of the virtuous. || 21 ||

O Mistress of the Kula, the Guru should avoid a disciple who is loathsome on account of family wealth and the like, who is conceited regarding his service to the Guru, who hates women, who has fallen from the observances (samaya), and who is cursed by the Guru; indeed, one possessed of such evil qualities as these should be shunned.

O Mistress of the Family, [entrust] him to a true disciple who is endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of the practice of meditative absorption, and gifted with virtue and good character. || 23 ||
One who has a pure body and clothing, who is wise, righteous, and pure-minded, firm in his vows, of virtuous conduct, and endowed with faith and devotion. || 24 ||
One who is skillful, eats little, has a hidden mind, serves without guile, acts with deliberation, is heroic, and is free from the poverty of spirit. (25)
One who is highly skilled in all undertakings, pure, helpful to all, grateful, fearful of sin, and esteemed by the virtuous and the noble. || 26 ||
One who is a believer, virtuous in generosity, devoted to the welfare of all beings, endowed with trustworthiness and humility, and not a deceiver regarding wealth, body, and so forth— (27)
One who accomplishes the impossible, who is brave and endowed with the strength of perseverance, who is favorable, engaged in action, vigilant, and discerning; || 28 ||
Speech that is beneficial, truthful, measured, and smiling; free from faults; having its meaning grasped by a single utterance; and clever, expanding the intellect. (29)
O beloved, [I praise] one who is averse to self-praise and the disparagement of others, who has a gracious countenance,
has conquered the senses, is well-contented, wise, and observes celibacy.

Having abandoned mental anguish, physical disease, fickleness, suffering, delusion, and doubt, he was intent upon meditation on the Guru, praise, discourse, worship of the deity, and prostration. || 31 ||
One who is devoted to the Guru and the deity, a supreme worshiper of the Kāminī, always remaining in the presence of the Guru, and one who brings satisfaction to the Guru. || 32 ||
O Goddess, he who is constantly engaged in service through mind, speech, and body, who obeys the commands of the guru, and who proclaims the glory of the guru; || 33 ||

O Mistress of the Family, [entrust this] to one who knows the authority of the Guru’s words, who delights in service to the Guru, who follows the mind [of the Guru], and who performs his bidding. (34)

One who possesses noble birth yet is free from pride in wealth, who remains humble in the presence of the guru, who is indifferent toward the guru’s property, and who longs for the guru’s favor. || 35 ||

One who is devoted to the discourse on the family dharma (*kuladharma*), who is dear to the *yogins* and *yoginīs* of the *kaulika* tradition, who is intent upon the worship of the family (*kula*) and so forth, and who feels no disgust toward the substances of the family (*kuladravya*). || 36 ||

O Goddess, the Guru should accept as a disciple one who is endowed with such characteristics as being devoted to recitation, meditation, and so forth; who desires the path to liberation; who is fond of the Kula scriptures; and who turns his back on the scriptures of the fettered (paśu). || 37 ||
The venerable Guru, O Supreme Goddess, is dressed in pure garments, captivating to the mind, endowed with all auspicious marks, and beautiful in every limb. (38)
He knew the true meaning of all scriptures, was conversant with all mantras and their ritual procedures, could bewilder the world, and was as pleasing to behold as a god. || 39 ||
He has a pleasant countenance, is easy to approach, pure, and the destroyer of delusion and doubt;
he understands gestures and facial expressions, is wise, and is radiant with the knowledge of reasoning and refutation. || 40 ||
With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, he is omniscient and knows place and time;
he possesses the perfection of command, knows the three times, and is capable of both restraint and grace.
He is the piercer, the awakener, the peaceful one, devoted to compassion for all living beings, capable of mastering the sixfold group of the senses through the restraint of their movement. || 42 ||

Foremost among the assembly, exceedingly profound, a knower of the distinction between worthy and unworthy recipients, equal to Śiva and Viṣṇu, a saintly being who censures those of dull vision. || 43 ||
Stainless, eternally contented, independent, and possessed of the power of mantras; affectionate toward true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is full of smiles. (44)
He is fond of devotion, eternally generous, profound, and a practitioner of refined conduct;
he is ever eager to worship his chosen deity, his guru, his elders, and women. || 45 ||
Devoted to blameless actions— whether obligatory, occasional, or performed for desired ends—
he is free from passion, hatred, fear, affliction, hypocrisy, and egoism.
Devoted to the practice of his own knowledge, he is an acquirer of dharma and the other goals;
content with whatever comes by chance, he discerns between virtues and faults. || 47 ||
Unattached to women’s wealth and the like, as well as to evil associations and vices; entirely free from the sense of "I" (egoism), beyond the pairs of opposites, and firm in his vows. || 48 ||
For he is free from greed, impartial toward those who lack resolve, and discerning;
he does not sell wealth, learning, or the like, nor mantras, yantras, tantras, and so forth. || 49 ||

O Dear One, the venerable Guru is said to be endowed with such characteristics as being free from attachment, free from conceptual construction, having ascertained the ultimate reality, possessing supreme majesty, regarding praise and blame as equal, observing silence, being indifferent to worldly concerns, and being free from all affliction. (50)
O beloved, how can He be worshipped— he who is Śiva, all-pervading, subtle, beyond the mind (unmanā), partless, immutable, of the nature of space, unborn, and infinite?
For this very reason, O Goddess, Śiva himself has directly assumed the form of the Guru; when worshipped with devotion, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"I am Śiva, O Goddess, not a physical form, for I am not within the range of human vision;
therefore, in the form of the venerable Guru, He protects His meritorious disciples. (53)
Bound by human skin, Paraśiva himself wanders secretly upon the earth for the sake of bestowing grace upon worthy disciples. (54)
For the sake of protecting true devotees alone, Śiva—the formless one who assumes a form and the treasure-house of compassion—acts in the world like an ordinary transmigrating being. (55)
Having concealed my forehead-eye, the crescent moon, and my two arms,
I shall remain upon the earth in the form of a guru.
O beloved, it has been declared that Śiva is directly Atrinetra (the eye of Atri), Acyuta is directly the four-armed one, and the venerable Guru is Brahmā who does not possess four faces. 57.
O Bhavānī, in this world the glorious Guru is seen as a mere human by one of sinful deeds, but is seen as Śiva by one of meritorious deeds. (58)
Those of meager fortune do not behold the glorious Guru, the supreme reality, standing right before their eyes, just as the blind do not see the risen sun.
The Guru is Sadāśiva himself; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
If the Guru were not Śiva himself, who else could bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation? (60)
Pārvatī belongs to both Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Guru;
there is no difference between the two, and he who makes such a distinction is a sinner.
O Goddess, having assumed the form of a guide and having severed all the fetters of the bound soul without exception, the Guru leads him to the supreme state. || 62 ||
Because he acts for the benefit of all, the Lord, whose mind is filled with compassion, assumes the form of a teacher and liberates the bound souls through initiation.
Just as "ghaṭa," "kalasa," and "kumbha" are words denoting the same object, so too "deva," "mantra," and "guru" are said to have one and the same meaning.
As is the deity, so is the mantra; as is the mantra, so is the guru.
The fruit resulting from the worship of the deity, the mantra, and the guru is identical.
Assuming the form of Śiva, O Pārvatī, I accept the worship;
assuming the form of the Guru, I sever the bonds of worldly existence.
One who knows the essence of the Siddhānta, who is the seed [of all], and who imparts awakening—uninterrupted and always joyful at heart—is called a Guru. (67)
O beloved, he who, having transcended the stages of life and the social orders, always abides in the Self alone— that yogi is declared to be a Jyotir-varṇāśramī, and he is the Guru.
O Dear One, he who knows the six paths, the six supports, and the determination of the sixteen supports according to the prescribed rule, is declared to be a Guru.
O beloved, he whose vision remains steady without an object to be seen, whose mind remains without a support,
and whose breath remains steady without effort— he is a Guru.
O Mistress of the Kula, he by whom that reality is known—which generates consciousness and arises from supreme bliss—is a Guru. (71)

O Goddess, he who knows the past and the future, the Tantras and the Mantras, as well as the Śākta and Śāmbhava [initiations] and the sixfold piercing (vedha), is indeed the Guru who performs the piercing.
O Dear One, he who purifies the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan)— which consist of the reality of the planes, mantras, kalās, yantras, tattvas, and worlds— is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who thoroughly understands piercing, the step, opposition, seizing, and likewise releasing— he is declared to be a Guru.
"Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state, and that which transcends it—he who knows these five, O Goddess, is declared to be a Guru, O Beloved. (75)
O Dear One, he who correctly understands the fourfold— namely, the mass (piṇḍa), the word (pada), the form (rūpa), and that which transcends form (rūpātīta)— is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who understands this quartet—the outward-looking [Parā], the Intermediate (Madhyamā), and the Articulated (Vaikharī)—is declared to be a Guru. 77.
"Self, Knowledge, Śiva, and All—these are the four principles.
O Parameśānī, he who knows them is a guru, and no other, O Dear One. (78)
He who understands the threefold process—the severing of bonds, the initiation by piercing, and the grasping of the bound soul—is considered the supreme Guru. (79)
O beloved, he who knows the word, the noose, and the secret meaning of the fettered souls according to the prescribed rule, O lady of beautiful hips, is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who understands this triad— the mantra of the cakra-saṅketa and likewise the pūjā-saṅketa— is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who understands in truth the abiding of the triad of liṅgas known as Vāṇa, Itara, and Svayambhū, is declared to be a Guru.
He who is capable of purifying the three impurities—the individual (āṇava), the karmic (kārmaṇa), and the illusory (māyīya)—is considered the supreme Guru. || 83 ||
O Great Goddess, he who knows the three types of latent impressions (vāsanā) belonging to the feet called "reddish," "white," and "mixed" (or "black"), is considered the supreme Guru.
He who knows Mahāmudrā, the Sky-Seal (nabhomudrā), Uḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, and Mūlabandha is considered the supreme Guru. (85)
He who understands in its true essence the determination of the thirty-six principles, from Śiva down to the earth, is considered the supreme Guru. (86)
O Dear One, he who knows the internal sacrifice, the external sacrifice, the state of knowledge of the *kalās*, and the arrangement of the beautiful machine (*yantra*), he is a Guru, O Dear One. (87)
O Dear One, he who knows in truth the identity of the microcosm and the macrocosm, as well as the number of his veins, bones, and hairs—he alone is the Guru, and no other. 88.
He who is skilled in the eighty-four various postures, such as the lotus posture and others,
and who knows the eight-limbed yoga beginning with restraint (yama), is considered the supreme Guru.
Compassion, suspicion, fear, shame, and disgust as the fifth;
family, conduct, and likewise birth—these eight are proclaimed to be the snares (pāśas). || 90 ||
That which is bound by the fetter is to be known as the fettered (paśu), while the one liberated from the fetter is Maheśvara;
therefore, he who removes the fetter is considered the supreme Guru. || 91 ||
O Dear One, he who knows the binding [of the breath], the *yonimudrā*, the vision of the consciousness of the mantra, and the true nature of the *yantra* and the mantra, is a Guru. 92.
O Dear One, he who knows the fourfold state of the mind— cast down, gone and returned, afflicted, and disciplined— is a Guru.

O beloved, he who knows the fruits of the movement of the individual soul (jīva) within the seven lotus petals, from the root-center (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), is a guru; no other is such.
O Dear One, he who has obtained the full accumulation of reality through the lineage succession beginning with Śiva and ending with his own guru is a true teacher; no other is so. 95.
O Dear One, he by whom reality is perceived such that one becomes identical with it at that very moment,
and who considers himself liberated— he alone is the Guru, and no other.
Those gurus who, by bestowing innate bliss, destroy the pleasure born of the senses, should be served by disciples; others, who are deceivers, should be abandoned. || 97 ||
A teacher who, out of respect, restrains a disciple who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra through vows, fasts, and observances—he is considered a true guru. 98.
One should recognize that Guru, the savior from saṃsāra, as difficult to find—he who, when pleased, bestows the glory of liberation in half a moment. (99)
He who, in an instant, bestows his own spiritual power upon his disciple—power that is free from effort, exertion, and the like—is indeed a Guru, rare even among the gods. (100)
He who imparts the instruction of knowledge—which produces immediate conviction, is easily accessible, and bestows personal bliss—is a guru as rare as a god. 101.
O Goddess, just as one might travel from one island to another, so too is he who bestows knowledge free from practice and the like; he is the Guru. (102)
Just as satisfaction arises quickly for one who is hungry from food, so too does [knowledge arise] merely through instruction; such a teacher, a giver of knowledge, is difficult to find. 103.
There are many teachers, like lamps in every house;
but this teacher, O Goddess, is rare, for he is the illuminator of all, like the sun.
There are many gurus who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, Shastras, and other sciences;
but this guru, O Goddess, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the supreme reality, is difficult to find.
There are many teachers on earth who bestow things other than themselves;
but this teacher, O Goddess, who reveals the Self, is rare to find in all the worlds.
There are many gurus who know evil spells and medicines;
however, one who knows the mantras taught in the scriptures of the Vedas and Āgamas is rare on this earth.
There are many gurus who seize the wealth of their disciples;
but this guru, O Goddess, who removes the suffering of his disciples, is rare to find.
O Goddess, many on earth are devoted to the conduct of their caste, stage of life, and family; but he who is free from all conceptual constructions—that Guru is difficult to find.
A wise person should choose that very guru from whose contact supreme bliss arises; he should not choose anyone else. 110.
Whose intellect proceeds toward that which culminates in direct experience, and by the mere sight of whom one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. || 111 ||
The entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, was consumed by doubt;
he by whom that doubt itself has been consumed is a Guru, O Goddess, who is difficult to find.
Just as fresh butter melts when placed near fire, so too does sin melt in the presence of a true teacher. || 113 ||
Just as a blazing fire consumes both dry and moist wood,
so too does the heavy glance of the Guru burn away the disciple's sin in an instant.
Just as cotton blown by a great wind would go in the ten directions, even so does the mass of evil flee away through the intense compassion of the Guru. 115.
Just as darkness perishes by the mere sight of a lamp, O Goddess, so too does ignorance perish by the sight of the true Guru. 116.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, conversant with the injunctions of the Vedas and the Shastras,
and knowing the application of all means, he is indeed a Guru who possesses the knowledge of reality.

For one devoid of the ultimate reality, worship, fire-offerings, monastic conduct, austerity, pilgrimages, vows, and the like, as well as knowledge of mantras, scriptures, and so forth, are fruitless.
When the supreme reality is known by oneself, one knows one's own self as immovable;
since there is no favoring of oneself, how can there be favoring of another? (119)
How can he who does not know the form of Brahmā, which is of the nature of mind, directly manifest and residing within his own body, bestow liberation upon another? (120)
Even if devoid of all auspicious marks, one who knows reality is considered a guru;
therefore, in this world, the knower of reality alone is both liberated and the liberator. (121)
O Maheśānī, he who knows reality awakens even the bound soul (paśu);
for one devoid of reality, how can there be the acquisition of knowledge of the inner spiritual truth? 122.
O Goddess, those who are taught by the knowers of reality are themselves knowers of reality; of this there is no doubt.
But those who are taught by the bound (paśus), O Goddess, are remembered as being bound themselves.
O Goddess, one who is pierced may pierce; one who is not pierced cannot be a piercer.
One who is liberated may liberate the bound; how could one who is not liberated be a liberator?
One who possesses higher knowledge may rescue a fool, but a fool cannot rescue a fool.
Can a boat made of stone carry across another stone? Could a stone ever carry a stone across? 125.
O Dear One, having obtained a teacher devoid of reality, that man who is solely intent on worldly existence shall obtain no fruit whatsoever, either in this world or the next.
In the Śaiva tradition, three gurus are prescribed; in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, five gurus;
in the Vedic scriptures, hundreds of gurus; and in the Kula lineage, there is but one guru.
The instigator, the indicator, the explainer, the demonstrator, the instructor, and the enlightener— these six are remembered as gurus.

These five may be the effects, while the one who bestows the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is the cause; O Maheśānī, there is no doubt that the sandals of that very Guru alone are to be worshipped, even if there be many [Gurus]. 129.
O Goddess, having obtained a glorious Guru who possesses the required characteristics, who severs all doubt, and who bestows knowledge, one should not seek another guru.
Having obtained a teacher who is ignorant and always a source of doubt, one may go to another teacher; he is not tainted by that fault. (131)
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should go from one teacher to another teacher. (132)
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have briefly described to you some of the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple; what more do you wish to hear? 133.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Guru and the Disciple," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, which contains one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses and concerns the gateway to liberation through Nirvāṇa. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said: "O Lord of the Kula, I desire to hear about the examination of the teacher and the disciple."
O Lord, tell me the sequence of instructions and the various types of initiation.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, purification of the mind arises. (2)
"Without initiation there can be no liberation; this is stated in the teaching of Śiva. And that [initiation] cannot exist without a teacher; thus there is a lineage of teachers. (3)
Therefore, having attained the established doctrine through the reasons of tradition and so forth, [one should act];
for without an instructor, mantras would be fruitless.
The gods praise such a person alone as the one who transmits the lineage:
the Guru, who is learned in the mantras and scriptures, and who observes the rules of conduct and observances. || 5 ||
Even though he is detached, the Guru, by the command of Śiva, should perform this for a short time for the sake of the disciple's qualification and then entrust it to his own disciple.
"For him who has thus attained authority, there is yoga directly with the supreme Śiva;
at the end of the body, there is eternal liberation—so it was spoken by Śaṅkara. (7)
Therefore, O Beloved, with every effort, the Guru should always maintain the unbroken tradition directly proclaimed by Paraśiva.

Having examined [the disciple] according to the rules for the sake of attaining power, accomplishment, and supreme accomplishment, the Guru should subsequently impart the mantra; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
O Goddess, he who gives by unjust means and he who receives by unjust means— by giving and by receiving, a curse upon the lineage will come to pass.
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, give or receive instruction without examining one another, they shall both attain the state of a piśāca.
Both he who receives and he who gives instruction that is contrary to the scriptures shall experience twenty-one terrible hells.
And he who imparts instruction on the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is a sinner;
his mantra perishes like a grain of rice sown in sandy soil. || 13 ||
The knowledge of mantras never remains in one who is unworthy;
therefore, it must be performed after examination, otherwise it will be fruitless. || 14 ||
Having performed the initiation into the pledges and having bestowed the pledge-sandal,
and having brought the disciple into his own presence, he should impart the mantra and not otherwise.
That knowledge which is imparted to a true disciple who is exceedingly devoted—that knowledge is indeed the meaning of the scriptures; one should practice that without interruption.
The knowledge that is imparted to unworthy disciples who lack devotion becomes defiled, just as cow's milk [becomes unfit] when poured into dog's ghee and the like. 17 //
If one should initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, greed, or the like, he incurs the curse of the deity and the rite becomes fruitless. || 18 ||
One should diligently examine the disciple through either knowledge or action for a year, or half of that, or half of that again. (19)
One should employ the superior in low tasks and the lowly in superior tasks;
and one should personally direct them with equal commands regarding life, property, prostrations, and so forth. (20)
By means of words indicating those actions, through illusions, cruel deeds, and by taking sides or remaining indifferent, [he acted] repeatedly and in many ways. || 21 ||
Whether he is pulled or even struck, he who does not fall into despondency should always reflect with joy: "The Guru is showing compassion. (22)
Also in the remembrance of the glorious Guru, in chanting his praises, in seeing him, in bowing to him, in service, in summoning him, in sending him forth, and in what is pleasing to him; (23)
Those who experience transformations such as bliss, trembling, horripilation, and changes in voice or eyes are fit for the rite of initiation and consecration here.

The disciple, too, should perform an examination of the guru by means of these characteristics [of bliss and so forth] during the practices of recitation, praise, meditation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like. || 25 ||

O Goddess, having fully recognized the capacity for imparting knowledge, the accomplishment of mantras, and the power of piercing [the vital centers], the disciple shall become [a true one], and not otherwise.

O Goddess, disciples are proclaimed to be of three kinds— inferior, middling, and superior— according to whether they are fit at the beginning, middle, or end [of their practice], and according to the degree to which they have been struck by [the descent of] power (śakti).
O Goddess, those who first possess devotion and seek initiation become once again greatly joyful; they are declared to be fit for the primordial [practice]. (28)

Those who have attained the initiation and the observance (*samaya*), who are endowed with knowledge and realization (*jñāna-vijñāna*), and whose mental fluctuations (*paryāya*) have been destroyed through devotion—they are remembered as those who are fit for the middle [level]. (29)

O Dear One, those men who are devoid of devotion at the beginning, but possess moderate devotion in the middle, and have fully matured devotion at the end, become fit for the final goal; they are designated as possessing the highest knowledge—such is the threefold instruction. (30)
Just as an ant reaches a fruit at the top of a tree very slowly over a long time, so too is the instruction on karma traditionally understood.
Just as a monkey, by diligently leaping from branch to branch,
obtains fruit, so too, my dear, is the instruction of the Dharma.
Just as a bird traveling through the sky quickly alights upon its fruit,
so too, O Mistress of the Kula, has this instruction on knowledge been declared.

O Goddess, the initiation known as *sparśa* is called *dṛk*, and that known as *mānasa*, O Maheśvarī, is free from effort and exertion; thus, O Goddess, initiation is remembered as being threefold. (34)
Just as a bird gradually nourishes its young with its two wings, O Dear One, such is said to be the instruction of the initiation by touch. 35.
O Supreme Goddess, just as a fish might nourish its own offspring merely by gazing upon them, such is the initiation and instruction through the two eyes.
Just as a tortoise might nourish its own offspring through mere meditation, so too should the piercing initiation (vedhadīkṣā) and the oral instruction (upadeśa) be mental in nature. || 37 ||
A disciple deserves grace according to the descent of power (śaktipāta);
where power does not descend, there no accomplishment (siddhi) arises. || 38 ||
O Goddess, initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows liberation, is proclaimed to be sevenfold by way of action, color, digit, touch, speech, sight, and mind. (39)

The one called Samayā, the distinguished one, the one named Sādhikā, the one called Putrikā, the one known as Vedhakā, the one with the name Pūrṇā, the one called Ācāryā, and the one designated as Nirvāṇā. (40)

The initiation by ritual action (kriyādīkṣā) is said to be eightfold, preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit and the pavilion, and equipped with the water-pot and other implements; it should be performed by the Guru outside [the temple].
O Goddess of Gods, for the sake of purifying the body, one should perform it according to the previously stated rule. 41.
O Goddess, the initiation of the letters (varṇadīkṣā) is said to be threefold: by means of forty-two syllables, or by fifty syllables, or indeed by sixty-two scripts.
Having projected the phonemes onto the body of the disciple, the Guru, O Dear One, should withdraw them in reverse order and unite that consciousness with the Supreme Self.
Therefore, having generated those phonemes, one should again place them within the body of the disciple;
according to the rule of the sequence of emanation, one should also apply consciousness.
The state of divinity, consisting of supreme bliss, arises in the disciple;
this, O beloved, is declared to be the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇa), which removes the bonds (pāśa).
O Dear One, the *kalādīkṣā* should be known to be threefold and must be performed according to the rules:
*nivṛtti* is established starting from the soles of the feet up to the knees.
From the knees up to the navel is *Pratiṣṭhā*, which abides in what is dear;
from the navel up to the throat is *Vidyā*; beyond that is *Śānti*.
Pervading from the throat up to the forehead, and from there up to the crown of the head, is this Kalā known as Śāntyatītā; thus is the pervasion of the Kalās described.

O Dear One, by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal, the knower of the ritual should properly and according to rule join [the breath] from one station to another, up to the crown of the head.
This, O Mistress of the Kula, has been declared as that which bestows the divine state;
it may consist of thirty-eight kalās or even fifty.

Having learned from the mouth of the Guru the Goddess according to the sequence of the deposition of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) and by way of both emanation and reabsorption, one should unite her with the disciple and pierce him. 51.
The state of divinity arises, along with the union of the Yoginīs and the Vīras;
this is declared to be the initiation of Kalā, which removes the bonds of the bound soul (paśu). || 52 ||
Having meditated upon his auspicious Guru, he should mutter the Mūla- and Aṅga-mālinīs.
The Guru should touch the body of the disciple; this shall be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
Having concentrated the mind on reality, one should utter the combined mantras augmented by the supreme reality; this is called the "initiation of speech" (vāgdīkṣā).
Closing his eyes and meditating with a mind serene through the supreme reality, the Guru should clearly behold the disciple; O Dear One, this shall constitute the initiation by sight.
Through the mere glance of the Guru, through his speech, or even through touch, knowledge arises immediately; that is considered the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Initiation by means of the mind (manodīkṣā) is said to be twofold: intense and even more intense.
Having known the sixfold path, O Dear One, one should contemplate it within the body of the disciple.

O Ambikā, one should contemplate the world, the principle (tattva), the digit (kalā), the phoneme (varṇa), the word (pada), and the mantra, extending from the knees, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the palate up to the crown of the head.
The wise one should perform the piercing (*vedha*) by way of the path taught by the Guru. Bound by fetters, the disciple becomes one whose fetters are severed in an instant.
This is declared to be the bestower of liberation, O Mistress of the Kula, known as the intense initiation (*tīvradīkṣā*). 59.
O Goddess, even when [the practice] is extremely intense, as soon as it is remembered by the Guru,
the disciple who possesses perfect realization shall then become one whose sins are severed.
Freed from external activity, he falls to the ground at that very moment;
having attained a divine state, he knows everything according to the Śāmbhava way.
O Goddess, that which exists at the time of piercing is experienced by oneself alone; being awakened, one is not able to describe that bliss.
Śiva himself, when pierced by the piercing [of initiation], shall not be subject to rebirth.
This is the most intense initiation, which liberates one from the bonds of existence and directly bestows the state of Śiva; I swear this to you, O Mistress of the Kula! (63)
Bliss, trembling, becoming, whirling, sleep, and fainting— O Kuleśvarī, these are proclaimed as the six states of the Creator.
O Mistress of the Kula, these six qualities are indeed seen at the time of piercing;
wherever one has been pierced, one remains liberated—of this there is no doubt. (65)
O Dear One, the venerable Guru who performs the initiation of piercing (vedhadīkṣā) is rare in this world;
likewise, such a disciple is also rare and is obtained only through the conjunction of merit.
O Supreme Goddess, it is the command that one should not bestow [this initiation] upon just anyone.
Having worshipped the Kula-cakra according to the prescribed ritual with the substances of the Kula, one should show it to the disciple, O Goddess; this is known as the Kaulika initiation.
The Guru should first pour family substances mixed with the nectar of the five products of the cow into the mouth of the disciple; this is proclaimed as the rite known as *gaṇḍūṣa*.
Then,

O beloved, one should perform the external consecration with a conch or a water-pot filled with wine and containing live fish, or completely filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); that is what has been taught.
O Goddess, the fish is the uvula, and the mouth is called the jar;
filled with the nectar of the five products of the cow, one should consecrate the disciple with that.
O Pārvatī, this shall be the perfected consecration even for the Ācārya;
and [he should perform] the rite of the tooth-stick at the three times of day, as well as the offering of a handful of flowers, O beloved. (71)
In the conch, there is the placement of the Vedic kalās and their knowledge becomes eightfold;
[the rites of] the commitment (samaya) are performed with a tooth-stick, and the practitioner (sādhaka) offers a handful of flowers.
The son [is consecrated] by the conch-consecration, the *vedhas* by the name of the *bodhaka*, and the *ācārya* by the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*); thus the five states are proclaimed. (73)
Those who are solely devoted to family traditions, devoted to their gurus, firm in their vows, and purified by the complete initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka)—they are liberated in this very birth. 74.
O Mistress of the Kula, those who have died purified by the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) obtain once again a supreme birth through the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva. (75)
"Purified by the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) which bestows union with Śiva,
they shall thereby attain liberation"— thus spoke the speech of Śambhu.
If a Kaulika who is devoid of the Pūrṇā initiation and consecration dies,
he attains the state of a Piśāca until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the aeon.
Initiation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal;
the external is the initiation through ritual action (kriyādīkṣā), while that which is called piercing (vedha) is considered internal.
Purity is proclaimed to be twofold: internal purity and external purity;
internal purity arises from ritual action, while external purity arises from initiation.
By initiation and by the lamp of liberation, even a caṇḍāla is liberated;
without these two, O Mistress of the Kula, a follower of the Kaula path is never liberated.
Neither for the body nor for the ritual action is there any formal consecration; one should cause the Self to perform the initiation of the beginningless Kulakuṇḍalinī.

For these initiations, O Goddess, although they convey different purposes, result in the same effect regarding the ritual action when there is a mutual agreement between the supreme teacher and the disciple. 82.
Just as the power of poison may be destroyed by means of mantras and medicinal herbs, O Kuleśvarī,
so too the knower of mantras may, through initiation, instantly sever the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
From this extensive bondage, which causes one to perceive the state of another, initiation alone shall liberate; it also leads one to the divine abode previously [attained].

O Goddess of gods, initiation performed according to the prescribed rite indeed burns away hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka) and tens of millions of major sins (mahāpātaka) in an instant.
O Goddess, that by which the bound souls (paśus) become awakened and auspicious (śiva) is indeed declared to be initiation (dīkṣā), the liberator from the fetters of the bound. (86)
O Beloved, that initiation by which realizations arise merely upon being initiated should be known as the bestower of liberation; all others, however, are merely services for worldly existence.

One should diligently take recourse in that initiation from the venerable Guru for the sake of attaining mantra-perfection—that without which one does not succeed even by a hundredfold practice of worship. (88)
Just as iron, when pierced by the best of mercury, attains the state of gold,
so too, O beloved, the self, when pierced by initiation, attains the state of Śiva.
With his karma burnt by the fire of initiation (dīkṣā), his bonds severed by Māyā,
and having reached the supreme pinnacle of knowledge, he becomes Śiva, free from seeds (nirbīja).
The Śūdra-hood of the Śūdra has departed, and the Brahmin-hood of the Brahmin as well;
when one is perfected through the purificatory rite of initiation, no distinction of caste exists. (91)
Whatever sin one incurs by perceiving a Śiva-liṅga as a mere stone,
even an initiated person would incur that same sin through the recollection of its prior [material] nature.
Whether established as a liṅga made of wood, stone, iron, clay, or precious gems,
all castes who have been initiated are pure, just as it has been declared.
By the mere act of worshipping this, everything as far as the realm of Brahmā becomes worshipped by that initiated person; of this there is no doubt. (94)
For one who has been initiated, there is no need for austerities, nor for restrictive vows; neither by journeys to sacred fords and shrines, nor by bodily mortifications. (95)
O Dear One, those who perform rites such as recitation and worship without having been initiated do not bear fruit, like seeds sown upon a stone.
O Goddess, for one devoid of initiation there is neither spiritual perfection nor a good rebirth;
therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru. 97.

If a twice-born man is initiated later while a person of the lowest caste was initiated earlier, that twice-born man is the junior; he is considered senior only according to the determination of scriptural meaning. (98)

One's own teacher, the [teacher's] consort, and [the teacher's] sons, as well as anyone who has been previously initiated, should be honored by him like the teacher; they must never be treated with disrespect under any circumstances.
If the disciple has only just been initiated and the Guru has gone to heaven,
he should perform the complete consecration by means of a single lineage alone.
O Dear One, among all philosophical systems, he who has been initiated according to the rule by a guru endowed with knowledge is truly disciplined, and no other.
But preceded by the formal acceptance [of the request] and followed by the worship of the wheel, one should purify the disciple through initiation; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
For those born of the Śūdra caste and mixed castes, the rule for primordial purification is ordained;
one should effect their liberation from sin by means such as the offering of water for the feet. 103.
A twice-born man becomes fit in one year, a Kṣatriya in two years,
a Vaiśya in three years, and a Śūdra in four years.
A woman has no independent authority; a widow acts by the direction of her son, a maiden by the command of her father, and a wife by the permission of her husband. (105)
O beloved Kuleśvarī, just as a Śūdra would have no entitlement to the study of the Vedas, likewise one who is uninitiated has no entitlement [to this practice]. 106.
O Goddess, having been initiated, one should satisfy the venerable Guru, the Guru’s wife, his son, the Śakti, and the Kaulikas, according to the full extent of one's wealth.
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you something regarding the examination of the teacher and the disciple, as well as the various types of initiation; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Examination of the Guru and the Disciple," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the supreme among all scriptures, the great secret concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said: "O Lord of Kula, I desire to hear the characteristics of *puraścaraṇa*."
O Supreme Lord, tell me also about the distinctions regarding their abodes, food, and so forth.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the true essence of mantra is revealed.
There is no sacrifice here in this world superior to the sacrifice of recitation (japa);
therefore, one should accomplish dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa through recitation. || 3 ||
Having completely renounced all other steps, one should practice the step of the mantra.
Through vigilance, success will arise; through negligence, there is an inauspicious result.
The recitation (japa) is auspicious when it consists of vows and mental constructs aimed at worldly enjoyment, liberation, or both;
therefore, O Goddess, one should practice that yoga which consists of recitation and meditation.
O Dear One, all defects arising from the seed-syllables up to Brahmā, those produced by the transgression of observances,
and all those committed through knowledge or ignorance, perish through the practice of recitation (japa).
If one desires one's own success in this saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering, the reciter of mantras shall attain happiness solely through the worship of the five limbs. (7)
Daily worship performed at the three times of day, as well as recitation (japa),
libation (tarpaṇa), fire-offering (homa), and feeding Brahmins— this is called *puraścaraṇa*.
O Dear One, whenever any limb [of the mantra] is omitted, the practitioner should perform a recitation twice that number;
or else, O Beloved, he may perform it two, three, four, or five times.
One should perform [the ancillaries] for the sake of achieving the limbs; if one is unable to do so, one should perform them with devotion.
If that limb is omitted, the practitioner of mantra will not attain the desired goal. (10)
O Goddess, when the Brahmins have been well-fed with the four kinds of food and substances endowed with the six flavors, everything indeed becomes fruitful. || 11 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, by means of the perfect accomplishment of a single mantra and through the worship of its five limbs, all mantras are mastered through your grace.
Through the power of the instruction, by the grace of the venerable Guru, through the potency of the mantra, and by means of devotion, the perfection of the mantra arises. (13)
A mantra obtained from a guru whose own mantra is perfected will lead to success;
or, due to practice performed in previous births, a mantra may grant swift accomplishment. (14)
O Mistress of the Kula, that mantra which is preceded by initiation, transmitted through the lineage of succession, and obtained through the proper method, is undoubtedly perfected. || 15 ||
One should recite the mantra one thousand times, encapsulated by the letters of the Mātṛkā;
by doing so in both direct and reverse order, the perfection of the mantra is produced. || 16 ||

Combined with sixty-three syllables and encapsulated by the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā), its mantra becomes perfected through one thousand recitations performed in both forward and reverse order.
By the mere recitation of the Mātṛkā, tens of millions upon tens of millions of mantras are undoubtedly recited, since everything originates from it. 18.
There are many millions of mantras that cause the mind to become agitated;
yet a single mantra obtained through the guru’s grace shall grant all accomplishments. (19)
A mantra that is heard by chance, or even seen through deception, or one that is learned from a written document—reciting such a mantra is productive of no benefit. (20)
Those who recite mantras after merely looking at them written in a book incur a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin, which brings about disease and suffering. (21)
A field of merit, a riverbank, a cave, a mountain peak, sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, and a purifying forest. (22)
Secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, the slope of a mountain, a temple, the shore of the ocean, and one's own home—[these are places for meditation]. (23)
These places are recommended for practitioners as sites for their spiritual accomplishments;
alternatively, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Recitation is praised when performed in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, and the families of cows and brahmins, as well as sacred trees. (25)
One should know that the merit is a hundredfold at home, it becomes a hundred-thousandfold in a cow-pen, ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva. 26.
Free from fear and anxiety caused by barbarians, wicked beasts, and predatory animals, [one should practice] in a solitary, pure place that is free from censure and filled with devotion. || 27 ||
One should dwell in one's own country, in a righteous land, where there is plenty of food and no calamities, in a place inhabited by people devoted to the king, and in a refuge for ascetics. 28.
The path along which kings, ministers, the king's men, and powerful persons travel—that is a path where one who knows the secret counsel should not dwell. (29)
One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, houses, or at the foot of trees; nor should one live by rivers, ponds, wells, or in cavities in the earth and similar places.
If one performs recitation, worship, and so forth after having worshipped the Lord of the Lamp, he receives the fruit of that [lamp-worship]; his own exertion shall become the fruit. || 31 ||
A wise person should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, earth, wood, grass, or leaves, as it bestows the suffering of poverty and disease.
A wise person should prepare a seat from cotton wool, blankets, or garments, or from the skins of lions, tigers, or deer; this bestows good fortune and increases wisdom.
Having sat down in postures such as the lotus, the svastika, or the hero’s posture, one should perform recitation, worship, and other rites; otherwise, they will be fruitless. (34)
Revolving twelve times with the intellect, one should utter the *praṇava* consisting of three morae;
releasing the internal air through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], it becomes *recaka*.
Repeating the *tāra* sixteen times, one should fill the external air;
having slowly bound it with the *iḍā*, this is proclaimed as *pūraka*.

Reciting the *tāra* (om) twelve times, one should retain the breath in the middle [of the body] and dry up the body by means of the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*); this is declared to be the drying of the body.

Furthermore, as before, having exhaled the breath and inhaled it, one should retain it; one should burn [the impurities] with the seed-syllable of fire—this is declared to be the burning of the body. || 38 ||
Again, as before, having exhaled the breath and inhaled it, one should perform the retention (*kumbhaka*).
O Goddess, by means of the stream of nectar flowing from the chariot of the union of Śiva and Kuṇḍalinī, one should flood [the body] from the feet to the head; thus the flooding occurs. (39)
