Without recitation and meditation it is "without the embryo" (agarbha); with those two it is "with the embryo" (sagarbha).
Prāṇāyāma conjoined with the "embryo" is more than a hundred times superior to that which is without the embryo.
Austerities such as pilgrimages, sacrifices, gifts, vows, and the like, do not equal even a sixteenth part of that breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 41 ||
O Śivā, three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) quickly burn away all sin—whether mental, verbal, or even physical—that has been committed. 42.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses consumed through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). 43.
Indeed, whatever action one whose self is purified by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) performs, that very thing bears fruit without a doubt, whether it was done intentionally or unintentionally. || 44 ||
He who constantly practices according to the path taught in the scriptures attains the state of the deity, and the accomplishment of mantra arises.
O Dear One, when one recites the mantra consisting of the Nyāsa and Kavaca verses, obstacles flee upon seeing him, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion. (46)
The foolish-minded person who recites the mantra without first performing the network of ritual placements (nyāsa) is overcome by all obstacles, just as a fawn is by tigers. (47)
The rosary (akṣamālā) is said to be of two kinds: the constructed (kalpitā) and the unconstructed (akalpitā).
The constructed is fashioned from beads, while the unconstructed is the Mātṛkā itself.
Because it consists of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', it is celebrated as the "Akṣamālā" (the rosary of letters).
The best of mantra-knowers should count [it] both in direct and reverse order. 49.
The fruit may be tenfold by each individual finger,
a hundred thousandfold by the lines, and it is said to be infinite by means of rubies (maṇi).
With thirty [beads] there is wealth; with twenty-seven, nourishment (puṣṭi) occurs;
with twenty-five, liberation (mokṣa); and for malevolent rites (abhicāraka), with fifteen.
O Kuleśānī, with fifty [beads], all supernatural powers (sarvasiddhi) are proclaimed.
Liberation is attained through the thumb; the index finger destroys enemies;
one should know the middle finger as the giver of wealth; the ring finger is for rites of pacification; and the little finger is well-proclaimed as the means for paralyzing and attracting.
Having formed the resolve, "I shall recite this," the best of mantra-knowers,
having performed the recitation while seated firmly, should then offer water to the Goddess.
Loud recitation is declared the lowest; whispered recitation is remembered as the middle;
and mental recitation, O Goddess, is the highest—thus the threefold recitation has been described. (54)
One that is too short is a cause of disease; one that is too long is a cause of the exhaustion of ascetic merit.
A mantra that is joined with both the imperishable and the perishable does not succeed.
O Goddess, he who merely remembers the hymn in his mind or mutters the mantra with his voice—both are fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel. (56)
First there is the birth-impurity (jāta-sūtaka), and at its end is the death-impurity (mṛta-sūtaka);
a mantra joined with both types of impurity does not succeed. (57)
Having rendered the mantra devoid of beginning and end, one should indeed revolve it with the intellect;
that mantra which is liberated from the two impurities (sūtaka) bestows all accomplishments.
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*, will find no accomplishment even through a hundred million recitations. (59)
And those mantras which are like dormant seeds, O beloved, will not yield fruit;
it is taught that mantras endowed with consciousness bring about all accomplishments.
Mantras are said to be devoid of consciousness; they are merely phonemes.
They do not bestow fruit at all, even from a million or ten million recitations.
Whatever form the mantra initially assumes when it is uttered,
that same result is obtained by reciting it a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million times.

The breaking of the knots at the heart and throat, the expansion of all limbs, tears of bliss, horripilation, possession of the body, O Kuleśvarī, and faltering speech arise suddenly; of this there is no doubt. (63)
When even a single recitation of a mantra endowed with consciousness produces such realizations,
that is called "transmission" (pāramparya).
Obstructed, cryptic, deluded, bound, enraged, and split;
childish, youthful, adolescent, mature, and old—thus it is proclaimed. (65)
Stunned, fainted, intoxicated, pinned, shattered, rogue, sluggish, averted, severed, deaf, blind, and unconscious. (66)
A servant who is hungry, stubborn, fallen from his position, and oppressed;
one who is devoid of affection, incapacitated, ruined, lifeless, and one whose enemies have been shattered. (67)
He is asleep, contemptible, base, and impure; he is difficult to approach, devoid of courage, defeated, a burnt-out fool, and terrifying. (68)
The sword is censured as cruel, fruitless, and a mere cutter;
it is powerless, whirled about, cursed, wounded, miserable, and lacking limbs.
It is dull, an enemy, indifferent, ashamed, deluded, and lazy. (69)
If one recites a mantra without knowing these sixty defects of mantra,
no accomplishment arises for him, even from a hundred thousand or ten million recitations.
O beloved, ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) that remove defects in mantra are described:
first, birth (janana), then life-giving (jīvana), followed by striking (tāḍana), and thereafter awakening (bodhana). || 71 ||
O Mistress of the Kula, the consecration, then the purification, the nourishment, as well as the satiation, the kindling, and the protection—these are the purificatory rites (saṃskāras). (72)
Just as weapons sharpened on a whetstone become truly keen, so too do mantras attain their full potency through the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras). || 73 ||
Edible offerings, sacrificial oblations, vegetables and the like, prescribed fruits,
roots, and barley flour— these are recommended for practitioners of mantra.
When one whose limbs are nourished by another's food and drink performs an accumulation of merit, half of the fruit belongs to the giver of food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt. (75)
Therefore, O Īśvarī, a wise person should avoid the food of others with every effort, both during the period of *puraścaraṇa* and in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*).

The tongue is scorched by eating another's food, the hands are scorched by accepting gifts, and the mind is scorched by the wives of others; how, then, can there be success in one's undertakings? (77)

[The results are determined] in the eight directions—Indra, Agni, Rudra, the Planets, the Vedas, the Sun, and the Quarters—as well as in the sixteen, five, four, fifteen, and thirteen [houses]. || 78 ||
The wise practitioner should write the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet within sixteen squares,
starting from the first letter of his own name until the appearance of the first letter of the mantra.
The mantra-practitioner should determine the *siddha* and other categories, and then again perform the calculation with the *sādhya* and others;
he should count the *siddha* and so forth again by means of fourfold divisions.
A *siddha-siddha* mantra becomes effective through recitation; a *siddha-sādhya* becomes effective through double that amount;
a *siddha-susiddha* becomes effective through half that recitation; but a *siddha-ari* destroys one's kinsmen.
A *sādhyasiddha* causes extreme affliction; a *sādhyasādhya* is useless;
a *sādhyasusiddha* brings benefit through devotion; and a *sādhyāri* destroys those of one's own lineage.
The Susiddha-siddha [mantra] is accomplished by half the recitation; the Sādhya [mantra] is accomplished according to the stated rule;
the Susiddha [mantra] is accomplished from the very first attempt; and the enemy of the Susiddha destroys one's own lineage.
One who is *arisiddha* kills one's son; one who is *arisādhya* kills one's wife; one who is *susiddha* destroys one's entire family; and one who is *tadripu* (the enemy) kills one's own self. (84)
The *siddha* vowels are said to be kinsmen; the *sādhya* vowels are remembered as servants.
The *susiddha* vowels should be known as nourishers, while the *śatru* vowels are remembered as destroyers. (85)
The relatives are nine; the servants are twelve, six, and ten;
the nourishers are three, eleven, and seven; and the destroyers are twelve, eight, and four.
[86] *Prāpa*, *lobhā*, *paṭu*, *prāhyaṃ*, *rudrasya*, *adri*, and *uru* are the syllables. *Kara*.

O beloved, when the letters, generally skilled in the dissolution of the world, are separated by a host of wicked ones and end with vowels in their respective order, then they have entered the portion of Revatī. 87.
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, achiever, death, friend, and great friend—these states, beginning with birth, recur again and again. (88)

In the [twelve] signs of the zodiac, the letters are divided in order as follows: *vā* (white) and *laṃ* (white) in Aries; *khu* (red) and *raṃ* (red) in Taurus; *śa* (beautiful) and *mī* (beautiful) in Gemini; and in Virgo, the letters beginning with *śa* are prescribed. (89)
The Ascendant, Wealth, Brothers, Siblings, Children, Enemies, Wife, Death, Dharma, Action, Fortune, and Expenditure are the twelve houses (rāśis). (90)
The wise should calculate the end of the mantra from one's own zodiac sign;
however, when the zodiac sign and birth star are unknown, the calculation should be made from the zodiac sign corresponding to the first letter of the name. (91)
Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, one should divide it into three parts and split them with vowels; the other [method] is the reverse of that.
If the debtor is the most excellent knower of mantras, it should be understood that the debt is increased;
for if one is oneself a debtor, one should first recite that mantra, since one is [indebted] from before.
Air, fire, earth, water, and space correspond respectively to fifty letters:

five short vowels, five long vowels ending with the bindu (anusvāra) and arising from their combinations; and the consonants beginning with *ka*, divided into groups of five, ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. || 94 ||
Earth and water are friendly toward each other, as are wind and fire;
however, they are enemies in the opposite case, and otherwise, there is friendship everywhere. 95.
O Mistress of the Family, one should avoid such a mantra in which there is a conjunction of mutually contradictory phonemes; for that brings about destruction. 96.

In the case of a single-syllable mantra, likewise in a *kūṭa* mantra, or in a *mantranāyikā* of the *Traipura* class—whether bestowed by a woman or obtained in a dream—one should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories of efficacy] at all. (97)

O Goddess of the Gods, regarding the garland-mantras taught by those who have attained mantra-perfection and those born of the four traditions (āmnāyas), one should not at all examine their status as "perfected" (siddha) and so forth. 98.

One should not examine the Siddha and other categories for the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, the Prāsāda, the Praṇava, or those mantras consisting of syllables together with their seed-syllables (piṇḍa). || 99 ||
If the mind is in one place, Śiva in another, Śakti in another, and the vital breath (māruta) elsewhere,
O beautiful lady, success is not attained even by ten million recitations of the mantra.

Knowledge is studied for the sake of debate, recitation is performed for the sake of others, and gifts are given for the sake of fame; O fair-faced one, how can there be spiritual accomplishment in such cases? (101)

One goes to a sacred ford for the sake of wealth, one performs austerity for the sake of hypocrisy, and one worships the deities for the sake of some worldly purpose; how, then, can spiritual perfection ever arise?
If fools perform ritual placement (nyāsa), worship of the deity, recitation (japa), or fire-offerings (homa) with an impure body, all of that shall be fruitless. || 103 ||

O Dear One, whatever ritual action one performs while still engaged in the discharge of feces and urine and other such impurities—whether it be recitation, worship, or anything else—all of it becomes impure. 104.
If one who is possessed of foul-smelling breath and soiled garments, hair, and other parts should perform recitation, the deity—being utterly loathsome—will quickly burn him. 105.
At the time of recitation, one should avoid laziness, yawning, sleep, sneezing, spitting, fear, touching the lower parts of the body, and anger. (106)
Excessive eating, idle chatter, frivolous talk, adherence to restrictive rules, attachment to others, and fickleness—by these six, the mantra is not accomplished. (107)

One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one surrounded by a crowd, one with an impure upper garment, one who is unclean, and one who is walking—these should not recite [the mantra]. (108)
During the time of recitation, one should avoid dullness, suffering, cutting grass, engaging in dispute, or pursuing worldly desires, as well as externalizing the bodily breath. 109.

Peaceful, pure, moderate in diet, sleeping on the ground, devoted, self-controlled, free from the pairs of opposites, steady-minded, silent, and with a restrained self, one should mutter [the mantra], O Dear One. (110)

Endowed with faith, conviction, compassion, devotion, self-restraint, and resolve, as well as with the virtues of contentment, zeal, righteousness, and so forth, a person should perform the recitation. 111.
Adorned with fragrant flowers, ornaments, garments, and the like, success comes into his hands; it does not come to another even from ten million recitations.
Established in that, with his life-force absorbed in that, his mind fixed on that, and having that as his supreme goal, O Dear One,
he should mutter the mantra while contemplating the meaning of that state.
When weary from recitation, one should meditate again; when weary from meditation, one should recite again.
For one engaged in recitation, meditation, and so forth, the mantra is quickly perfected.
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have told you something of the characteristics of *puraścaraṇa* in brief; what more do you wish to hear? (115)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Puraścaraṇa and Other Rites," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, concerning the gateway to liberation through Nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Kula, ocean of the nectar of compassion, I desire to hear [this].
And tell me, O Supreme Lord, the injunction for rites performed for the sake of desired fruits.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one becomes skilled in the practical application [of yoga]. (2)

O Dear One, the minister, possessing a pure heart and endowed with the previously mentioned observances, should recite the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda one hundred thousand times according to the reality (tattva).
O Goddess, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire for one-tenth of the total number;
one should then satisfy [the deities] with milk, water, and rice grains for one-tenth [of that].
O Dear One, with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, ornaments, wealth, garments, and so forth, as well as with various edible foods, drinks, and other charming sacrificial substances; || 5 ||
One should satisfy the circle of Yoginīs with as much elaboration as one’s means allow;
thus [proceeding] with the ritual placement (nyāsa), recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), fire-offering (homa), worship (arcana), and libation (tarpaṇa).
O Goddess, the practitioner who seeks success shall become manifest Paraśiva himself;
thereafter, O Mistress of the Kula, he may perform the ritual applications desired by his own mind.
With this mantra, the wise one should accomplish [the goal] for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
For one whose mantra is perfected, the six rites are accomplished without a doubt;
for one whose mantra is not perfected, they are not accomplished at all, and he shall incur the curse of the deity.
For those who perform rites for the sake of desire, no other world exists;
O beloved, the fruit for them is only the success of the rite, and nothing else.
O Goddess of gods, not even for a single injunction is a double fruit ever seen anywhere; therefore, one should worship the deity without desire.
Through the mantras for oblations and libations, and by means of specific ritual placements (nyāsa) and meditations (dhyāna),
one should perform the six rites for both oneself and others.

At the conclusion of the practice, one should perform the worship of the wheel according to the prescribed rite; endowed with the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. || 12 ||
For the purpose of pacifying defects in the ritual application and for the sake of self-protection,
if one does not obtain the fruit, one shall incur the curse of the deity.

Having understood the lunar day (tithi), the weekday (vāra), the asterism (nakṣatra), the yoga, the month, the season, the fortnight (pakṣa), the lord of the lamp (dīpeśa), and the wheels of the lineage (kulacakras), one should accomplish the ritual acts. || 14 ||

Having understood the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), the deity (devatā), the ritual placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), worship (arcana), and so forth, as well as the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka), one should accomplish the mantras. || 15 ||

Having understood that one's sons, kinsmen, and wife, as well as the compatibility of the zodiac signs and colors, and likewise the friendship of the elements, one should practice the mantras when they are rising.

Having understood that the knowledge of mantras is non-different from [the Self] in form, that sleep is of the nature of consciousness, and [the distinctions of] female, male, neuter, and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual acts. || 17 ||
The wise know that the doubling of vowels, consonants, and words is the "progenitor of consciousness";
having understood the short, long, and protracted [vowels] and so forth, one should accomplish the mantras.
Having understood the five purifications, the postures, breath control, ritual placements, the rosary, the defects, the consecrations, the mudrās, and so forth, one should accomplish the rites. (19)

In the same way, having understood the connection between the postures, the binding of directions, the binding of the channels (nāḍī), and so forth, as well as the deities, times, and mudrās, one should accomplish the ritual acts.

Having understood the actions of the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment— the fivefold materials for writing, the location, the diagram, and the measurement— one should perform the rites.

Having understood the origin, the latent impressions (vāsanā), the description, the form, and the consecration, as well as the sacrificial pit, the materials, the measurements, and so forth, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Having observed the radiance of the fire, its smoke-colored sound, smell, and the shape of its flames, as well as its auspicious movements and so forth, one should determine whether it is favorable or unfavorable.

Having understood the distinctions in the utterance of mantras, characterized by the investigation of the reality of the mantra and the entry of the body [into the deity], one should accomplish the ritual acts.

Having understood the mandala, the purification of the ritual vessel and its substances, the eight perfumes and so forth, as well as the initiation, the bestowing of the name, and other rites, one should perform the initiation.

Having understood the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, as well as the observances (niyama), latent impressions (vāsanā), worship, supports, yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual actions.

Having understood the characteristics of the family worshiper, such as entering the house of worship and so forth, as well as the purification of the family substances and other requirements, one should perform the worship. (27)

O Goddess, having understood the inner sacrifice, the outer sacrifice, the placement of the vessel for the arghya offering and so forth, and the fivefold handful of flowers, one should accomplish the ritual acts.

O Goddess, having understood the vessel, the support, the writing, the flesh, the digit, the mudrā, the paths, the union, and the offering to the *baṭuka*s and others, one should accomplish the ritual actions.

The characteristic [of the consort] is the differentiation of the innate power (sahaja-śakti) known as *kulākula*. Having understood the auspicious characteristics, the consecration of the woman, her worship, and the time for union, O Goddess, one should accept the power (śakti). || 30 ||

Having understood the varieties of drink, the measure of the manifestation of the fruit, the characteristics of its persistence, and the acceptance of the three principles, one should drink the nectar of the Kula.
O Dear One, by knowing the entry into the wheel, the prostration, the abiding, and the emergence, as well as the enjoyment and activities of the Yoginīs, one becomes a Kaulika.
Having recognized the time for the arousal of passion, the offering that illuminates the Kula,
and the recitation of peaceful hymns and so forth, one becomes a Kula-teacher.

Having understood the worship of the maiden [Goddess] who possesses eight times eight flowers for the sake of favoring the pairs [of deities], as well as the worship on specific lunar days, one should accomplish the ritual acts.
Having understood the different traditions, the conventions, the closing of the flowers, the three gurus, and the oral lineage, one should accomplish the ritual acts. || 35 ||
O Goddess, having understood the Vedic knowledge, the family traditions, the various Mantras, the Pādukā, and the three feet (caraṇas), one should accomplish the ritual acts.

Having understood the procedure for worshiping one's own superior [deity] and those of equal or inferior status, as well as the worship of the perfected mudrās and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual actions.

Having understood the rites for the consecration of the guru, fire, and the deceased; the funeral ceremonies; the sequence of offerings to the quarters; and the procedures for the *mokṣadīpa* and other such rituals, one should accomplish these actions.
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, some specific details have been told;
this is the common procedure for the ritual of all mantras whatsoever. (39)
O Dear One, mantras are male deities and vidyās are female deities.
Mantras for males end with *huṃ phaṭ* when the vital breath moves in the right [nostril],
while vidyās for female deities awaken when they end with *agnijāyā* (svāhā), O Dear One.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) awakens in the left [channel], the neuter mantras end with "namaḥ";
when the vital breath has entered both channels, all [mantras] attain awakening. || 41 ||

In rites for pacification (śāntika), the mantras should be gentle, predominantly consisting of syllables of nectar (amṛta), and ending with "svāhā"; those for rites of power (vīrya) are mostly Vāyavya, while those for cruel acts (krūra-karma) are Āgneya.
*Phaṭ* is used for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), *vaṣaṭ* for subjugation (*vaśya*), and *huṃ phaṭ* for killing (*māraṇa*).
*Namaḥ* is prescribed for paralyzing (*stambhana*), while *svāhā* is for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). (43)

The practitioner should append *svāhā* at the end of the mantra during the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the satiation (*tarpaṇa*), and *namaḥ* during the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship (*pūjana*);
these should be joined as they stand during the time of recitation (*japa*).
For rites of pacification (śāntika), [the leaf] should be silver or copper; for subjugation (vaśyaka), birch bark;
for all purposes, gold; and for fierce rites (krūra), it should be a cloth from a corpse.
Three fragrances are prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), five fragrances for subjugation (vaśyaka),
eight fragrances for all activities, and the eight poisons for fierce rites (krūra).

For pacifying rites, the pen should be made of dūrvā grass; for subjugation and similar rites, it should be made of a peacock's tail. For all activities, however, it should be made of gold; for cruel rites, it should be made of a crow's tail.

Rites for pacification (śāntika) should be performed in one's own home; rites for subjugation (vaśya) and so forth in the temple of Caṇḍikā; all types of rites in a temple of the gods; and cruel rites (krūra-karma) in a cremation ground.
O Dear One, having learned these characteristics and others from the mouth of the Guru, the practitioner of mantra should perform all rites for the sake of attaining their respective fruits. (49)
At the base is the seed-syllable of the temple, resembling the rising sun;
at the head is the supreme seed-syllable, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons.
Filled with the bliss born from the mutual touch of the people, [he perceived] from the base of the body up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) as forms of uninterrupted continuity. 51 //
One should constantly contemplate oneself as being sprinkled from head to foot with the supreme nectar-essence; such a person shall become free from old age and death.
Having meditated thus, O Mistress of the Family, one should accomplish all rites;
they are swiftly accomplished, O Goddess, there is no need for deliberation here. (53)
O Dear One, I shall explain the classification of meditative absorption (dhyāna), which brings about all accomplishments;
by means of this, one obtains one's desired goal even without worship, fire-offerings (homa), and the like. (54)
O Goddess, in a pleasant place, the practitioner, with a steady mind, seated upon a soft cushion, should meditate after first performing the salutation to the Guru. || 55 ||
Situated in the center of the full moon-maṇḍala located on the head is the supreme seed-syllable of the Śrī-prāsāda, conjoined with the sixteenth vowel.
O beloved, [the form] is as white as pure crystal, camphor, the kunda flower, and the moon;
its body is bathed in the nectar produced from the orb of the true moon. || 57 ||
One should constantly cultivate the self with an unwavering inner mind;
all misfortunes will dissolve, and it brings about auspiciousness, glory, and nourishment. (58)
O Dear One, accompanied by youthful exuberance, one should worship the Maṇḍala with the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda recited one thousand and eight times.
The fear born of untimely death, great diseases, old age, and death;
the fear born of malevolent planets, epilepsy, vetālas, spirits, madness, and so forth. (60)
Having conquered [all obstacles], free from mental and physical ailments, and endowed with sons and grandsons, he shall live for more than a hundred years, honored by all mankind. || 61 ||
One understands scriptures never before heard, one's poetry becomes stainless, and one truly becomes composed of consciousness; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. 62.
In cases of diseases such as fever and insanity, one should recite while contemplating [the deity] upon the head;
when colic, wind-disorders, ulcers, tumors, dysuria, and the like occur, O Goddess of Gods, one should recite while contemplating [the deity] on those respective locations as before.
When great diseases have arisen affecting all the limbs, one should contemplate [the deity];
at that very moment, all diseases will attain pacification—of this there is no doubt. || 64 ||
Whoever meditates upon the ten sense organs shall obtain excellence of the senses;
wherever one remembers the seed-syllable, there its fruit certainly comes to pass.
O Dear One, he who constantly contemplates this upon his head shall become free from old age and death;
it is the destroyer of all diseases and the bestower of knowledge and health.
There is no meditation higher than this; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
O Goddess, this is declared to be the fruit born of *sāttvika* meditation.
One should perform all rites for pacification according to this procedure;
by this procedure, O Goddess of the Gods, incomparable good fortune shall arise. (68)
He who meditates upon the seed-syllable conjoined with the twelve vowels within the twelve supporting lotuses shall become free from old age and death. || 69 ||
One should contemplate the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels within the six supports;
O Mistress of the Kula, she is worshipped by the goddesses residing in the six supports. (70)
In the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, situated within a solar disc,
is the seed-syllable of the Parā-prāsāda, resembling the hue of the rising sun.
O Ambikā, it is radiant with the luster of the Javā flower, Bandhūka, Sindūra, and Padmarāga gems,
and is encircled by twenty-five letters of touch.
O Goddess, with an unwavering inner self, one should meditate upon oneself as having made the three worlds manifest through the shadow of the mass of that [divine] radiance.
The wise practitioner, endowed with youthful exuberance, should recite the seed-mantra of Parāprasāda one thousand and eight times over the maṇḍala.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, kinnaras, and guhyakas;
the vidyādharas, sages, yakṣas, nāgas, and the women who are apsarases. || 75 ||
He brings under his control, without a doubt, lions, tigers, lordly serpents, and other such wicked beasts; how much more so, then, humans and the like? (76)
O beloved, one attains great sovereignty, such as the enjoyments of heaven and so forth;
by remembering and reciting [the mantra] over the head of someone, that person indeed becomes submissive by force.
O Goddess, this fruit arising from meditation on the Rājasa [quality] has been declared.
One should perform all rites of subjugation according to this procedure. || 78 ||
O Goddess, this brings everything under control and bestows the fruit of all sovereignty;
there is no meditation higher than this—this is the truth, there is no doubt.
One should draw a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-spoked wheel, and a square enclosure;
one should write the root mantra in the center, accompanied by the name of the person for whom the rite is intended.
O Supreme Goddess, one should write the six limbs in the six corners;
O Pārvatī, the eight vowels on the filaments and the [consonant] groups on the petals.
O Mother, one should draw the root mantra within the four corners of the underground chamber using five-colored powders, making it auspicious and pleasing to the sight.
Having thus drawn the yantra according to the rules, O Dear One, the best of mantra-knowers should place one, three, six, eight, and four water-pots (kalaśas).
O Dear One, from the center to the edge of the square, there are thirty-two pitchers;
or else, O Mistress of the Eighteen, there may be seven or ten, O Dear One.
The best of practitioners should prepare either four or one [of these]:
unstable blood, vessels and sinews, earth and flesh, blood, and water. (85)

One should worship the deity of the water-pot (kalaśa), who is endowed with mantra and vital breath, [visualized] as having a head consisting of leather, cloth, stone, tortoise-shell, and coconut fruit. 86.
O beloved, one should worship the limbs of Sāvitrī, the Mothers accompanied by Bhairava, and the Guru, Vighneśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapati in the intermediate directions.
Having worshipped [the deities] in the jars according to the rule, the best among those who know the mantras should consecrate his beloved disciple for the pacification of all sins. (88)
Longevity, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, knowledge, health, and so forth shall come to pass;
one consecrated as king obtains the earth bounded by the four oceans. (89)
One who possesses nothing, when consecrated, shall attain great sovereignty;
and a barren woman, when consecrated, obtains a son endowed with all virtues.
Spirits, untimely death, diseases, and the like will undoubtedly perish;
having written this supreme yantra on either triloha (an alloy of three metals) or on birch bark. || 91 ||
O Goddess, when held in the arm, it shall provide all forms of protection;
it bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, the acquisition of knowledge, fame, and victory. 92.
Whatever is desired by one's own mind, that one obtains without doubt: the power over the sword, the subjugation of youth, the yakṣiṇī, the ointment, and the sandals. (93)
The eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the great elixirs and rejuvenators, and all the accomplishments headed by the *sañjīva* medicinal pill; || 94 ||
They are seen by those who know the mantras for bringing others under one's control; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should employ the six rites, O Dear One, for it does not happen otherwise. 95.

The practitioner of mantras, intent on the visualization of the deity, should perform oblations as before with yellow substances such as turmeric, along with sacrificial wood, leaves, fruits, and so forth. (96)
O Dear One, O Goddess, one shall paralyze speech, hearing, movement, sight, armies, rivers, planets, enemies, and various wicked beasts; of this there is no doubt. (97)
O beloved, there is no meditation superior to this for destroying those afflicted by the influence of planets and other such evils; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
O Goddess, this fruit born of *tāmasa* meditation has been declared; by means of this procedure, one should accomplish rites for the destruction of the wicked. 99.
Having understood these and other distinctions of meditation from the mouth of the Guru, O beloved, one should employ the six rites, O Goddess worshipped by heroes; not otherwise. (100)
With the excellent fuel-sticks of khadira, śveta, mandāra, and sitabhānu, and with the inner bark of palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and apāmārga. || 101 ||
With *nandyāvarta*, white lotuses, *hayāri* flowers,
and other white, auspicious substances, interspersed with sacrificial fuel, leaves, and fruits.
O Mistress of the Kula, the knower of mantras [should offer] eatables such as milk-rice mixed with dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and rice, combined with the three sweets. 103.
O Goddess, having ascertained the relative weight or lightness of that task— whether by means of one [mantra] or all [of them]— one should then perform a thousand or five oblations.

O Mistress of the Family, whether it be ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even a million oblations, [they are offered] into the consecrated fire within a sacrificial pit prepared for those respective rites. (105)
O beloved goddess, having invoked the deity into this [liṅga] and meditated upon her along with her retinue,
one should perform the oblation according to the rules, O Goddess, with an inner self absorbed in that.
It pacifies all diseases, wounds, insanity, epilepsy, portents, and consumption;
it alleviates all suffering at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (107)
By this, O beloved, one shall obtain all peace, as well as knowledge and vidyā;
[using flowers] born from the kadamba, aśoka, vakula, punnāga, mango, and madhūka trees. || 108 ||
With two kinds of *campaka*, *pālāśa*, *pāṭala*, and beautiful *kapittha* trees; with *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, *bandhūka*, and red lotuses.
With white water-lilies, red mandāra flowers, yūthikā, kunda, and javā, as well as coconuts, plantains, grapes, sugarcane, and parched grain; || 110 ||
With sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, saffron,
and other such auspicious red substances, as well as with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and fruits.
O Goddess, the best of those who know mantras should offer oblations according to the rules as before, [for the sake of] kings, men, and women celebrated for their youth. (112)

O Mistress of the Kula, one shall bring under control intoxicated lions, as well as tigers, wild beasts, and even elephants, along with Siddhas, gods, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and the women of the Gandharvas—even the gods themselves; of this there is no doubt. (113)
By means of an oblation of *vājīlavaṇa*, one shall certainly attract a woman;
by this rite, O Goddess of Gods, one shall obtain supreme good fortune. (114)
What need is there for much speaking here? Among the practitioners of mantra in the three worlds, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this king of mantras. (115)
O Kuleśvarī, he who is thoroughly proficient in the Ūrdhvāmnāya, who knows the mantra of the supreme temple (Prāsāda),
and who understands the true meaning of the Kula-ocean, is liberated while living.

Whether dwelling at a sacred bathing place, or at a non-sacred place, or even in the midst of water, one who knows the mantra of the Supreme Abode is certainly liberated; of this there is no doubt. (117)
O Pārvatī, the directions, seats, fields, mudrās, trees, creepers, monasteries, and so forth,
as well as the Bhairavas and goddesses, are to be known as belonging to the Ūrdhvāmnāya.
With nimba, kāraskara, unmatta, kaṇṭakī, vipra, dantin, and other trees such as those with thorny bones, which are substances that accomplish inauspicious ends; || 119 ||
With *vaṭuka* [offerings] that are black in color, consisting of fuel-sticks, leaves, and fruits;
with house-soot, charcoal from a funeral pyre, the three pungent spices (*trikaṭu*), sour substances, and funeral-ashes; || 120 ||

Having thoroughly ground [the ingredients] sprinkled with the juice of the *unmatta* plant and well-watered, one should combine them with the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the ashes of a funeral pyre. || 121 ||
One should fashion an image of the person to be accomplished from the wood of a tree corresponding to a single asterism;
having properly established its vital breaths, one should suspend it above the sacrificial pit.
The mantra-practitioner, with a turbid mind, fierce gaze, and impatient spirit, should dig out that image beneath the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rite. || 123 ||

O Goddess, the best of those who know mantras should, according to the prescribed rite, offer oblations with those very substances into the funeral fire, which has been intensified by the seven kinds of poisonous trees as fuel.
One should perform acts of inciting hatred, expulsion, and killing; of this there is no doubt.
For pacification, O Goddess, one should contemplate [the deity] as sattvic and white in color. 125.
O Goddess, for the purpose of subjugation, one should contemplate [the deity] as having a rajasic nature and a red color;
for cruel deeds, one should contemplate [the deity] as having a tamasic nature and a black color. || 126 ||
Having first performed the protection of oneself, one should afterwards accomplish the ritual acts;
he who performs otherwise out of delusion becomes a beast for the deity.
Therefore, O Goddess, worshipped by heroes, a wise person, having performed the great Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa, the worship, and the bali offering, should then carry out his ritual activities; not otherwise.
O Dear One, within the lotus of the mūlādhāra, situated in the midst of the fire,
is that seed-syllable of the Parā-prāsāda mantra, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an aeon.
Clad in garments made from those born in the inverse order, he is enveloped by the ten pervasive syllables;
he himself is like the fire of universal destruction, causing terror to all beings.
Facing the southern direction, with a gaze made turbid by extreme ferocity and accompanied by the exuberance of youth, he [performed] that which is known as the supreme grace (*parā-prāsāda*).
One should recite the mantra over the mandala one thousand and eight times for those beings who cause misfortune and who provoke quarrels and distress. (132)
[One should subdue] those who cause useless hatred, the cruel, those who create obstacles to worship, and the spirits, grahas, vetālas, piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas. || 133 ||
One should contemplate those wicked beings and others who constantly cause affliction as being fallen into that fire and utterly consumed;
they meet their destruction in an instant, like moths in a flame. (134)
He who remembers the seed-syllable upon her crown encounters death;
by this meditation, O Goddess of gods, one may destroy even Time and the other [factors]. 135.
Thus, O beloved Kuleśānī, I have briefly described to you the ritual procedure for optional rites (kāmyakarman). What more do you wish to hear? 136.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Rites for Desired Ends," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrīkulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, containing one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, concerning the gateway to liberation and final beatitude. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Kula, I wish to hear about the latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding the names and other attributes of the Gurus."
O Supreme Lord, tell me the true nature of the categories of the Kula.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, the knowledge of the Kula is revealed.
Salutations to you, O Lord, O Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru, who has assumed manifold forms for the sake of successfully bringing forth the descent of knowledge. 3.
Salutations to the one whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, who is the embodiment of the Supreme Self,
the sun that dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and to Consciousness itself.
To the omniscient one, whose form is fashioned out of compassion, whose nature is auspiciousness,
and who bestows the state of liberation upon devoted and fortunate beings both in this world and the next.
In front, at my sides, behind, above, and below, may I always perform homage; through the form of a virtuous mind, may I eternally practice the state of being your servant.
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* signifies its obstruction;
because it obstructs darkness, it is called *guru*.
The letter *ga* is said to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*); the letter *ra* is the burner of sin;
the letter *u* is called Viṣṇu; the Guru is the supreme embodiment of these three.
The letter *ga* signifies the perfection of knowledge; the letter *ra* therein is the illuminator;
the letter *u* signifies identity with Śiva—this is designated as the Guru. (9)

Because he awakens those who are impoverished by the lack of knowledge regarding the reality of the self according to the secret scriptures, and because he possesses the nature of the gods beginning with Rudra, he is designated as the "Guru. (10)
He practices [right conduct] himself, establishes his disciples in right conduct, and gathers the meanings of the scriptures here; for that reason, he is called an *ācārya*. 11.

He who himself teaches that which is near to all things moving and unmoving, and who is called an *ācārya* because of his perfection in the yoga of the restraints (*yama*) and other limbs, [is the one]. || 12 ||

Because he has offered his own body, because he has abandoned passion, hatred, and the like, and because his mind is solely devoted to meditation, he is said to be "one who has propitiated [the Buddha]. || 13 ||
O Dear One, because he assumes the form of a deity, for the sake of favoring his disciples,
and because his body consists of compassion, he is called the Teacher (deśika).

O Dear One, because he contemplates the meaning of the Supreme Reality— which unfolds within his own heart through inner peace— and because he is free from false knowledge, he is called "Svāmī" (the Lord).

Because he is far removed from defects of mind and the like, because he avoids causal discourse and such, and because of his similarity to dogs and other animals as well as his state of bliss, he is Maheśvara. || 16 ||

O Dear One, he is called Śrīnātha because he bestows the knowledge of liberation, because he awakens one to the Self as the Sound-Brahman (Nādabrahman), and because he has suppressed the marks of ignorance.

Because he abides in accordance with place and time according to the traditional lineage (kulāgama), and because he has brought under his control the living beings of the world, he is called "Devah" (the Lord). 18.
Because he pacifies the bonds of existence, because he bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, and because he protects and is desirable, he is called Bhaṭṭāraka. || 19 ||
Because he reveals the secret meaning of the Vedānta contained in the hidden scriptures and because he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, he is called the Lord (Prabhu).
O Dear One, because of his continuous application of the *yonimudrā*, because of the manifest power of the mantra,
and because he is worshiped by the hosts of gods, he is called a *yogin*.
By abandoning the suffering of attachment, by resorting to any hermitage whatsoever, and because of his mutual binding of the self, he is designated as a "self-restrained one" (saṃyamī). || 22 ||
Because of reflecting upon the nature of reality, because of being free from censure and the like, and because of undertaking auspicious deeds, one is designated as an ascetic (tapasvin). || 23 ||
Because he is imperishable, because he is most excellent, because he has shaken off the bonds of saṃsāra,
and because he has realized the meaning of "That thou art," he is called an Avadhūta.
Because he is free from passion, intoxication, afflictions, anger, envy, and delusion, and because he stands far removed from *rajas* and *tamas*, he is called a "Hero" (*vīra*). || 25 ||

The family (kula) and the lineage (gotra) have been fully explained, and that originates from Śakti and Śiva; he who possesses the knowledge that "by this [lineage] comes liberation" is designated as a Kaulika.
Akula is said to be Śiva, and Kula is proclaimed to be Śakti;
O Dear One, the Kaulikas are those who are skillful through the contemplation of both Kula and Akula.
Because he gathers the essence, because he sets forth the path of dharma, and because he restrains the collection of the organs, he is called a practitioner (sādhaka). || 28 ||
By worshipping with supreme devotion through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one crosses over all sufferings; therefore, such a person is called a devotee (bhakta). || 29 ||
He who, having offered his body, wealth, and life-breaths to the true gurus,
learns yoga from those gurus, is called a disciple (śiṣya).

Through the continuous practice of the *yonimudrā*, through serving at the feet of Girijā, and through the dissolution of the power of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), she is designated as a Yoginī. (31)
Because she causes delight to the hundred million great divine yoginīs and because she bestows intense liberation, she is designated as Śakti.
Because she protects, because she cuts away misfortune, and because she increases one's desired objects,
she is designated as "Pādukā"— this is my truth for you, O beloved.
Because it destroys the sins committed over thousands of previous births and because it reveals the Supreme Deity, it is called *japa*.
O Goddess, because it causes supreme joy to the mind even by small degrees and because it delivers those who offer praise, it is called a "stotra" (hymn of praise).
Having restrained the mind from the distress of the senses,
the contemplation of one's chosen deity with a tranquil heart is called *dhyāna*.
O Pārvatī, O beloved, it is called "caraṇa" because its purpose is fulfilled through expansion, because of protection, and because it takes the form of men and women.

Because it makes known the meaning of all scriptures through its determination of the purpose of the True Dharma, and because it is the authority for all philosophical systems, it is called the Veda. (38)
It is called a *purāṇa* because it describes merit and demerit, wards off demons and other evils, and generates the ninefold devotion and other virtues. (39)
O Goddess, because it constantly instructs those dwelling in the [four] castes and [four] stages of life, and because it delivers them from all sins, it is called a "śāstra. (40)
O Goddess, because it defines dharma and adharma for those whose ultimate goal is the longing for remembrance, and because it tears away the cataract [of ignorance], it is called "Smṛti. (41)
Because it describes the desired dharmas and other matters, because it shatters the darkness of ignorance,
and because it removes all sufferings, it is remembered as an *itihāsa* (history/epic).
O Dear One, the Āgama has been declared through the description of conduct, as the cause for attaining the divine state,
and through the exposition of the reality of the Great Self.
Because he is worshipped by the hosts of Śākinīs, because he delivers [beings] from the ocean of worldly existence,
and because of the presence of the supreme power (Parā-śakti) and others, he is designated as "Śākta."

Because it brings about the cessation of the states beginning with Kaumāra, because it shatters dissolution, birth, and so forth, and because it encompasses the entirety of the Kula lineages, it is designated as "Kaula. || 45 ||
O Goddess, because it severs the bonds, because it is beyond the passion of other splendors,
and because it is contemplated by ascetics, it is called the "Succession" (Paramparā).
Because it constitutes the very essence of saṃsāra, because it bestows light and bliss,
and because it brings about fame and good fortune, it is called the "Sampradāya" (the Tradition).
Because it is the beginning of all paths, because it increases the joy of the mind, and because it is the cause of dharma such as sacrifice, it is celebrated as the Āmnāya. || 48 ||
That which has been heard from various great mantras, yantras, tantras, and deities,
and which remains unbroken in one's hearing, is called *śrauta*.

Because it consists of the essence of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), because it defines the fourfold purpose, and because it pacifies passion, hatred, and the like, it is celebrated as "conduct" (ācāra). || 50 ||
Because it bestows a divine state, because it washes away impurity,
and because it releases one from the bondage of worldly existence, it is called *dīkṣā* by the wise.
It is known as *abhiṣeka* (consecration) because it removes the sense of "I," because it destroys fear, because it sprinkles [the soul], and because it generates trembling, bliss, and other states.
Because of its intensity, its superiority, its bestowal of delight to the deity, and because it is caused by the descent of power (śaktipāta), it is known as "instruction" (upadeśa). || 53 ||
Because it protects from all fears that which has the nature of reality— the God of immeasurable splendor— it is therefore called "mantra."
O Pārvatī, because she assumes a body to grant boons to her devotees and because she pacifies the three types of suffering, she is celebrated as a deity.
O Goddess, because it places wealth acquired through righteous means into one's limbs and provides protection from all [dangers], it is called *nyāsa*. (56)
They produce joy and cause the minds of the gods to run [toward them];
therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, they are known as mudrās and should be observed. 57.
Because it bestows infinite fruit, because it exhausts all impurities,
and because it brings about attainment through its nature as the Mother (mātṛkā), it is called the "Akṣamālā" (the Rosary of Syllables).
O Goddess of the Gods, it is proclaimed as a mandala because it is auspicious, because it is the refuge for the hosts of dakinis and yoginis, and because it is graceful. (59)
Because it possesses the form of the Lotus-Seated One (Viṣṇu), because it destroys the subtle elements and so forth,
and because it has quelled boundless sins, it is celebrated as the *kalaśa* (the vessel).
O Mistress of the Family, because it constantly protects one from all fears, such as those of Yama and the elemental spirits (bhūtas), it is therefore called a *yantra*.
O Dear One, the seat (āsana) is so called because it bestows the realization of the Self, wards off all diseases, and grants the nine supernatural powers (navasiddhi).
Because it pacifies the net of illusion and the like, because it defines the path to liberation,
and because it removes the eight types of suffering and other afflictions, it is called "madya" (the intoxicant).
O Goddess, because it has the nature of a great gift, because it is the singular cause for the sacrificial ground,
and because it generates my own state of being, it is called *madya*.
Because she is served by the *sumanas* (gods), because she bestows sovereignty, and because she is ever dear, she is called "Sumanas.
Because she grants the form of the gods (*sura*), she is celebrated as "Sure" (the Goddess). 65.
O Dear One, it is called "Amṛta" (the Nectar) because its nature is like that of the moon, because it wards off the fear of death, and because it is the cause for the illumination of reality.

O Goddess, because he possesses the universal form of the limbs of drink, because he is the locus of the three and four kalās, and because he protects those who have fallen, he is called a "vessel" (pātra).
Because it has the nature of fire (āśuśukṣaṇi), because it is dear to the god Dhātṛ,
and because it protects that which is to be supported, the wise know it as the substratum (ādhāra).
O Goddess, because it generates auspiciousness, bestows the bliss of perfect awakening,
and is beloved by all the gods, it is called *māṃsa* (flesh).
O beloved, it is called "pūjā" because it pacifies past births, prevents birth and death, and bestows the complete fruit [of one's actions]. (70)
Because it bestows desired fruits and because it is the locus of the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga),
worship at Nandana, the grove of all the gods, has been fully described.
The satiation of the deity, who consists of reality and is surrounded by his retinue,
is declared to be the generation of the ninefold bliss.
Because it causes the destruction of deep-seated misfortune and afflictions,
and because it bestows the knowledge of the Dharma, it is called "scent" (gandha).
Because it provides fragrance, procreation, the revelation of the path to liberation,
and the subduing of suffering and other afflictions through its burning power, it is called Āmoda.
O Mistress of the Family, because all impurities have been destroyed through the gift of food,
and because they bring about identification [with the divine], O Goddess, they are proclaimed as "unbroken" (akṣata).
Because it increases merit, because it wards off the flood of sins,
and because it bestows abundant wealth, it is called "puṣpa" (flower).
Because it has the power to remove the foul odor of all great defects and because it generates supreme bliss, it is called "dhūpa" (incense).
Because it completely dispels the great darkness of long-standing ignorance and egoism,
and because it illuminates the supreme reality, it is called a "lamp."
Because it pacifies the darkness of delusion, because it wards off the exhaustion of worldly existence,
because it bestows a divine form, and because it illuminates the supreme reality,
liberation is renowned as the "lamp," the sole means for achieving the path to liberation. (79)
O Mistress of the Family, there are four kinds of substances endowed with the six flavors;
through their offering, satisfaction arises—this is declared to be the *naivedya*.
Because it causes joy to the multitude of beings wandering in many ways and because it pacifies the sins that have stained them, it is called Bali.
O beloved, the purification of the three principles occurs through your service alone;
it is called the "three principles" because they are the cause for the manifestation of reality. || 82 ||
O beloved, it is called *caluka* because it yields the fruit of the fourfold aims of life, because it has plundered the bonds of ignorance, and because it is the root of all auspicious qualities.
Because it generates light and bliss, because it bestows the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya), and because it is the vision of the supreme reality, it is called "grace" (prasāda). || 84 ||
O Goddess, because it cuts the bonds, because it wards off hell, and because it purifies, O Supreme Sovereign, it is called *pāna*. (85)
Service performed through action, mind, and speech at all times and in all conditions, according to the prescribed rule, is called *upāsti* (worship). || 86 ||
O Dear One, when the beloved deity is pleased through worship with five limbs and by the giving of desired gifts, that which precedes [the main rite] for the devotee is called *puraścaraṇa*.
The performance of the sixteen rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with twelve is declared to be the ritual procedure; this is traditionally known as the "offering" (upahāra).
O Dear One, having worshipped the God along with His Śakti with the sixteen types of offerings, the dismissal to His own abode is declared; this is called the "soft seat" (mṛdvāsana).
The invocation for the purpose of worshipping the deity is known as *āvāhana*;
O Mistress of the Kula, the act of seating [the deity] upon the seat is *sthāpana*. (90)
Facing one another is said to be "bringing near" (sannidhāpana);
remaining motionless wherever one may be is said to be "restraining" (sannirodhana). || 91 ||
The placement of the six limbs upon the body of the deity is the sakalīkṛti;
the covering is designated as the avaguṇṭhana.
O Dear One, the sight of the Dhenu-mudrā is the act of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*);

O Goddess, the gesture of joined palms with the words "forgive me" is the act of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*), O Dear One. One should utter a greeting and inquire after the deity's welfare in its presence.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā;
that for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is said to be prepared with jāti, cloves, and kakkola.
Because it pacifies all sins, increases one's wealth, sons, and progeny,
and bestows priceless fruit, it is called *arghya*.
Siddhārtha (white mustard seeds), unbroken rice grains, the tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, barley, fragrance, fruit, and flowers—this is proclaimed as the eightfold offering (arghya). || 96 ||
O Mistress of the Family, the *madhuparka* is said to consist of honey, clarified butter, and curd;
bathing (*snāna*) consists of the washing of the body with fragrant waters. (97)
O beloved, salutation is said to consist of moonlight, sandalwood, musk, and black agallochum; it is described as the eight-limbed prostration.
All this, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is designated as the "field" (kṣetra).
He by whom that field is protected is called the "Protector of the Field" (Kṣetrapāla). || 99 ||
Thus, O Great Goddess, I have briefly described to you some of the latent impressions regarding the names and origins of the Gurus; he who knows this is a true worshiper.
O Maheśvarī, this is the secret among secrets;
this Ūrdhvāmnāya has been declared both in brief and in detail.
This scripture, the Kulārṇava, resides within the hearts of the Yoginīs;
it has been revealed by me today, and must be guarded with great effort.

O Great Goddess, one should not place the book in the house of a *paśu*, nor give it into the hand of a *paśu*, nor recite it in the presence of a *paśu*. One should not recite the text concerning the exhilaration of *āsava* [alcohol], nor cast it upon the ground. (103)
One should worship [it] constantly with devotion and learn it from the mouth of the guru; it must never be taught to one who is not a son [of the lineage], nor to one who is not a disciple. 104.
Having spoken out of affection, greed, or fear, he will certainly perish before long.
O wise Goddess, whatever exists has been stated by me in some measure. 105.
For the benefit of practitioners who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation,
whoever recites this greatness of the *ūrdhvāmnāya* in the presence of the Śrīcakra— 106.
O Goddess, he who listens with supreme devotion is a Kaulika;
[he is so even] regarding vows, ritual bathing, austerity, pilgrimage sites, sacrifices, and the worship of deities. 107.
One obtains that fruit multiplied ten millionfold; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should dwell in your presence; no deliberation is required here. (108)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of Rituals for Desired Aims," in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*, within the fifth section of the *Śrī-kulārṇava*— the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures, concerning the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 17.
